traps.too_broad: Too broad: claims more than the text supports
traps.too_narrow: Too narrow: a detail, not the whole point
traps.not_in_text: Not in the text: brings in an idea the text never states
traps.reversed: Reversed: flips the relationship or the author's view
traps.true_irrelevant: True but irrelevant: accurate, but does not answer the question
traps.wrong_tone: Wrong tone or shade: a near-synonym that does not fit the context
traps.wrong_logic: Wrong logic: the wrong relationship between ideas
traps.misses_goal: Misses the goal: uses the notes but not for the stated purpose
traps.grammar_rule: Grammar rule broken: does not follow Standard English conventions

items.subject: science
items.passage: Honeybees tell their hive mates where to find food by performing a movement called the waggle ______ angle of the dance shows the direction of the food, and the length of each waggle shows how far away the food is.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: dance, the
choices.B: dance the
choices.C: dance. The
choices.D: dance and the

explanation.why: "Honeybees tell their hive mates … called the waggle dance" is a complete sentence, and "the angle of the dance shows the direction of the food …" is another complete sentence. Two independent clauses need a strong boundary, such as a period, between them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.C: Correct. A period ends the first independent clause, and the second one starts as a new sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Kintsugi is a Japanese method of repairing broken pottery with lacquer dusted with powdered gold. Instead of hiding the cracks, the ______ them, treating the damage as part of the object's history.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: method highlights
choices.B: method, highlights
choices.C: method; highlights
choices.D: method: highlights

explanation.why: "The method" is the subject of the sentence and "highlights" is its verb. No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, so nothing goes between "method" and "highlights."
explanation.A: Correct. The subject "the method" flows straight into its verb "highlights" with no punctuation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A single comma can't separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses; here it would cut the subject off from its verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "Instead of hiding the cracks, the method" is not one.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Karakoram Highway, which links Pakistan and China, climbs to more than 4,600 meters at the Khunjerab ______ it is one of the highest paved international roads in the world.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Pass,
choices.B: Pass;
choices.C: Pass and
choices.D: Pass

explanation.why: The text has two complete sentences: "The Karakoram Highway … climbs to more than 4,600 meters at the Khunjerab Pass" and "it is one of the highest paved international roads in the world." Two independent clauses can be joined with a semicolon.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Correct. A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The axolotl, a salamander native to a few lakes and canals near Mexico ______ can regrow lost limbs, parts of its heart, and even sections of its spinal cord. Unlike most salamanders, however, it normally spends its whole life in the water, keeping its feathery external gills even as an adult.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: City
choices.B: City;
choices.C: City—
choices.D: City,

explanation.why: "A salamander native to a few lakes and canals near Mexico City" is extra information that describes the axolotl. It opens with a comma after "axolotl," so it must close with a comma too before the verb "can regrow."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The axolotl" from its verb "can regrow."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Correct. The closing comma matches the opening comma after "axolotl" and completes the pair around the extra information.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Indian physicist Jagadish Chandra Bose, remembered for his pioneering experiments with radio waves, later turned his attention to plants, arguing that their responses to light, touch, and temperature could be measured as precisely as those of animals. The crescograph—an instrument he designed to magnify the minute movements of a growing plant by a factor of about ten ______ allowed him to record changes in growth rate that would otherwise have been far too small to detect.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: thousand,
choices.B: thousand—
choices.C: thousand;
choices.D: thousand

explanation.why: The words between "The crescograph" and "allowed" are extra information describing the instrument. That information opens with a dash, so it must close with a matching dash before the main verb "allowed."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a dash can't close with a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.B: Correct. The second dash closes the pair of dashes around the extra information, and the subject "The crescograph" connects to its verb "allowed."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "The crescograph" from its verb "allowed," and what comes before it is not an independent clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the extra information is never set off and runs into the main verb "allowed."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Although Ludwig van Beethoven had lost nearly all of his hearing by the time he completed his Ninth Symphony in ______ the work is among the most ambitious he ever attempted: its final movement adds vocal soloists and a full chorus to the orchestra, an unusual choice for a symphony at the time. Scholars generally credit the achievement to an inner ear trained by decades of composing, which let him imagine sounds he could no longer hear.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

explanation.why: The first sentence begins with "Although," so everything up to "in 1824" is a dependent clause, and "the work is among the most ambitious he ever attempted" is the main clause. A dependent clause that comes first is joined to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. A comma correctly links the introductory "Although" clause to the main clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "Although" clause is dependent.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A period would leave "Although Ludwig van Beethoven … in 1824" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and the "Although" clause is not one.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Ada Lovelace's notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, a general-purpose mechanical computer that Babbage designed but never ______ appended to her 1843 English translation of an article about the machine by the Italian engineer Luigi Menabrea. Running to roughly three times the length of the article itself, the notes include a step-by-step method for calculating Bernoulli numbers, which many historians describe as the first published computer program.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: completed; were
choices.B: completed—were
choices.C: completed, were
choices.D: completed were

explanation.why: The subject of the first sentence is "Ada Lovelace's notes," and its verb is "were appended." In between, "a general-purpose mechanical computer that Babbage designed but never completed" is extra information about the Analytical Engine. It opens with a comma after "Engine," so it must close with a comma before "were."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "Ada Lovelace's notes" from its verb "were appended," and neither side would be an independent clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.C: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "Engine," setting off the extra information so the subject connects to "were appended."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and the verb "were" seems to belong to "Babbage designed but never completed."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Sigiriya, a granite outcrop rising some 180 meters above the plains of central Sri Lanka, was transformed in the late fifth century CE into a royal stronghold by King Kashyapa, who ringed its base with terraced gardens, pools, and moats. Halfway up the rock, visitors today pass through the remains of a monumental ______ pair of enormous paws, built of brick and plaster, that once belonged to a lion figure through whose open mouth the final staircase climbed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: gateway; a
choices.B: gateway a
choices.C: gateway. A
choices.D: gateway: a

explanation.why: "Halfway up the rock, visitors today pass through the remains of a monumental gateway" is a complete independent clause. What follows, "a pair of enormous paws … that once belonged to a lion figure …," is a long noun phrase, not a clause: "belonged" and "climbed" sit inside relative clauses, so it has no main verb of its own. It explains what the gateway is, and a colon after an independent clause is the right mark to introduce such an explanation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "a pair of enormous paws … that once belonged to a lion figure" has no main verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the explanation runs straight into "gateway" and the sentence can't be read clearly.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A period would leave "A pair of enormous paws … the final staircase climbed" as a sentence fragment, because it has no main verb.
explanation.D: Correct. A colon follows the independent clause and introduces the phrase that explains what the gateway is.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most mammals keep their bodies at a steady, warm temperature, but the arctic ground squirrel is a striking exception. During its winter hibernation in Alaska and northern Canada, the squirrel's body temperature can drop below the freezing point of water, the lowest body temperature measured in any mammal. Even so, the animal does not freeze solid: every few weeks it wakes briefly, warms itself up by shivering, and then cools down again.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Arctic ground squirrels hibernate for longer periods than any other mammal in the far north.
choices.B: The arctic ground squirrel survives unusually low body temperatures while it hibernates.
choices.C: The arctic ground squirrel wakes every few weeks during winter to warm itself up.
choices.D: Most mammals cannot keep a steady body temperature in very cold climates.

explanation.why: The text opens by calling the arctic ground squirrel "a striking exception" to the steady body temperature of most mammals, then explains that during hibernation its temperature can fall below freezing. The last sentence adds how it survives this. The main idea must cover the whole text: the squirrel endures extremely low body temperatures in hibernation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never compares how long different mammals hibernate.
explanation.B: Correct. Every sentence supports this point: the squirrel is an exception, its temperature drops below freezing, and it still survives.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Waking every few weeks is one detail from the last sentence, not the main point of the whole text.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the opposite: most mammals do keep a steady, warm temperature.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For centuries, weavers near Dhaka, in what is now Bangladesh, made a cotton cloth so fine and light that it was traded across Asia and Europe. The cloth, known as Dhaka muslin, was spun from a local cotton plant that grew along the banks of the Meghna River. By the early 1900s, however, the craft had disappeared, partly because cheaper machine-made fabric from Britain had replaced it in many markets.
items.stem: According to the text, what was one reason Dhaka muslin stopped being made?

choices.A: Its weavers left the region to look for work in European cities.
choices.B: The local cotton plant used to spin it became too costly to grow.
choices.C: The cloth was too delicate to survive long trade journeys.
choices.D: Cheaper fabric made by machines replaced it in many markets.

explanation.why: The question asks for a reason the craft ended. The last sentence gives it directly: the craft disappeared "partly because cheaper machine-made fabric from Britain had replaced it in many markets." The correct choice restates this in other words.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the cloth was traded to Europe, not that the weavers moved there.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text mentions the local cotton plant but never says it became expensive.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the cloth was traded across Asia and Europe, so it clearly survived long journeys.
explanation.D: Correct. "Cheaper fabric made by machines" restates "cheaper machine-made fabric from Britain," which the text names as a reason the craft disappeared.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Completed in the 120s CE, the dome of the Pantheon in Rome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Its builders had no steel bars to strengthen the concrete, so they controlled the dome's weight in other ways. Near the base, where the structure carries the greatest load, the concrete contains heavy stone and the walls are several meters thick. Toward the top, the walls grow thinner, and the builders mixed in pumice, a light volcanic rock, so that the upper dome presses down far less on the structure below.
items.stem: Based on the text, why did the Pantheon's builders use pumice in the upper part of the dome?

choices.A: To reduce the weight that the top of the dome placed on the parts beneath it
choices.B: To make the upper walls of the dome thicker than the walls near its base
choices.C: To replace the steel bars that Roman builders usually placed in concrete
choices.D: To make the dome larger than any other concrete dome built in Rome at the time

explanation.why: The text says the builders "controlled the dome's weight" without steel. It then explains that they mixed in pumice, "a light volcanic rock, so that the upper dome presses down far less on the structure below." So the pumice was used to lighten the top of the dome and reduce the load on the lower parts.
explanation.A: Correct. The text states that pumice was used "so that the upper dome presses down far less on the structure below."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the walls grow thinner toward the top, not thicker.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the builders had no steel bars at all, so pumice could not be replacing a usual practice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text notes the dome's record size but never says pumice was used to achieve it.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Tomás had expected the work at his grandmother's pottery to be quick. On the first morning he shaped six bowls, each one lopsided, and pushed them aside in frustration. His grandmother said nothing; she simply cut the last bowl from the wheel and handed him a fresh lump of clay. By the end of the week, Tomás had made only two bowls, but he had stopped counting. He found himself listening to the hum of the wheel and the soft drag of his fingers through the wet clay, and he no longer glanced at the clock.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Tomás grows frustrated because his grandmother refuses to show him how to use the wheel.
choices.B: Tomás learns to shape bowls much more quickly as the week goes on.
choices.C: Tomás shifts from rushing his work to becoming absorbed in the process of making it.
choices.D: Tomás's grandmother is disappointed by the lopsided bowls he makes on the first morning.

explanation.why: At the start, Tomás expects the work "to be quick," makes six bowls, and is frustrated. By the end of the week he makes fewer bowls, has "stopped counting," and "no longer glanced at the clock." The text as a whole traces this change from hurrying to being absorbed in the work.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The grandmother says nothing, but the text never says she refuses to teach him; she hands him more clay to keep working.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Tomás actually makes fewer bowls by the end of the week (two, compared with six on the first morning).
explanation.C: Correct. This covers both the beginning (expecting quick work, frustration) and the end (stopping counting, ignoring the clock).
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text does not describe the grandmother's feelings about the bowls, and the point concerns Tomás's change.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the seasonally flooded forests of the Amazon basin, some trees drop their fruit into the water, where it is eaten by fish such as the tambaqui. Because seeds can pass through a fish's gut intact and be released far from the parent tree, ecologists have long suspected that these fish help disperse seeds. Tracking studies now suggest that the largest individuals, which swim farther and hold seeds longer, may carry seeds several kilometers. This finding has an uncomfortable implication: fishing tends to remove precisely the biggest fish, so even where tambaqui remain common, the forest may be losing its most effective long-distance seed dispersers, a loss that population counts alone would not reveal.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Fishing has made tambaqui rare in flooded forests by removing the species' largest individuals.
choices.B: Ecologists have long suspected that fish such as the tambaqui help spread the seeds of flooded-forest trees.
choices.C: Large tambaqui carry seeds farther than any other animal living in the Amazon's flooded forests.
choices.D: Fishing may reduce long-distance seed dispersal in flooded forests even where tambaqui remain common.

explanation.why: The text builds to its final sentence: because the largest tambaqui "may carry seeds several kilometers" and fishing "tends to remove precisely the biggest fish," the forest "may be losing its most effective long-distance seed dispersers" even "where tambaqui remain common." The main idea is this possible hidden effect of fishing on seed dispersal, stated with the text's own caution ("may").
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the loss could happen "even where tambaqui remain common," so it does not claim the fish have become rare.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is background from the second sentence; it leaves out the new finding about large fish and its implication.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text compares large tambaqui only with smaller tambaqui, not with every other animal in the forest.
explanation.D: Correct. This captures the text's main point, including its hedge ("may") and the key condition that the fish can still be common.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Many illustrated manuscripts produced in the workshop of the Mughal emperor Akbar in the late sixteenth century carry small notes in their margins naming the artists involved. These notes frequently list more than one name for a single painting: one artist is credited with the design of the composition, another with the coloring, and occasionally a third with the faces. For art historians, the inscriptions complicate a habit inherited from the study of European painting, in which a work is attributed to a single master whose personal style it expresses. In Akbar's workshop, the notes suggest, a painting's distinctive qualities may have emerged from collaboration rather than from any one hand.
items.stem: According to the text, what do the notes in the margins of many manuscripts from Akbar's workshop indicate?

choices.A: Artists in Akbar's workshop, like European masters, were each credited with whole paintings.
choices.B: A single painting was often produced by several artists who handled different tasks.
choices.C: European painters had trained many of the artists who worked in Akbar's workshop.
choices.D: Every painting in Akbar's workshop was produced by at least three separate artists.

explanation.why: The text says the notes "frequently list more than one name for a single painting," with different artists credited for the design, the coloring, and "occasionally" the faces. So the notes show that paintings were often made by several artists with different jobs. Watch the qualifiers: "frequently" and "occasionally" rule out any choice that says "every."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The notes show the opposite: paintings were credited to more than one artist, which is why they complicate the European single-master habit.
explanation.B: Correct. This restates "more than one name for a single painting," with separate credits for design, coloring, and sometimes faces.
explanation.C: Incorrect. European painting is mentioned only as the source of art historians' habits, not as an influence on Akbar's artists.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A third artist is credited only "occasionally," and multiple names appear "frequently," not always.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mrs. Halloran had long prided herself on receiving bad news as she received the post: promptly, and without remark. When her brother's letter arrived announcing that the old family house at Kilrush was to be sold, she read it once at the breakfast table, folded it along its original creases, and asked the maid whether the bread had come. Only later, when she found herself in the garden at an hour she never went there, standing before the gooseberry bushes she had grown from cuttings taken at that very house, did she understand that she had been composing, all morning, a reply she had no intention of sending.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Mrs. Halloran is secretly relieved that the old family house at Kilrush is finally to be sold.
choices.B: Mrs. Halloran resents her brother for deciding to sell the house without asking her.
choices.C: Mrs. Halloran's calm response to the news hides, even from herself, how much it affects her.
choices.D: Mrs. Halloran's lifelong composure finally gives way when she breaks down in the garden.

explanation.why: Two parts of the text must be read together. At breakfast she reacts "without remark," folding the letter and asking about the bread. Later, standing by bushes grown from the house's cuttings, she realizes she has been "composing, all morning, a reply." The words "Only later ... did she understand" show that her calm surface hid her feelings even from her own awareness.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Her drift to the gooseberry bushes from the old house and her mental reply suggest she is unsettled by the sale, not relieved.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says the brother failed to consult her, and it does not reveal what her unsent reply says.
explanation.C: Correct. Her outward calm at breakfast contrasts with her later realization; "only later ... did she understand" shows the feeling was hidden even from her.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This overstates the garden scene: she quietly realizes something, but nothing suggests she breaks down.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: That Inca administrators used khipus, arrangements of knotted cords, to record numbers is not in dispute: the position and type of each knot correspond to a decimal system, and many khipus tally census figures or goods owed to the state. Whether some khipus also recorded language is a harder question. Spanish chroniclers of the sixteenth century reported that khipu keepers could "read" histories and family lines from the cords, yet such testimony, offered by observers who could not themselves interpret the cords, establishes only that keepers recited narratives while handling khipus, not that the narratives were encoded in them. A few surviving khipus whose cords vary in color and fiber far more than any numerical purpose would require have therefore drawn particular attention.
items.stem: Based on the text, why have certain surviving khipus drawn particular attention?

choices.A: Their variety of colors and fibers seems to exceed what recording numbers alone would require.
choices.B: They confirm chroniclers' reports that khipu keepers could read histories directly from cords.
choices.C: Their knots, unlike those of the census khipus, do not follow a decimal system of positions.
choices.D: Spanish observers saw keepers reciting narratives while handling these particular khipus.

explanation.why: The text says the chroniclers' reports cannot settle whether khipus recorded language. The last sentence, linked by "therefore," explains why some khipus stand out: their cords vary "far more than any numerical purpose would require." That extra variety is what makes them possible evidence of a non-numerical record.
explanation.A: Correct. This restates the final sentence: the variety goes beyond "any numerical purpose," which is why these khipus interest researchers asking whether khipus recorded language.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text calls the question of language open and says the reports prove less than they seem to; nothing confirms them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says these khipus' knots break from the decimal system; it points to color and fiber instead.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text discusses the chroniclers' testimony in general, not observations tied to these particular khipus.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Leafcutter ants can be seen marching through the tropical forests of Central and South America, each one carrying a piece of leaf much larger than its own head. Surprisingly, the ants do not eat these leaves. Instead, they chew them into a soft paste inside their nests and use the paste to grow a fungus. The fungus, not the leaf, is the colony's main food.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Leafcutter ants collect leaves in order to grow the fungus that they eat.
choices.B: Leafcutter ants can carry pieces of leaf larger than their own heads.
choices.C: Leafcutter ants eat the leaves they cut once the leaves soften in the nest.
choices.D: Leafcutter ants are the most common insects in tropical forests.

explanation.why: The text first describes ants carrying leaves, then explains the surprise: they "do not eat these leaves" but use them to grow a fungus, which is "the colony's main food." The main idea must cover this whole point: the leaves are used to grow the ants' food.
explanation.A: Correct. This sums up the whole text: the ants gather leaves, turn them into paste, and grow the fungus they actually eat.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The size of the leaf pieces is one detail from the first sentence, not the main point.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the ants "do not eat these leaves"; they eat the fungus grown on the paste.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never compares leafcutter ants with other insects.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Kofi had expected his aunt's bicycle shop to be quiet on a Saturday morning. Instead, customers were already waiting at the door when she unlocked it. One needed a new chain; another wanted a flat tire fixed. His aunt handed him a wrench and a tin of grease without a word. By noon his hands were black, his shirt was ruined, and he had repaired his first tire by himself.
items.stem: According to the text, how was the morning at the shop different from what Kofi had expected?

choices.A: His aunt asked him to open the shop by himself.
choices.B: Customers were already waiting when the shop opened.
choices.C: His aunt would not let him work on any bicycles.
choices.D: The shop had run out of new chains and tires.

explanation.why: The first sentence tells us what Kofi expected: a quiet Saturday morning. The next sentence begins with "Instead," which signals the difference: "customers were already waiting at the door when she unlocked it."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says his aunt unlocked the shop; it never says Kofi opened it alone.
explanation.B: Correct. This restates the sentence that begins with "Instead": the shop was busy, not quiet, from the moment it opened.
explanation.C: Incorrect. His aunt handed him tools, and he repaired a tire, so she clearly let him work.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A customer needed a new chain, but the text never says the shop had none.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The greater one-horned rhinoceros once roamed widely across the grasslands of northern India and Nepal. By the 1960s, however, hunting and the loss of grassland to farms had left only a small number in Nepal. In 1973, the government created Chitwan National Park and assigned guards to protect the animals. The effort has worked: a national count in 2021 found more than 700 of the rhinos in Nepal.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The greater one-horned rhinoceros once lived widely in northern India and Nepal.
choices.B: Farms now cover most of the grassland where rhinos once lived in Nepal.
choices.C: Protection efforts helped Nepal's rhinos recover after a sharp decline.
choices.D: Rhinos in Nepal are now protected mainly by farmers rather than by guards.

explanation.why: The text moves from a decline (only a small number of rhinos left by the 1960s) to a response (a national park with guards) to a result: "The effort has worked," with more than 700 rhinos counted in 2021. The main idea is that protection helped the population recover.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is background from the first sentence; it leaves out the decline and the recovery.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says grassland was lost to farms before the 1960s, but it never says farms cover most of it today.
explanation.C: Correct. This covers the whole text: a sharp decline, protection in Chitwan, and a recovery to more than 700 rhinos.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the government assigned guards; farmers are mentioned only as a cause of lost grassland.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A gamelan is a traditional Indonesian orchestra made up mostly of gongs, drums, and metal keyboard instruments, and its players are not expected to stand out as soloists. In one common Balinese technique, two musicians each play only some of the notes of a fast melody. Their parts fit together so closely that listeners hear a single, unbroken line. Neither part makes complete sense alone, so the music depends on every player fitting in with the others.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Gamelan musicians must train for many years before they may play solos.
choices.B: In one technique, two musicians each play part of a fast melody.
choices.C: Listeners usually find gamelan melodies too broken up to follow.
choices.D: Gamelan music depends on players combining parts rather than playing alone.

explanation.why: The text says gamelan players are "not expected to stand out as soloists" and gives an example of two players whose parts fit together into one line. It ends by stating the point: "the music depends on every player fitting in with the others."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says players are not expected to be soloists; it says nothing about training for solos.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the example the text uses, not the larger point the example supports.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says listeners hear "a single, unbroken line," the opposite of a broken-up melody.
explanation.D: Correct. Both the opening claim and the example show that the music works only when players' parts combine.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1941, Swiss engineer George de Mestral returned from a walk in the Alps and noticed that small burrs, the seed cases of a plant called burdock, were stuck to his clothes and to his dog's fur. Looking at a burr under a microscope, he saw that it was covered in tiny hooks that caught on loops of thread and hair. Years later, he used this idea to create the hook-and-loop fastener now sold as Velcro.
items.stem: According to the text, what did de Mestral see when he looked at a burr under a microscope?

choices.A: Loops of thread like the ones in his clothing
choices.B: Tiny hooks that could catch on thread and hair
choices.C: A sticky coating that held it to any surface
choices.D: Small holes that let it grip smooth fabric

explanation.why: The second sentence answers the question directly: under the microscope, the burr "was covered in tiny hooks that caught on loops of thread and hair." The correct choice restates this.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The loops were in the thread and hair; the burr itself had hooks.
explanation.B: Correct. This restates what de Mestral saw: tiny hooks that caught on thread and hair.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text explains the sticking with hooks, not with any sticky coating.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never mentions holes in the burr.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: From the rooftop, Sana could see dozens of kites rising over the old city of Lahore. Her own kite, the green one her brother had helped her build, kept dipping toward the water tanks below. Each time, she yanked the string too hard. Then she remembered her brother's advice and let the string out slowly. The kite steadied, caught the wind, and climbed until it was just one more bright square among the others.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Sana gets her kite to fly by following advice she had been given.
choices.B: Sana's brother flies his kite higher than anyone else in Lahore.
choices.C: Sana decides that her homemade kite cannot fly as well as the others.
choices.D: Sana watches the many kites that fill the sky above the old city.

explanation.why: Sana's kite keeps dipping while she yanks the string. The turning point comes when she "remembered her brother's advice and let the string out slowly"; after that, the kite "steadied" and "climbed." The main idea is that following the advice lets her fly the kite.
explanation.A: Correct. The passage shows a problem, the advice she remembers, and the kite's success once she follows it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The brother helped build the kite and gave advice, but he is not shown flying a kite at all.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Her kite ends up flying among the others, so the passage shows the opposite.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Seeing the other kites is only the opening detail, not what the passage is mainly about.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Before 1840, letters in Britain were usually paid for by the person who received them, and the cost depended on how far the letter had traveled. Some people simply refused letters they did not want to pay for. In 1840, a reform proposed by teacher Rowland Hill took effect: senders paid in advance with a small stamp, and a light letter cost one penny to send anywhere in the country. Soon, far more letters were being mailed.
items.stem: Based on the text, why did the number of letters mailed in Britain most likely rise after 1840?

choices.A: People could now refuse letters they did not want.
choices.B: Letters were now delivered faster than before.
choices.C: Prices now depended on how far a letter traveled.
choices.D: Senders paid one low price for any distance.

explanation.why: The text describes the old system (receivers paid, and the cost depended on distance) and then the 1840 reform: senders paid in advance, and a light letter cost "one penny to send anywhere in the country." The rise in letters came right after this change, so the new single low price is the most likely reason.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Refusing letters was possible under the old system, before 1840, when receivers paid.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never mentions how fast letters were delivered.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Distance-based prices belong to the old system; after the reform, one penny covered any distance.
explanation.D: Correct. The reform set a single penny price for a light letter sent anywhere, and letter numbers then rose sharply.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Hummingbirds burn energy very quickly, and during the day they must feed every few minutes. At night, when they cannot feed, many hummingbirds enter a state called torpor. Their body temperature drops, and their heart rate slows sharply. This deep rest greatly reduces the amount of energy they use, helping them survive until morning, when they can feed again.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Hummingbirds must feed every few minutes during the day.
choices.B: Hummingbirds sleep for more hours each night than other birds.
choices.C: Many hummingbirds survive the night by slowing their bodies to save energy.
choices.D: Hummingbirds' heart rates rise sharply when they rest at night.

explanation.why: The text sets up a problem (hummingbirds use energy fast but cannot feed at night) and then explains the solution: torpor, in which body temperature and heart rate drop, which "greatly reduces the amount of energy they use." The main idea is how torpor helps them survive the night.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Feeding every few minutes is a detail from the first sentence that sets up the main point.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never compares hummingbirds' sleep with that of other birds.
explanation.C: Correct. This covers the problem and the solution: during torpor their bodies slow down, saving energy until morning.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says their heart rate "slows sharply," not that it rises.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Braille, the raised-dot system that lets blind people read by touch, was developed in France by Louis Braille, who lost his sight as a young child. As a student, he learned of a code of raised dots invented by an army officer, Charles Barbier, so that messages could be read in the dark. Braille found the code too complicated, so he simplified it. By age fifteen, he had created a system in which each letter fit under a single fingertip.
items.stem: According to the text, what did Louis Braille do with Barbier's code?

choices.A: He simplified it to create an easier system.
choices.B: He taught it to soldiers who needed to read at night.
choices.C: He decided it was simple enough to use without changes.
choices.D: He replaced its raised dots with printed letters.

explanation.why: The text says Braille "found the code too complicated, so he simplified it," creating a system in which each letter fit under one fingertip. The correct choice restates this.
explanation.A: Correct. This restates "he simplified it," which led to his own easier system.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Barbier invented the code for reading in the dark, but the text never says Braille taught soldiers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Braille found the code "too complicated," so he did change it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Braille's own system still uses raised dots, as the first sentence says; nothing was replaced with printed letters.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every evening, Lucía's grandfather sat on the harbor wall mending fishing nets, and every evening she watched. Today, he handed her the wooden needle and moved aside. Her first knots were clumsy; they slipped loose as soon as she pulled them tight. Her grandfather said nothing, only guided her fingers once through the loop. Slowly the knots began to hold, and when she looked up, he was smiling.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Lucía's grandfather decides to stop fishing and gives his tools to her.
choices.B: Lucía tries mending a net for the first time and, with quiet help, succeeds.
choices.C: Lucía's grandfather grows impatient with her clumsy, loose knots.
choices.D: Lucía's first knots slip loose as soon as she pulls them tight.

explanation.why: Lucía has always watched, but "Today" her grandfather hands her the needle. Her knots slip at first; he silently guides her fingers; then "the knots began to hold" and he smiles. The main idea is her first successful attempt, helped quietly by her grandfather.
explanation.A: Incorrect. He lets her use the needle for one evening; nothing suggests he is giving up fishing.
explanation.B: Correct. This covers the whole passage: her first try, his silent help, and her success.
explanation.C: Incorrect. He stays quiet, guides her gently, and ends up smiling, so he is patient, not impatient.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The slipping knots are only one moment; the passage goes on to show her improving.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Amazon rainforest looks like one of the most fertile places on Earth, yet much of its soil is poor in phosphorus, a nutrient that plants need to grow. Heavy rains wash the nutrient away. Part of the missing phosphorus arrives from an unexpected source: the Sahara Desert. Each year, winds carry millions of tons of dust from the Sahara across the Atlantic Ocean, and some of that phosphorus-rich dust falls on the rainforest.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Scientists plan to add phosphorus to the Amazon's soil to help plants grow.
choices.B: The Amazon's soil is richer in nutrients than the soil of most forests.
choices.C: Winds carry millions of tons of dust across the Atlantic Ocean each year.
choices.D: Dust from the Sahara helps supply a nutrient that the Amazon's soil lacks.

explanation.why: The text explains a problem (the Amazon's soil is "poor in phosphorus" because rain washes it away) and then its surprising partial solution: phosphorus-rich dust blown from the Sahara. The main idea links the two: Saharan dust supplies a nutrient the soil lacks.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes a natural process; it never mentions scientists adding phosphorus.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the forest only looks fertile; its soil is actually "poor in phosphorus."
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is one supporting detail; it leaves out why the dust matters to the rainforest.
explanation.D: Correct. This connects both parts of the text: the soil's shortage of phosphorus and the dust that helps replace it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Timbuktu, in present-day Mali, was a major center of learning in the 1400s and 1500s. Scholars there wrote and copied thousands of manuscripts on subjects such as astronomy, mathematics, medicine, and law. Many of these manuscripts survived for centuries because local families kept them in their homes, passing them down from parents to children. Today, libraries in the city work to preserve and study them.
items.stem: According to the text, how did many of Timbuktu's manuscripts survive for centuries?

choices.A: They were sent to libraries in other countries.
choices.B: Scholars made fresh copies of them every few years.
choices.C: Families stored them at home and handed them down.
choices.D: City libraries guarded them from the 1400s onward.

explanation.why: The third sentence gives the reason directly: the manuscripts survived "because local families kept them in their homes, passing them down from parents to children." The correct choice says the same thing in other words.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says the manuscripts left Mali.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Scholars did write and copy manuscripts, but the text does not say that repeated copying is how they survived.
explanation.C: Correct. This restates the text's explanation: families kept the manuscripts at home and passed them down.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says libraries preserve the manuscripts "today"; for centuries it was families who kept them.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Sundarbans, a vast mangrove forest shared by Bangladesh and India, grows in muddy ground that is flooded by seawater twice a day. This mud holds very little oxygen, which plant roots need. Many of the forest's trees solve the problem with special roots called pneumatophores, which grow upward out of the mud like pencils. At low tide, these roots take in air for the rest of the tree.
items.stem: According to the text, what is the function of the pneumatophores?

choices.A: They take in air that the trees cannot get from the mud.
choices.B: They hold the trees firmly in place in the soft mud.
choices.C: They store seawater for the trees to use at low tide.
choices.D: They grow downward to reach oxygen deep in the soil.

explanation.why: The text names a problem, that the mud "holds very little oxygen," and says the trees "solve the problem" with pneumatophores, which "take in air for the rest of the tree." So their function is to supply air the mud cannot.
explanation.A: Correct. The roots take in air at low tide, solving the problem of oxygen-poor mud.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says these roots anchor the trees.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The roots take in air, not seawater, and the text never mentions storing water.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the roots grow "upward out of the mud," not downward.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Lukas reached the station twenty minutes early and checked the arrivals board again and again. His older brother had been away at university in another city for almost a year. When the train finally pulled in, Lukas searched every window. Then he spotted a familiar wave from the third car. He had planned to act calm, but before the doors had fully opened, he was already running down the platform.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Lukas worries that his brother's train will be canceled.
choices.B: Lukas is so eager to see his brother that he cannot stay calm.
choices.C: Lukas plans to greet his brother calmly and manages to do so.
choices.D: Lukas's brother has decided to leave university and move home.

explanation.why: Every detail shows Lukas's eagerness: he arrives "twenty minutes early," checks the board "again and again," and searches every window. The last sentence confirms it: he "had planned to act calm" but is "already running down the platform."
explanation.A: Incorrect. He checks the board often, but nothing suggests he fears a cancellation.
explanation.B: Correct. His early arrival, constant checking, and running down the platform all show an excitement he cannot hide.
explanation.C: Incorrect. He planned to act calm but ends up running, so he does not manage it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says only that the brother has been away for a year, not that he is leaving university.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Construction of the Sagrada Família, a church in Barcelona, Spain, began in 1882, and the architect Antoni Gaudí directed the work from 1883 until his death in 1926. Gaudí knew the building would not be finished in his lifetime, so he left detailed plaster models to guide later builders. Many of the models were broken in 1936, but workers patiently pieced the fragments back together. Today, builders use the repaired models along with computer design programs.
items.stem: According to the text, why did Gaudí leave detailed plaster models?

choices.A: He wanted to sell them to pay for the construction.
choices.B: He needed them to test his designs on computers.
choices.C: He expected others to finish the building after him.
choices.D: He hoped to replace the models broken in 1936.

explanation.why: The text gives the reason in one sentence: Gaudí "knew the building would not be finished in his lifetime, so he left detailed plaster models to guide later builders." The models were meant for the people who would continue the work.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never mentions selling the models or raising money.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Computer programs are used by builders "today," long after Gaudí's death.
explanation.C: Correct. He made the models because he knew later builders would have to complete the church.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Gaudí died in 1926, ten years before the models were broken.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Mehrgarh, on the Kachi Plain of Balochistan in Pakistan, is one of the earliest known farming villages in South Asia; people there grew barley and herded goats more than 8,000 years ago. The site is also known for a less expected discovery. In 2006, researchers reported that eleven molars from graves dated to roughly 7,500 to 9,000 years ago had small, neat holes drilled into them. Because the edges of the holes had been worn smooth by later chewing, the researchers concluded that the drilling was done on living people, an early form of dentistry.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Mehrgarh is one of the earliest known farming villages in South Asia.
choices.B: Teeth found at Mehrgarh suggest that people there practiced an early form of dentistry.
choices.C: Researchers found that the teeth from Mehrgarh had been drilled after their owners died.
choices.D: Farming at Mehrgarh caused tooth decay that forced villagers to drill their teeth.

explanation.why: After one sentence of background on farming, the text turns to "a less expected discovery" and spends the rest on it: drilled molars whose worn edges show the drilling was done on living people, which researchers read as "an early form of dentistry." That discovery is the text's main point.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is background from the first sentence; most of the text is about the drilled teeth.
explanation.B: Correct. This captures the discovery the text focuses on and the conclusion the researchers drew from it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The worn edges led researchers to conclude the opposite: the drilling was done while the people were alive.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never says farming caused tooth decay or explains why the teeth were drilled.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Ngozi studied the board for a long time before tipping over her king, the sign that she had lost. Across the table, the regional champion, a man three times her age, shook her hand and was silent for a moment. Then he reset the pieces to where they had stood twenty moves earlier and pointed at her knight. "Here," he said quietly. "Here you almost had me." Ngozi left the hall having lost the game, but she was already replaying that move in her head, and she was smiling.
items.stem: Based on the text, why is Ngozi smiling as she leaves the hall?

choices.A: She believes the champion let her win part of the game out of kindness.
choices.B: She is relieved that the long and difficult tournament is finally over.
choices.C: She has noticed a serious mistake the champion made late in the game.
choices.D: She has learned from a strong opponent that she came close to beating him.

explanation.why: Ngozi loses, but the champion shows her a position from earlier in the game and tells her, "Here you almost had me." She leaves "replaying that move in her head" and smiling, so her smile comes from learning that she nearly beat a strong player.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Nothing suggests the champion went easy on her; he simply points out where she nearly won.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says the tournament is over or that she feels relieved.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The champion points to her knight twenty moves back, a chance she had, not a late mistake of his own.
explanation.D: Correct. The champion's words show her how close she came, and she leaves thinking about that move with a smile.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Wombats, burrowing marsupials native to Australia, are the only animals known to produce cube-shaped droppings. One might expect such a shape to be formed at the body's exit, the way a square nozzle shapes icing squeezed from a bag. In 2018, however, a team of researchers examining wombat intestines found that the cubes take shape earlier, inside the intestine itself, where some sections of the wall are stiffer than others. As the intestine contracts, these uneven walls press the contents into blocks with flat sides and fairly sharp corners.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Wombats' cube-shaped droppings are formed inside the intestine by walls of uneven stiffness.
choices.B: Wombats' droppings take their cube shape only at the body's exit, like icing from a nozzle.
choices.C: Researchers now understand how the intestines of all animals shape their droppings.
choices.D: Wombats are burrowing marsupials that are native to the continent of Australia.

explanation.why: The text introduces the wombat's unusual cube-shaped droppings, raises an expectation (the shape forms at the body's exit), and then, with "however," reports what researchers actually found: the cubes form inside the intestine, where uneven walls press the contents into blocks. The main idea is this finding about how the cubes form.
explanation.A: Correct. This states the researchers' finding, which is what the whole text builds toward.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the expectation that the 2018 research showed to be wrong.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The research concerned wombats only; the text makes no claim about all animals.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This background detail leaves out the text's point about how the cube shape forms.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When William Shakespeare died in 1616, only about half of his plays had appeared in print, often in cheap editions of uneven quality. Seven years later, two actors from his company, John Heminges and Henry Condell, gathered thirty-six of his plays into a single large volume now known as the First Folio. Without their effort, roughly eighteen plays, including Macbeth and The Tempest, might have been lost, since no earlier printed version of them is known to exist.
items.stem: Based on the text, what is the main reason the First Folio is considered important?

choices.A: It was the first book to include any of Shakespeare's plays.
choices.B: It corrected the errors found in cheap earlier editions of his plays.
choices.C: It preserved many plays that had never been printed before.
choices.D: It included every play that Shakespeare is known to have written.

explanation.why: The text's last sentence explains the volume's importance: without it, "roughly eighteen plays" might have been lost, because "no earlier printed version of them is known to exist." So the Folio matters mainly because it saved plays that had never been printed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. About half of the plays had already appeared in print before Shakespeare died, so the Folio was not the first.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text mentions that earlier editions were of uneven quality but never says the Folio corrected them.
explanation.C: Correct. The text credits the Folio with saving about eighteen plays that had no earlier printed version.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the Folio contains thirty-six plays but never claims this was every play Shakespeare wrote.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In his treatise the Aryabhatiya, completed in 499 CE, the Indian mathematician and astronomer Aryabhata proposed that the stars only appear to move westward across the night sky. The real motion, he argued, is the Earth turning on its axis, much as a person in a moving boat sees trees on the shore seem to move backward. Most astronomers of his era, in India and elsewhere, held that the Earth stood still, and several later Indian scholars rejected his idea. The view that the Earth rotates gained wide acceptance only many centuries afterward.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Aryabhata was the first person in history to suggest that the Earth moves.
choices.B: Most astronomers in Aryabhata's era believed that the Earth stood still.
choices.C: Later Indian scholars improved Aryabhata's idea until it was widely accepted.
choices.D: Aryabhata argued that the Earth rotates, an idea that was not widely accepted in his time.

explanation.why: The text first presents Aryabhata's proposal that the Earth turns on its axis and then qualifies it: most astronomers of his era disagreed, later scholars rejected it, and the idea was widely accepted "only many centuries afterward." The main idea combines his claim with its cool reception.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never compares Aryabhata with anyone earlier, so it does not support "first person in history."
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is a supporting detail; it leaves out Aryabhata's own proposal, which is the text's focus.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says several later Indian scholars rejected the idea, not that they improved it.
explanation.D: Correct. This captures both parts of the text: Aryabhata's argument and the fact that it was not widely accepted for centuries.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Señor Ibarra had closed his tailor shop in Buenos Aires years ago, and he told anyone who asked that he did not miss it. So when his granddaughter brought him her torn winter coat, he grumbled that she should simply buy another. Still, he turned the coat over in his hands, studying the seam. By evening he had found his old spool of gray thread, cleared the kitchen table, and bent over the work, humming a tune she had not heard him hum in years.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A retired tailor who claims not to miss his work seems to enjoy returning to it.
choices.B: A grandfather refuses to mend his granddaughter's coat because he has retired.
choices.C: A retired tailor regrets closing his shop and decides to open it once again.
choices.D: A granddaughter tears her winter coat and asks her grandfather to repair it.

explanation.why: Ibarra says he does not miss tailoring and grumbles about the coat, but his actions tell a different story: he studies the seam, finds his old thread, and works while "humming a tune she had not heard him hum in years." The main idea is the contrast between what he claims and the pleasure he shows.
explanation.A: Correct. This captures the contrast at the heart of the passage: his claim not to miss the work versus his evident pleasure in doing it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. He grumbles at first, but by evening he is mending the coat.
explanation.C: Incorrect. He enjoys one repair job, but nothing suggests he regrets closing the shop or plans to reopen it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is only the event that starts the passage; it leaves out how Ibarra responds.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In April 1815, Mount Tambora, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, erupted with enormous force, sending vast amounts of ash and gas high into the atmosphere. The following year, people in Europe and North America lived through a strangely cold summer: frosts damaged crops in New England in June, and harvests failed in parts of Europe. At the time, few people suspected that the two events were linked. Only in the twentieth century did scientists show that particles from large eruptions can spread around the globe and block some sunlight, cooling distant regions.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The eruption of Mount Tambora caused frosts and crop failures across Indonesia in 1816.
choices.B: A cold summer far from Tambora was likely caused by its eruption, a link recognized only later.
choices.C: People in 1816 quickly realized that a distant volcanic eruption had cooled their summer.
choices.D: Frosts damaged crops in New England during June of the year after Tambora erupted.

explanation.why: The text pairs two events, the 1815 eruption and the cold summer that followed in Europe and North America, and then explains that the link between them was not understood until the twentieth century, when scientists showed how eruption particles can cool distant regions. The main idea combines the connection with the late recognition of it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes cold and crop failures in Europe and North America, not in Indonesia.
explanation.B: Correct. This joins the text's two parts: the eruption probably caused the distant cold summer, and scientists made the connection much later.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says that at the time "few people suspected that the two events were linked."
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is one example of the cold summer; it leaves out the eruption's role and the later scientific explanation.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The moai of Rapa Nui (Easter Island), huge stone statues carved between roughly 1250 and 1500 CE, stand kilometers from the quarry where most of them were carved. Because the islanders had no wheels or large draft animals, the question of how the statues were moved long puzzled researchers. Oral traditions on the island say that the moai "walked." In 2012, archaeologists tested this idea with a concrete replica weighing more than four tons. Pulling on ropes tied to its head from alternating sides, a team of eighteen people rocked the upright statue forward, making it waddle along a path.
items.stem: According to the text, what did the 2012 test show?

choices.A: The moai were most likely dragged from the quarry on wooden sleds.
choices.B: The island's stories of walking moai were invented by later visitors.
choices.C: A small team using ropes could move an upright statue by rocking it.
choices.D: Every moai on the island was moved by being walked upright to its site.

explanation.why: The text describes the test in its last sentence: by pulling ropes "from alternating sides," eighteen people "rocked the upright statue forward, making it waddle along a path." The test showed that such a method could work, which fits the oral traditions that the moai "walked."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never mentions sleds; the test moved the statue standing upright.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The test supported the island's oral traditions rather than showing they were invented.
explanation.C: Correct. This restates the result: eighteen people with ropes moved an upright replica by rocking it forward.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A test with one replica shows the method was possible, not that every statue was moved this way.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Nimali had imagined her grandfather's tea estate in the hills near Nuwara Eliya as a place of quiet green rows and slow mornings. Instead, on her first day, she was awake before dawn, following the pluckers up slopes so steep she had to grip the bushes to keep her balance. Her grandfather showed her how to pinch off only the top two leaves and a bud. By noon her basket held barely a handful, while the women around her had filled theirs twice. She did not complain; she only watched their hands more closely.
items.stem: Based on the text, how does Nimali respond to the difficulty of the work?

choices.A: She tries to improve by paying closer attention to the skilled pluckers.
choices.B: She regrets coming to the estate because it is not as quiet as she imagined.
choices.C: She complains to her grandfather that the slopes are too steep to work on.
choices.D: She asks her grandfather to give her an easier job somewhere on the estate.

explanation.why: The question asks how Nimali reacts to falling behind. The last sentence answers it: "She did not complain; she only watched their hands more closely." Watching the experienced women's hands suggests she is trying to learn their skill.
explanation.A: Correct. Watching the pluckers' hands "more closely" after falling behind shows she is trying to learn from them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The estate differs from what she imagined, but the text never says she regrets coming.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text states directly that "She did not complain."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nimali never asks for a different job; she keeps watching and learning.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The snapping shrimp, a sea creature only a few centimeters long, is among the loudest animals in the ocean, and large colonies of them can interfere with underwater sonar. For years, researchers assumed the sound came from the two halves of the shrimp's oversized claw striking each other. High-speed video and sound recordings told a different story. When the claw snaps shut, it shoots out a jet of water so fast that a bubble of very low pressure forms. The loud crack is made when that bubble collapses, not when the claw closes.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Snapping shrimp are louder than any other animal that lives in the ocean.
choices.B: Large colonies of snapping shrimp can interfere with underwater sonar.
choices.C: The shrimp's crack is produced when the two halves of its claw strike together.
choices.D: Research showed that the shrimp's snap comes from a collapsing bubble, not the claw.

explanation.why: The text sets up an old assumption (the sound comes from the claw's halves striking) and then reports what high-speed video and recordings "told" instead: the crack comes from a collapsing low-pressure bubble. The main idea is this corrected explanation of the sound.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the shrimp is "among the loudest" animals, not the loudest of all.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The sonar detail shows how loud the shrimp are, but it is not what the text is mainly about.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is the old assumption that the newer research overturned.
explanation.D: Correct. This states the text's central finding, which replaces the earlier assumption about the claw.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Silent films were rarely watched in silence. In the 1910s and 1920s, most theaters employed a pianist or organist, and large city theaters sometimes hired full orchestras. Because musicians often had to match music to scenes they were seeing for the first time, film studios began sending out cue sheets: lists of a film's scenes with suggested pieces and moods for each. The sheets did not dictate every note, though, and many players continued to improvise, so the same film could sound quite different from one theater to the next.
items.stem: According to the text, why could the same silent film sound different from one theater to another?

choices.A: Studios sent each theater its own cue sheet with different music.
choices.B: Many musicians improvised rather than playing set music note for note.
choices.C: Pianists in small theaters played louder to make up for having no orchestra.
choices.D: Cue sheets listed the exact notes each musician was expected to play.

explanation.why: The final sentence gives the cause directly: cue sheets "did not dictate every note," and "many players continued to improvise, so the same film could sound quite different from one theater to the next." The word "so" links the improvising to the differences.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes cue sheets for each film, not different cue sheets for different theaters.
explanation.B: Correct. The text links the differences directly to musicians' improvising.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never discusses how loudly anyone played.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the cue sheets "did not dictate every note"; they suggested pieces and moods.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the early 1900s, the Harvard College Observatory hired women, known as "computers," to examine thousands of photographic plates of the night sky. The work was considered routine, and the pay was modest. Yet one of these women, Henrietta Swan Leavitt, noticed a pattern in a type of star whose brightness rises and falls: the longer such a star took to complete a cycle, the brighter it truly was. Her finding, published in 1912, later gave astronomers a way to measure distances to faraway stars and even to other galaxies.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Leavitt, hired for supposedly routine work, made a finding that helped astronomers measure great distances.
choices.B: The women hired as "computers" at Harvard were paid modest wages to examine photographs of the sky.
choices.C: Leavitt used her own finding to measure the distances to several galaxies beyond our own.
choices.D: Leavitt found that stars whose brightness rises and falls are farther away than other stars.

explanation.why: The text contrasts the job's low status ("considered routine," "modest" pay) with what Leavitt achieved through it, signaled by "Yet": she found a pattern that "later gave astronomers a way to measure distances." The main idea joins that contrast with the importance of her finding.
explanation.A: Correct. This captures the contrast between the routine job and the far-reaching discovery Leavitt made.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This describes the working conditions in the first two sentences but leaves out Leavitt's discovery.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says her finding "later gave astronomers" a method; it does not say she measured galaxies herself.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Leavitt linked a star's cycle length to its true brightness; the text never says such stars are farther away.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mei had agreed to help her uncle with his beehives only because her parents insisted. For the first hour she stood well back, flinching whenever a bee drifted near her veil. Her uncle worked slowly and spoke to the bees in a low voice, as if they were old friends. When he lifted out a frame heavy with honeycomb and offered it to her, she hesitated, then took it. The bees crawled calmly over the comb, and Mei, holding her breath, realized that her hands had stopped shaking.
items.stem: Based on the text, how do Mei's feelings change over the course of the text?

choices.A: She starts out eager to help but grows bored by her uncle's slow work.
choices.B: She starts out afraid of the bees but decides to keep bees of her own.
choices.C: She starts out fearful of the bees but grows calmer as she handles them.
choices.D: She starts out confident but becomes nervous once the bees cover the comb.

explanation.why: At first Mei stands "well back," "flinching" whenever a bee comes near. By the end, holding the comb, she realizes "her hands had stopped shaking." Her feelings move from fear toward calm.
explanation.A: Incorrect. She helps only because her parents insist, so she is not eager, and the text never mentions boredom.
explanation.B: Incorrect. She becomes calmer, but nothing suggests she plans to keep bees herself.
explanation.C: Correct. Her flinching at the start and her steady hands at the end show fear giving way to calm.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the change: she begins nervous and ends calmer.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Elephants communicate partly through rumbles so low in pitch that humans cannot hear them. These sounds, known as infrasound, lose little energy as they travel and can carry several kilometers. Researchers studying African elephants have also found that the rumbles send vibrations through the ground. Elephants appear to detect these vibrations with sensitive nerve endings in their feet and trunks, sometimes freezing in place and leaning forward as if listening. This ability may help herds keep track of distant groups that are far out of sight.
items.stem: Based on the text, why might elephants freeze in place and lean forward?

choices.A: To produce low rumbles that travel through the ground
choices.B: To better sense vibrations traveling through the ground
choices.C: To hear airborne sounds too low for their ears to catch
choices.D: To rest their feet after walking several kilometers

explanation.why: The text says elephants "appear to detect these vibrations with sensitive nerve endings in their feet and trunks," and that they freeze and lean forward "as if listening." Since the vibrations are sensed through the feet, this listening posture most likely helps them pick up the signals.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The freezing is linked to detecting vibrations, not to making the rumbles.
explanation.B: Correct. The text connects the freezing and leaning directly to detecting ground vibrations through the feet and trunk.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says humans cannot hear the rumbles; it never says elephants' ears cannot, and it ties the behavior to ground vibrations.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text gives no sign that the behavior has anything to do with tiredness.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Library of Alexandria, founded in Egypt in the third century BCE, is often remembered as having vanished in a single great fire. Ancient writers do report that books burned when fires set by Julius Caesar's forces spread through part of the city in 48 BCE. Many historians, however, think the library's end was slower and less dramatic. Over the centuries, royal support for scholars weakened, some scholars were driven out during political conflicts, and fewer new copies were made of the collection's papyrus scrolls, which decay with age.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Fires set by Julius Caesar's forces destroyed the entire library in 48 BCE.
choices.B: Papyrus scrolls decay with age unless new copies of them are made.
choices.C: The library held more books than any other library in the ancient world.
choices.D: Many historians think the library declined gradually rather than in one fire.

explanation.why: The text opens with a popular memory (the library "vanished in a single great fire"), grants that some books did burn in 48 BCE, and then, with "however," gives historians' view that the end "was slower and less dramatic," listing causes over centuries. The main idea is this gradual-decline view.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says only that some books burned in 48 BCE; it presents total destruction by one fire as the popular memory historians doubt.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The decay of papyrus is one of several causes listed, not the main point.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never compares the library's size with that of other ancient libraries.
explanation.D: Correct. This captures the contrast the text builds: the popular single-fire story versus historians' view of a slow decline.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Basil is a warm-season herb, so gardeners often wonder how warm the soil should be before they plant it. Horticulturist Lucía Ferreira sowed 50 basil seeds in each of four trays, kept each tray at a different soil temperature, and recorded how many seeds sprouted. In her test, the greatest number of seeds sprouted at a soil temperature of ______

data.title: Basil Seeds Sprouted at Four Soil Temperatures (50 seeds per tray)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: 25°C, where 46 of the 50 seeds sprouted.
choices.B: 30°C, where seeds sprouted in an average of 4.8 days.
choices.C: 15°C, where 21 of the 50 seeds sprouted.
choices.D: 35°C, where nearly all of the 50 seeds sprouted.

explanation.why: The statement is about which temperature produced the greatest number of sprouted seeds, so look at the "Seeds sprouted" column and find the largest value. The largest number is 46, in the 25°C row.
explanation.A: Correct. At 25°C, 46 of 50 seeds sprouted, more than at any other temperature in the table.
explanation.B: Incorrect. 30°C gave the fastest sprouting time, but the statement is about how many seeds sprouted, and 44 is fewer than 46.
explanation.C: Incorrect. 15°C produced the fewest sprouted seeds, not the most.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table does not include a tray kept at 35°C.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: At the start of March 2023, a community library in Kathmandu, Nepal, opened a reading corner with low shelves and floor cushions for children. Librarian Sushila Thapa counted how many books were borrowed each month to see whether the new space made a difference. The graph suggests that borrowing increased after the reading corner opened: ______

data.title: Books Borrowed per Month at a Kathmandu Community Library, 2023

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: borrowing was highest in January, when about 410 books were borrowed.
choices.B: most of the extra books borrowed were picture books for young children.
choices.C: monthly borrowing rose from about 400 books to more than 650 books.
choices.D: about 410 books were borrowed in January and about 400 in February.

explanation.why: The statement says borrowing increased after the corner opened in March, so the choice must compare the months before (January and February) with the months after (March and April). The graph shows about 400 books in each of the first two months and more than 650 in each of the last two.
explanation.A: Incorrect. January is one of the lowest months on the graph; April is the highest.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The graph shows only the total number of books borrowed, not what kinds of books they were.
explanation.C: Correct. Borrowing went from about 400 books per month in January and February to 655 and 731 books in March and April.
explanation.D: Incorrect. These numbers are accurate, but they describe only the months before the corner opened, so they do not show an increase.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Museum visitors often spend only a few seconds in front of a painting. Curator Ingrid Solberg suspected that this was partly because wall labels give only basic facts, such as a work's title and date. She hypothesized that adding a short card telling the story behind a painting would increase viewing time for every painting in her test, not just for the most popular ones.
