data.title: Average Time Visitors Spent Viewing Each Painting

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Solberg's hypothesis?

choices.A: Visitors spent 38 seconds viewing Portrait of a Weaver with a story card, longer than they spent on any other painting.
choices.B: Still Life with Lemons received less viewing time than any other painting, with or without a story card.
choices.C: Visitors viewed The Orchard Wall for longer when it had only a label than when it also had a story card.
choices.D: Each of the four paintings was viewed longer on average with a story card than with only a label.

explanation.why: Solberg's hypothesis is that story cards increase viewing time for every painting, not only the popular ones. Support must therefore compare the two columns for all four paintings. In every row, the "Label and story card" time is greater than the "Label only" time.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only one painting and does not compare its time with the label-only time, so it cannot show an effect on every painting.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares paintings with one another instead of comparing each painting with and without a story card.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The Orchard Wall was viewed for 26 seconds with a story card and only 18 seconds with a label alone, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Correct. All four paintings gained viewing time with a story card (14 to 31, 22 to 38, 9 to 17 and 18 to 26 seconds), which is what "every painting" requires.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A green roof is covered with soil and low plants, which shade the surface and release water vapor that cools the air around them. Engineer Rangi Parata measured the surface temperature of a green roof and a conventional black roof in Auckland, New Zealand, every three hours on a sunny summer day. Parata found that the gap between the two roofs was largest in the afternoon: ______

data.title: Roof Surface Temperature over One Summer Day

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: at 6 p.m., the black roof was 44°C, while the green roof was 30°C.
choices.B: at 3 p.m., the black roof reached 66°C, while the green roof reached only 35°C.
choices.C: at 3 p.m., the green roof reached 66°C, while the black roof reached only 35°C.
choices.D: at 9 a.m., the green roof was more than 10°C cooler than the black roof.

explanation.why: The statement needs the afternoon time when the difference between the two lines is greatest. At 3 p.m. the gap is 66 − 35 = 31°C, larger than at noon (28°C) or 6 p.m. (14°C). The choice must also give the values the right way around: the black roof is the hotter one.
explanation.A: Incorrect. These values are accurate, but the gap at 6 p.m. is only 14°C, much smaller than the gap at 3 p.m.
explanation.B: Correct. At 3 p.m. the black roof (66°C) was 31°C hotter than the green roof (35°C), the largest gap shown.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This swaps the two roofs; the graph shows the black roof, not the green roof, reaching 66°C.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The 11°C gap at 9 a.m. is real, but 9 a.m. is morning, and the gap then is far smaller than in the afternoon.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When a midsize city expanded its bike-share network between 2019 and 2023, officials celebrated the rise in total trips as evidence that residents were embracing cycling for leisure. Urban planner Tomás Iturralde reads the same records differently. Because the new docking stations were placed mostly near offices and transit hubs, he argues, the growth in ridership came overwhelmingly from people riding on workdays, while recreational weekend use stayed nearly flat. In his view, the network had become chiefly a commuting tool.

data.title: Bike-Share Trips in a Midsize City

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Iturralde's argument?

choices.A: Total trips rose from 600,000 in 2019 to 905,000 in 2023.
choices.B: Weekday trips rose by 280,000 from 2019 to 2023, while weekend trips rose by only 25,000.
choices.C: Weekend trips increased in every year shown, from 190,000 in 2019 to 215,000 in 2023.
choices.D: Weekday trips more than doubled between 2019 and 2023, while weekend trips did not.

explanation.why: Iturralde does not dispute that total trips grew; his claim is about where the growth came from: mostly weekday trips, with weekend trips nearly flat. Support therefore has to compare the change in the two columns. Weekday trips rose from 410 to 690 thousand (+280,000), while weekend trips rose from 190 to 215 thousand (+25,000).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but officials and Iturralde both accept that total trips grew; the total does not show which kind of trip produced the growth.
explanation.B: Correct. It compares the growth in the two columns and shows that nearly all of the increase came from weekday trips.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes weekend trips alone and stresses their growth, which does not show that weekday trips drove the increase.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Weekday trips rose from 410,000 to 690,000, which is less than double, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In parts of Bangladesh, flash floods can leave young rice plants completely underwater for days, and many conventional varieties die if submerged for much longer than a week. Agronomist Farzana Haque compared a conventional variety with a flood-tolerant variety by holding seedlings of each underwater for different lengths of time and then counting the survivors. Haque concluded that although the tolerant variety offers only a slight benefit in brief floods, its advantage over the conventional variety grows considerably as flooding lasts longer.

data.title: Rice Seedling Survival after Submergence

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Haque's conclusion?

choices.A: The tolerant variety had a higher survival rate than the conventional variety after every flooding period tested.
choices.B: Survival rates for both varieties declined as the number of days underwater increased.
choices.C: Between 3 and 14 days underwater, the tolerant variety's survival rate fell by more percentage points than the conventional variety's did.
choices.D: The tolerant variety's survival rate was 3 percentage points higher than the conventional variety's after 3 days but 55 points higher after 14 days.

explanation.why: Haque's conclusion has two parts: the tolerant variety's advantage is small in short floods, and that advantage grows as floods last longer. Support must show the gap between the two bars at a short and a long flooding period. The gap is 95 − 92 = 3 points at 3 days and 64 − 9 = 55 points at 14 days.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that the tolerant variety always did better, not that its advantage was slight at first and then grew.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes both varieties together and says nothing about the difference between them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The tolerant variety fell 31 points (95 to 64), while the conventional variety fell 83 points (92 to 9), so this reverses the data.
explanation.D: Correct. A 3-point gap after a short flood and a 55-point gap after a long one shows both parts of the conclusion: a slight early benefit and a much larger later one.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Because lizards cannot generate much body heat internally, they were long described as being at the mercy of their surroundings, warming and cooling with the air. Herpetologist Elif Karaca, who fitted Mediterranean wall lizards in a rocky hillside population with miniature temperature sensors and recorded their average body temperature every two hours through a clear summer day, rejects that characterization. By shuttling between sunlit rock and shaded crevices, she contends, the lizards confine their body temperature to a band considerably narrower than the daily swing in the temperature of the air around them, rather than simply tracking that swing.

data.title: Air Temperature and Average Lizard Body Temperature over One Day

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Karaca's claim?

choices.A: Between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., the lizards' body temperature stayed within about 10°C, whereas air temperature spanned nearly 20°C.
choices.B: At every time of day shown, the lizards' average body temperature was higher than the temperature of the surrounding air.
choices.C: From 8 a.m. to noon, the temperature of the air rose by fewer degrees than the lizards' body temperature did.
choices.D: The lizards spent more of the hottest afternoon hours in shaded crevices than they did in the cool early morning.

explanation.why: Karaca's specific claim is about range: body temperature varies within a narrower band than air temperature does. To support it, compare the spread of each line across the day. Body temperature runs from 25°C to 35°C (about 10 degrees), while air temperature runs from 14°C to 33°C (19 degrees).
explanation.A: Correct. Comparing the two ranges, about 10°C for the lizards versus about 19°C for the air, shows exactly the narrower band Karaca describes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but being warmer than the air is a different claim; a lizard could be warmer than the air at every hour and still swing as widely as the air does.
explanation.C: Incorrect. From 8 a.m. to noon the air warmed by 15°C (14 to 29), while the lizards warmed by only 10°C (25 to 35), so this reverses the data.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Shuttling into shade fits Karaca's explanation, but the graph shows only temperatures, not where the lizards spent their time.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In a fishing town on the coast of Galicia, in northwestern Spain, older residents use a rich set of local words for particular winds and sea conditions, words that younger residents rarely say aloud. One might assume that this vocabulary is simply being forgotten. Linguist Xoana Castro, who surveyed residents of four age groups, proposes a different account: younger speakers, she argues, still know the traditional words about as well as their grandparents do but choose standard terms instead, so the shift reflects a change in preference rather than a loss of knowledge.

data.title: Survey of Traditional Wind and Sea Words in a Galician Fishing Town

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Castro's account?

choices.A: The share of speakers who regularly used the traditional words fell steadily from 88% in the oldest group to 23% in the youngest group.
choices.B: Among speakers aged 65 and older, 88% regularly used the traditional words and 97% recognized them.
choices.C: Speakers aged 15–24 used the traditional words at roughly a quarter of the rate of those 65 and older, yet recognized them at nearly the same rate.
choices.D: Recognition of the traditional words fell about as sharply from the oldest to the youngest group as regular use of the words did.

explanation.why: Castro's account has two parts that must both appear: younger speakers use the words much less than older speakers, and yet they know the words about as well. That requires comparing the youngest and oldest groups in both columns. Use falls from 88% to 23% (about a quarter), while recognition changes only from 97% to 90%.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but a drop in use is what both explanations accept; without the recognition figures it cannot show that the words are not being forgotten.
explanation.B: Incorrect. These figures are accurate and use both columns, but they describe only the oldest speakers, while Castro's account is about what younger speakers know.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows a large gap in use (23% versus 88%) alongside a small gap in recognition (90% versus 97%), which is exactly the pattern a change in preference would produce.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Recognition fell only 7 points (97% to 90%), while use fell 65 points (88% to 23%), so this misreads the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Hummingbirds feed on flower nectar, which is mostly sugar dissolved in water. To learn which sugar mixture ruby-throated hummingbirds prefer, biologist Nadia Kowalczyk hung four feeders in a garden in Ontario, Canada, each filled with a different mixture, and counted the birds' visits over one week. The feeder that received the most visits held a mixture that was ______

data.title: Hummingbird Visits to Four Feeders over One Week

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: 10 percent sugar, which received 84 visits.
choices.B: 30 percent sugar, which received 211 visits.
choices.C: 20 percent sugar, which received 211 visits.
choices.D: taken from wild flowers, which received the most visits.

explanation.why: The statement asks which mixture was in the feeder with the most visits, so find the largest number in the "Visits" column. That number is 211, in the 20% row.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The 10% feeder received the fewest visits, not the most.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The 30% feeder received 167 visits; the 211 visits belong to the 20% feeder, so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Correct. The 20% feeder received 211 visits, the largest number in the "Visits" column.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table lists only sugar mixtures in feeders; it gives no data about wild flower nectar.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 2019, education officials in Bahawalpur District, Pakistan, began fitting rooftop solar panels to government schools that often lost electricity during the day. Engineer Faisal Qureshi recorded how many schools in the district had panels at the end of each year. According to the graph, from 2019 to 2022 the number of schools with solar panels ______

data.title: Schools with Rooftop Solar Panels in Bahawalpur District

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: rose every year, from 35 schools to 245 schools.
choices.B: stayed at about 90 schools in every year.
choices.C: fell every year, from 245 schools to 35 schools.
choices.D: rose fastest among schools for girls.

explanation.why: The statement describes how the number of schools changed from 2019 to 2022, so read the bars from left to right. They rise from 35 in 2019 to 90, then 160, then 245 in 2022.
explanation.A: Correct. The bars grow taller each year: 35, 90, 160 and 245 schools.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Only 2020 shows about 90 schools; the other years show 35, 160 and 245.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the graph: 35 schools is the 2019 value and 245 is the 2022 value.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The graph shows only the total number of schools; it does not separate schools for girls and boys.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In June 2024, a small community theater in Buenos Aires, Argentina, began offering half-price tickets to students. Theater manager Julieta Ramos wanted to know whether audiences grew afterward, so she recorded the number of tickets sold each month from March to August. According to the graph, monthly ticket sales first rose above 1,500 in ______

data.title: Tickets Sold per Month at a Community Theater in Buenos Aires, 2024

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: March, when 1,150 tickets were sold.
choices.B: August, when 1,910 tickets were sold.
choices.C: May, when 1,180 tickets were sold.
choices.D: June, when 1,640 tickets were sold.

explanation.why: The statement asks for the first month in which sales were above 1,500, so read the line from left to right and stop at the first point higher than 1,500. March, April and May are all under 1,200; June is 1,640.
explanation.A: Incorrect. 1,150 is below 1,500, so sales had not yet passed that level in March.
explanation.B: Incorrect. August's sales were above 1,500, but they had already passed that level in June and July, so August was not the first such month.
explanation.C: Incorrect. 1,180 is below 1,500; May was the last month before sales rose above that level.
explanation.D: Correct. March, April and May are all below 1,500, and June, at 1,640, is the first month above it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Earthworms loosen and mix soil, so park managers often want to know which ground covers suit them. Soil scientist Grace Liu marked out plots of 1 square meter under four different covers in a park in Melbourne, Australia, and counted the earthworms she dug up in each plot. She found the fewest earthworms under ______

data.title: Earthworms Found in 1-Square-Meter Plots under Four Ground Covers

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: leaf litter, where 64 earthworms were counted.
choices.B: bare soil, where only 9 earthworms were counted.
choices.C: grass lawn, where soil moisture was the lowest.
choices.D: wood chips, where 52 earthworms were counted.

explanation.why: The statement is about the fewest earthworms, so look for the smallest number in the "Earthworms counted" column. That number is 9, in the bare soil row.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Leaf litter had the most earthworms, not the fewest.
explanation.B: Correct. Bare soil had 9 earthworms, the smallest number in the "Earthworms counted" column.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Bare soil, at 14%, had the lowest soil moisture, and the grass lawn did not have the fewest earthworms.
explanation.D: Incorrect. 52 earthworms is more than the counts for the grass lawn and bare soil, so wood chips did not have the fewest.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Shea butter, made from the nuts of the shea tree, is sold around the world for use in foods and skin creams. In northern Ghana, much of it is produced by women who work together in cooperatives. Economist Abena Owusu followed one cooperative in Tamale from 2019 to 2023. According to the graph, the cooperative's membership in 2023 was twice its membership in ______

data.title: Members of a Shea Butter Cooperative in Tamale, Ghana

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: 2019, when the cooperative had 120 members.
choices.B: 2021, when the cooperative had 190 members.
choices.C: 2018, before the study began.
choices.D: 2020, when the cooperative had 145 members.

explanation.why: The 2023 bar shows 240 members, so the statement needs the year with half that number, 120. The 2019 bar shows 120 members.
explanation.A: Correct. The cooperative had 240 members in 2023, and 240 is twice 120, the 2019 total.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Twice 190 is 380, far more than the 240 members in 2023.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The graph begins in 2019, so it gives no membership figure for 2018.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Twice 145 is 290, not 240, so 2023's membership was less than twice the 2020 figure.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mangoes picked while still green ripen in storage, and the temperature of the storeroom affects how quickly they do so. Food scientist Hina Baloch stored four batches of Chaunsa mangoes from Multan, Pakistan, at different temperatures and recorded how many days each batch took to ripen. The batch that ripened the fastest was stored at ______

data.title: Ripening of Chaunsa Mangoes at Four Storage Temperatures (40 fruits per batch)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: 15°C, where the fewest fruits spoiled.
choices.B: 25°C, where the mangoes ripened in 4 days.
choices.C: 30°C, where the mangoes ripened in 5 days.
choices.D: 15°C, where the mangoes took 14 days to ripen.

explanation.why: "Ripened the fastest" means the fewest days to ripen, so look for the smallest number in the "Days to ripen" column. That number is 5, in the 30°C row.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It is true that only 1 fruit spoiled at 15°C, but the statement is about ripening speed, and that batch took the longest to ripen.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The 25°C batch ripened in 6 days; the 4 is the number of fruits that spoiled, so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Correct. At 30°C the mangoes took 5 days, the smallest number in the "Days to ripen" column.
explanation.D: Incorrect. 14 days is the longest ripening time in the table, so this batch ripened the slowest, not the fastest.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Since 2017, a children's magazine in Wellington, New Zealand, has held a yearly poetry contest for students aged 8 to 14. In 2020, the contest began accepting poems written in te reo Māori as well as in English. According to the graph, the number of entries rose the most from one year to the next between ______

data.title: Entries in a Children's Poetry Contest, 2017–2023

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: 2017 and 2018, when entries rose from 340 to 365.
choices.B: 2020 and 2021, when entries rose from 410 to 590.
choices.C: 2019 and 2020, when entries rose from 352 to 410.
choices.D: 2022 and 2023, when entries rose from 640 to 705.

explanation.why: The statement asks where the number of entries rose by the largest amount in a single year. Subtract each pair of neighboring years: the largest jump is from 410 in 2020 to 590 in 2021, a rise of 180.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This rise was only 25 entries, one of the smallest on the graph.
explanation.B: Correct. Entries rose by 180 from 2020 to 2021, more than in any other one-year step.
explanation.C: Incorrect. 2020 is the year the rule changed, but entries rose by only 58 from 2019 to 2020, far less than the next year's rise.
explanation.D: Incorrect. 2023 had the most entries in total, but the rise from 2022 was only 65.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many insects gather around white streetlights at night, and some bats hunt them there. To see whether the color of the light matters, ecologist Pieter de Vries placed bat detectors under streetlights of four colors along a country road in the Netherlands and counted bat calls each night. The detectors recorded the most bat calls under ______

data.title: Average Bat Calls Recorded per Night under Streetlights of Four Colors

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: red lights, with about 120 calls per night.
choices.B: amber lights, with about 190 calls per night.
choices.C: green lights, with about 410 calls per night.
choices.D: white lights, with about 410 calls per night.

explanation.why: The statement asks which light color had the most bat calls, so find the tallest bar. The white bar, at 412 calls per night, is taller than the green (365), amber (188) and red (121) bars.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Red lights recorded the fewest calls, not the most.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Amber lights recorded fewer calls than white or green lights.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Green lights recorded about 365 calls per night; the bar near 410 is the white one, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.D: Correct. The white bar is the tallest, at 412 calls per night.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Early in 2022, a town in the Atlas Mountains of Morocco gave every household free low-flow taps, which release less water per minute. Water engineer Youssef Amrani compared average household water use in the summer of 2021, before the program, with use in the summer of 2022. Of the three months shown, average daily water use fell the most in ______

data.title: Average Water Use per Household (liters per day)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: July, when it dropped from 455 to 372 liters.
choices.B: August, when it dropped from 470 to 401 liters.
choices.C: June, when it dropped from 412 to 351 liters.
choices.D: September, when it dropped by more than 100 liters.

explanation.why: To find where use fell the most, subtract the 2022 value from the 2021 value for each month: June 61, July 83 and August 69 liters. The largest drop is in July.
explanation.A: Correct. Use fell by 83 liters in July, more than in June (61 liters) or August (69 liters).
explanation.B: Incorrect. August had the highest use in both years, but it fell by only 69 liters, less than July's 83.
explanation.C: Incorrect. June's drop of 61 liters was the smallest of the three months.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The table gives no data for September.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is one of the driest places on Earth. With very little water vapor in the air to hold heat, the desert cools quickly once the sun goes down. Geographer Camila Rojas recorded the air temperature every three hours over one day in March. The lowest temperature of the day occurred at ______

data.title: Air Temperature over One Day in the Atacama Desert

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: 3 p.m., when it was about 27°C.
choices.B: 9 p.m., soon after sunset, when it was about 12°C.
choices.C: 6 a.m., when it was about 4°C.
choices.D: 12 a.m., when it fell below 0°C.

explanation.why: The statement asks when the temperature was lowest, so find the lowest point on the line. That point is at 6 a.m., at about 4°C.
explanation.A: Incorrect. 3 p.m. was the warmest time of the day, not the coldest.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The air was cooling at 9 p.m., but it kept falling for several more hours and was colder at 12 a.m., 3 a.m. and 6 a.m.
explanation.C: Correct. The line reaches its lowest point, about 4°C, at 6 a.m.
explanation.D: Incorrect. At 12 a.m. the temperature was about 9°C, and no point on the graph is below 0°C.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A music school in Kolkata, India, lends instruments to students who cannot afford their own. At the end of 2023, administrator Ananya Ghosh counted how many times each instrument had been borrowed that year. According to the graph, the instrument borrowed most often was the ______

data.title: Times Each Instrument Was Borrowed, 2023

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: tabla, which was borrowed 88 times.
choices.B: sarod, which was borrowed 23 times.
choices.C: sitar, which costs the most to buy.
choices.D: harmonium, which was borrowed 112 times.

explanation.why: To find the instrument borrowed most often, look for the tallest bar. The harmonium bar, at 112, is taller than every other bar.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The tabla was borrowed often, but 88 is less than the harmonium's 112.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The sarod was borrowed the fewest times, not the most.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The graph shows how often instruments were borrowed, not what they cost.
explanation.D: Correct. The harmonium bar is the tallest, at 112.

items.subject: science
items.passage: For a school science fair in Toronto, Canada, Mei Lin Zhou folded paper airplanes in four designs and threw each one ten times from the same spot. She recorded how far each design flew and how long it stayed in the air, on average. According to her results, the design that flew the farthest was the ______

data.title: Average Flight of Four Paper Airplane Designs (10 throws each)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: glider, which stayed in the air for 3.2 seconds.
choices.B: dart, which flew 9.4 meters on average.
choices.C: delta, which flew 9.4 meters on average.
choices.D: square-wing, which flew 5.6 meters on average.

explanation.why: "Flew the farthest" refers to distance, so look for the largest number in the "Distance (meters)" column. That number is 9.4, in the dart row.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The glider stayed up the longest, but the statement is about distance, and the glider flew only 7.1 meters.
explanation.B: Correct. 9.4 meters is the largest number in the "Distance" column.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The delta flew 8.2 meters; 9.4 meters belongs to the dart, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. 5.6 meters is the shortest distance in the table.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Officials in a neighborhood of Valparaíso, Chile, wanted to know which materials residents recycled most. For one year, environmental planner Diego Fuentes weighed the material collected from recycling bins and from regular trash bins. According to the table, the material collected for recycling in the largest amount was ______

data.title: Waste Collected in One Year in a Valparaíso Neighborhood (metric tons)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: paper and cardboard, with 340 metric tons.
choices.B: plastic, with 410 metric tons.
choices.C: metal cans, with 45 metric tons.
choices.D: food scraps, with 500 metric tons.

explanation.why: The statement is about material collected for recycling, so use only the "Collected for recycling" column and find its largest value. That value is 340 metric tons, for paper and cardboard.
explanation.A: Correct. 340 metric tons is the largest number in the "Collected for recycling" column.
explanation.B: Incorrect. 410 metric tons of plastic was thrown away as trash; only 90 metric tons was collected for recycling, so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. 45 metric tons is the smallest amount collected for recycling.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Food scraps do not appear in the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sunflowers can grow remarkably quickly in early summer. Working at a field station in central Ukraine, agronomist Olena Kovalenko measured the height of one sunflower plant at the end of each week after it sprouted. According to the graph, by the end of week 6 the plant had reached a height of ______

data.title: Height of a Sunflower Plant in the Eight Weeks after Sprouting

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: about 45 centimeters.
choices.B: about 170 centimeters.
choices.C: about 120 centimeters.
choices.D: about 80 centimeters.

explanation.why: Find week 6 on the horizontal axis and read the height of that point. It is at about 120 centimeters, between the week 5 value of 80 and the week 7 value of 155.
explanation.A: Incorrect. 45 centimeters is the plant's height at week 4, not week 6.
explanation.B: Incorrect. 170 centimeters is the plant's height at week 8, the end of the study, not at week 6.
explanation.C: Correct. The point for week 6 is at about 120 centimeters.
explanation.D: Incorrect. 80 centimeters is the plant's height at week 5, one week earlier.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Ethio-jazz, a style that blends Ethiopian musical scales with jazz and funk, flourished in Addis Ababa in the late 1960s and early 1970s. An archive in the city has been copying old reel-to-reel tapes of the music into digital files. Archivist Selam Tesfaye recorded how many recordings were copied each year. The archive copied the most recordings in ______

data.title: Recordings Copied into Digital Files by an Addis Ababa Archive

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: 2020, when the fewest tapes needed repair.
choices.B: 2021, when 210 recordings were copied.
choices.C: 2022, when 210 recordings were copied.
choices.D: 2019, when 140 recordings were copied.

explanation.why: The statement asks when the archive copied the most recordings, so look for the largest number in the "Recordings copied" column. That number is 210, in the 2021 row.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It is true that 2020 had the fewest repairs, but it also had the fewest recordings copied, so it does not complete the statement.
explanation.B: Correct. 210 is the largest number in the "Recordings copied" column.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The archive copied 185 recordings in 2022; the 210 belongs to 2021, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. 140 is less than the totals for 2021 and 2022, so 2019 was not the busiest year.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Coffee is often grown in full sun to maximize harvests, but some farmers in Colombia plant it beneath taller shade trees. Agronomist Luis Cárdenas compared plots grown in full sun, light shade and heavy shade. He concluded that shade involves a trade-off: shaded plots produce smaller harvests, but a greater share of their beans are large, a quality that coffee buyers value.

data.title: Coffee Plots Grown under Three Levels of Shade

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Cárdenas's conclusion?

choices.A: Plants under heavy shade grew to an average of 2.4 meters, taller than the 1.9 meters reached in full sun.
choices.B: Heavy-shade plots yielded 1,240 kg per hectare to full sun's 1,850 kg, but 63 percent of their beans were large, versus 38 percent.
choices.C: Plots in full sun yielded 1,850 kg of beans per hectare, more than the plots under either light shade or heavy shade.
choices.D: Plots under light shade yielded more beans per hectare than plots in full sun did, and a larger share of their beans were large.

explanation.why: A trade-off has two sides, so support for Cárdenas's conclusion must show both a smaller harvest and a larger share of large beans under shade. Only one choice compares both columns for shaded and unshaded plots.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but plant height is not part of the trade-off Cárdenas describes, which concerns harvest size and bean size.
explanation.B: Correct. It shows both halves of the trade-off: heavy shade produced a smaller harvest than full sun but a larger share of large beans.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true and shows that shade lowers the harvest, but it says nothing about bean size, so it supports only half of the trade-off.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Light-shade plots yielded 1,620 kg per hectare, less than the 1,850 kg from full-sun plots, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In Bangladesh, mobile banking services let people send, receive and save money using a basic phone. Economist Tahmina Akter surveyed villages in Rangpur Division in 2018 and again in 2022. She reports that younger adults were still the most likely to use mobile banking in 2022, but that the gap between age groups narrowed because use grew fastest among adults aged 50 and older.

data.title: Village Residents Using Mobile Banking in Rangpur Division, by Age Group

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Akter's explanation of why the gap narrowed?

choices.A: In 2022, 74 percent of residents aged 18–29 used mobile banking, the highest share of any age group that year.
choices.B: In both 2018 and 2022, residents aged 30–49 used mobile banking at a higher rate than residents aged 50 and older.
choices.C: The share of residents aged 18–29 who used mobile banking rose by more percentage points between 2018 and 2022 than did the share of any other age group.
choices.D: The share of residents aged 50 and older who used mobile banking rose from 12 percent to 41 percent, a larger increase than in either younger age group.

explanation.why: Akter explains the narrowing gap by saying that use grew fastest among adults aged 50 and older, so the support must compare the increases of the age groups. The oldest group rose from 12 to 41 percent (29 points), more than the 18–29 group (16 points) or the 30–49 group (19 points).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true and matches Akter's point that younger adults were still the most likely users, but it does not show why the gap narrowed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes a difference that existed in both years; it does not show which group's use grew fastest.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The 18–29 group rose by only 16 points, the smallest increase of the three, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.D: Correct. The oldest group rose by 29 percentage points, compared with 16 for ages 18–29 and 19 for ages 30–49, which shows that use grew fastest among older adults.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On many lakes in Finland, local observers have written down the dates of freezing and thawing for well over a century. Limnologist Aino Virtanen used such records from one lake to find the average number of days per winter that it stayed covered with ice in each decade since the 1950s. She argues that the lake's ice cover has not simply declined but that the decline has sped up in recent decades.

data.title: Average Days of Ice Cover per Winter on a Finnish Lake, by Decade

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Virtanen's argument?

choices.A: Average ice cover fell by 5 days in total from the 1950s to the 1970s but by 11 days from the 2000s to the 2010s alone.
choices.B: The lake was covered with ice for an average of 182 days per winter in the 1950s and 146 days in the 2010s.
choices.C: Average ice cover fell by about the same number of days from each decade to the next across the whole record.
choices.D: In the 1990s, the lake was covered with ice for an average of 165 days per winter, more than in the 2000s.

explanation.why: Virtanen claims more than a decline: she says the decline sped up. Support must therefore compare the size of the drop in an earlier period with the size of the drop in a recent one. From the 1950s to the 1970s ice cover fell from 182 to 177 days, but from the 2000s to the 2010s it fell from 157 to 146 days.
explanation.A: Correct. A 5-day drop over two decades early on, compared with an 11-day drop in a single recent decade, shows that the decline has sped up.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true and shows that ice cover declined, but comparing only the first and last decades cannot show whether the decline sped up.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The drops grew from 2 days (1950s to 1960s) to 11 days (2000s to 2010s), so they were not about the same.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but a single comparison between two decades says nothing about whether the rate of decline changed.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Some orchestras offer short talks before concerts to introduce the music. At four concerts in Lyon, France, arts researcher Camille Fournier recorded the share of listeners who returned to their seats after intermission, comparing those who had attended the talk with those who had not. The table lists the programs from most familiar to least familiar to typical audiences. Fournier concluded that the talks mattered most for the least familiar music.

data.title: Listeners Who Returned after Intermission at Four Concerts in Lyon

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Fournier's conclusion?

choices.A: At every concert, listeners who attended the talk returned after intermission at a higher rate than listeners who did not.
choices.B: Listeners who attended the talk returned after intermission at a lower rate for the Boulez concert than for any other concert.
choices.C: The gap between the two groups' return rates was 5 percentage points for Debussy and Ravel but 25 points for Boulez.
choices.D: Among listeners who skipped the talk, a higher share returned at the Messiaen concert than at the Stravinsky concert.

explanation.why: Fournier's conclusion is about where the talks mattered most, so the support must compare the gap between the two groups across programs. The gap is 5 points for Debussy and Ravel, 9 for Stravinsky, 18 for Messiaen and 25 for Boulez, growing as the music becomes less familiar.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true and suggests that the talks helped, but it does not show that they helped most for the least familiar music.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only one group and does not compare talk attendees with other listeners.
explanation.C: Correct. The gap between the groups grows from 5 points for the most familiar program to 25 points for the least familiar one, so the talks made the biggest difference where the music was least familiar.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Only 72 percent returned at the Messiaen concert, compared with 84 percent at the Stravinsky concert, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In England, many farmers now sow strips of wildflowers along the edges of their fields to provide food for pollinating insects. Ecologist Hannah Mercer counted bumblebees on four farms, comparing field edges sown with wildflowers and edges left as grass. She claims that the wildflower strips benefited bumblebees on every farm, though the size of the benefit differed greatly from one farm to another.

data.title: Bumblebees Counted along Field Edges on Four Farms

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Mercer's claim?

choices.A: The wildflower strip at Calder had 48 bumblebees, more than any other strip or grass edge in the study.
choices.B: More bumblebees were counted along wildflower strips than along grass edges on only three of the four farms.
choices.C: The grass edges had between 9 and 18 bumblebees, so the number of bumblebees varied from farm to farm.
choices.D: Wildflower strips had more bumblebees than grass edges on all four farms, by 6 at Bramley but by 39 at Calder.

explanation.why: Mercer's claim has two parts: the strips helped on every farm, and the size of the help varied. The support must compare the two bars for each farm. Wildflower strips beat grass edges everywhere, by 22 at Ashcombe, 6 at Bramley, 39 at Calder and 9 at Dunmore.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes one farm only and does not show a benefit on every farm.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Wildflower strips had more bumblebees on all four farms, so this misreads the graph and would weaken the claim about every farm.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the grass edges; it does not compare them with the wildflower strips, so it cannot show a benefit.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows a benefit on every farm and that the benefit ranged from 6 to 39 bumblebees, which covers both parts of Mercer's claim.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: After many office workers in Melbourne, Australia, began working from home several days a week, economist Ravi Chandrasekaran studied cafés in the city center, where many customers had once been office workers buying coffee and lunch. He hypothesized that these cafés depended heavily on such customers, so their sales would have fallen much more on weekdays than on weekends.

data.title: Average Daily Sales at City-Center Cafés in Melbourne (dollars)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Chandrasekaran's hypothesis?

choices.A: Average sales fell by $700 to $1,100 on each weekday shown but by only $50 on each weekend day.
choices.B: Average sales on Wednesdays were higher than on any other day shown, in both 2019 and 2023.
choices.C: Average sales on Sundays were lower than on any other day shown, in both 2019 and 2023.
choices.D: Average sales fell by more on Saturdays than on Wednesdays between 2019 and 2023.

explanation.why: The hypothesis predicts a larger drop in sales on weekdays than on weekends, so the support must compare the changes from 2019 to 2023. Weekday sales fell by $1,100 (Monday), $700 (Wednesday) and $1,100 (Friday), while Saturday and Sunday sales each fell by only $50.
explanation.A: Correct. It compares the drop on weekdays with the drop on weekends, which is exactly what the hypothesis predicts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares days within each year and does not show how much sales fell.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it does not compare the change in sales on weekdays with the change on weekends.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Saturday sales fell by only $50, while Wednesday sales fell by $700, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Air generally becomes cooler as altitude increases. In the Langtang Valley of Nepal, glaciologist Pemba Sherpa installed weather stations at five elevations and recorded the average air temperature at each one during July. She found that, along this valley, the temperature fell by roughly 6°C for every 1,000 meters of elevation gained. For example, the average July temperature was ______

data.title: Average July Air Temperature at Five Stations in the Langtang Valley

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: about 22°C at 1,500 meters, the warmest of the five stations.
choices.B: about 16°C at 2,500 meters and about 10°C at 3,500 meters.
choices.C: about 16°C at 2,500 meters and about 4°C at 3,500 meters.
choices.D: below freezing at 5,500 meters, the highest station.

explanation.why: Sherpa's finding is about a rate of change, so the example must give temperatures at two elevations and show a drop of about 6°C for each 1,000 meters. The stations at 2,500 and 3,500 meters average about 16°C and 10°C, a drop of about 6°C over 1,000 meters.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but a single temperature cannot show how much the temperature falls as elevation increases.
explanation.B: Correct. These two stations are 1,000 meters apart, and the temperature falls by about 6°C between them, which is an example of the pattern Sherpa describes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The 3,500-meter station averaged about 10°C; about 4°C was recorded at 4,500 meters, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it gives only one station's temperature and does not show a drop of about 6°C per 1,000 meters.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Swahili, spoken across much of East Africa, developed along a coast where traders from Arabia, Persia, India and, later, Portugal and Britain did business for centuries. Linguist Neema Mwakyusa traced the origins of 400 Swahili words related to trade and seafaring. She concluded that, in this vocabulary, words borrowed from Arabic outnumber the words borrowed from all other foreign languages combined.

data.title: Origins of 400 Swahili Words Related to Trade and Seafaring

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Mwakyusa's conclusion?

choices.A: Arabic contributed 150 of the words, while Persian, Indian languages, Portuguese and English together contributed 70.
choices.B: Words of Bantu origin, at 180, made up the largest single group among the 400 words in the sample.
choices.C: Arabic contributed 150 of the words, far more than the 20 words that came from Portuguese.
choices.D: Persian, Indian languages, Portuguese and English together contributed more of the words than Arabic did.

explanation.why: Mwakyusa compares Arabic with all other foreign languages combined, so add up the bars for Persian (20), Indian languages (15), Portuguese (20) and English (15): 70 words. Arabic's 150 words are more than that total, and only one choice makes this comparison.
explanation.A: Correct. It compares Arabic with all the other foreign sources combined (20 + 15 + 20 + 15 = 70), which is the comparison the conclusion makes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but Bantu words are native to Swahili, not borrowed, so they are not part of Mwakyusa's comparison.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares Arabic with only one other language, not with all the other foreign languages combined.
explanation.D: Incorrect. These four sources together contributed 70 words, fewer than Arabic's 150, so this misreads the graph.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Gardeners sometimes release lady beetles, which eat aphids, to protect plants without using pesticides. In a rose garden in Seville, Spain, horticulturist Sofía Navarro released lady beetles onto some rosebushes and left others untreated, then counted aphids every week. She concluded that the beetles reduced aphid numbers at first but that the effect had nearly disappeared within a few weeks.

data.title: Average Aphids per Rose Shoot after Lady Beetles Were Released

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Navarro's conclusion?

choices.A: Most of the lady beetles released onto the rosebushes had flown away to other parts of the garden by week 3.
choices.B: One week after release, bushes with beetles had 14 aphids per shoot, far fewer than the 46 on untreated bushes.
choices.C: In week 1, bushes with beetles had 14 aphids per shoot to untreated bushes' 46, but by week 4 they had 47 to 52.
choices.D: By week 4, bushes with beetles had more aphids per shoot than untreated bushes had in the same week.

explanation.why: Navarro's conclusion has two parts: an early drop in aphids and a later fading of that effect. The support must compare the two columns at an early week and at a late week. In week 1 the gap was 32 aphids per shoot (14 versus 46), but by week 4 it was only 5 (47 versus 52).
explanation.A: Incorrect. The table counts aphids only; it gives no information about where the beetles went.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true and shows the early reduction, but it does not show that the effect later nearly disappeared.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows both a large early reduction and a small difference by week 4, matching both parts of the conclusion.
explanation.D: Incorrect. In week 4, bushes with beetles had 47 aphids per shoot and untreated bushes had 52, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Geographer Chidi Okonkwo mapped the stalls of a large open-air market in Lagos, Nigeria, in 2012 and again in 2022. He reports that stalls selling mobile phones and accessories grew in number by far more than any other kind of stall over the decade, even though fabric and clothing sellers still held more stalls than any other group in 2022.

data.title: Stalls in an Open-Air Market in Lagos, by Goods Sold

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Okonkwo's report?

choices.A: In 2022, the market had 260 phone and accessory stalls and 330 food and spice stalls, out of 1,310 stalls in all.
choices.B: Fabric and clothing stalls were the most common type of stall in the market in both 2012 and 2022.
choices.C: Household goods stalls increased by more than phone and accessory stalls did between 2012 and 2022.
choices.D: Phone and accessory stalls rose by 215, yet fabric and clothing stalls, at 405, were still the most common type in 2022.

explanation.why: Okonkwo reports two things: phone stalls grew by far the most, and fabric and clothing stalls were still the most numerous in 2022. The support must show both. Phone stalls rose from 45 to 260 (an increase of 215), and fabric and clothing, at 405, remained the largest group.
explanation.A: Incorrect. These numbers are accurate, but they describe 2022 only and do not show how much any type of stall grew.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true and supports the second part of the report, but it says nothing about the growth of phone stalls.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Household goods stalls rose by only 25, while phone stalls rose by 215, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows both parts of the report: the largest increase (215, compared with at most 25 for any other type) and fabric and clothing still in first place.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Wheat in Pakistan's Punjab province is harvested in April and May, so an unusually hot March, when the grains are filling, can shrink the crop. Plant breeder Rubina Chaudhry compared a widely grown older variety with a newer variety bred to tolerate heat. She argues that the new variety's advantage is not constant: it matters most in years when March is especially hot.

data.title: Wheat Yields of Two Varieties at a Research Farm in Punjab, Pakistan

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Chaudhry's argument?

choices.A: The older variety's yield was highest in 2019, when it produced 3.4 metric tons of wheat per hectare.
choices.B: The newer variety outyielded the older one by 0.9 metric tons per hectare in 2022, the hottest March, but by only 0.1 in 2019, the coolest.
choices.C: The newer variety produced a higher yield than the older variety in every year from 2019 through 2023.
choices.D: The gap between the yields of the two varieties was smaller in 2022 than in any other year shown.

explanation.why: Chaudhry claims that the newer variety's advantage depends on March temperature, so the support must compare the gap between the varieties in hot and cool years. The gap was 0.1 metric tons per hectare in 2019 (24.1°C) but 0.9 in 2022 (28.9°C), and it was larger in 2021 and 2022, the two hottest years, than in any other year.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the older variety and does not compare the two varieties.
explanation.B: Correct. The newer variety's advantage was largest in the hottest year and smallest in the coolest one, which shows that its advantage grows when March is hot.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true and shows that the newer variety did better, but it does not show that its advantage was largest in hot years.
explanation.D: Incorrect. In 2022 the gap was 0.9 metric tons per hectare, the largest of any year, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In 2016, a city in central Mexico began paying for murals on public walls. Art historian Paloma Ortiz argues that a rule added in 2019, which gave grants to murals designed together with neighborhood residents, changed the program's character: before the rule, most of its murals were the work of invited professional artists, but afterward, most were designed with residents.

data.title: Murals Painted per Year through a City Mural Program

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Ortiz's argument?

choices.A: Invited artists painted most murals from 2016 through 2018, but resident-designed murals were the majority every year from 2019 on.
choices.B: The program produced more murals in 2022, a total of 29, than in any earlier year shown on the graph.
choices.C: The number of murals designed with residents rose sharply after the 2019 rule, from 3 in 2018 to 13 in 2019.
choices.D: Murals by invited artists outnumbered murals designed with residents in every year shown, from 2016 through 2022.

explanation.why: Ortiz claims that the majority switched from invited artists' murals to resident-designed murals after 2019, so the support must compare the two lines before and after that year. Invited artists led in 2016–2018, and resident-designed murals led in every year from 2019 to 2022.
explanation.A: Correct. In 2016–2018 invited artists led (12 to 2, 14 to 3, 15 to 3), and from 2019 on resident-designed murals led (13 to 9, 15 to 8, 18 to 7, 21 to 8), which is the change Ortiz describes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (29 murals), but it concerns the total number of murals, not who designed them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only one line; without comparing it with the invited artists' murals, it cannot show which kind made up most of the murals before and after 2019.
explanation.D: Incorrect. From 2019 on, murals designed with residents outnumbered those by invited artists, so this misreads the graph.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In sea turtles, whether an egg hatches as a male or a female depends on the temperature of the sand around the nest: warmer nests produce more females. On a beach in Bahia, Brazil, biologist Mariana Teixeira found that nests in open sand were warmer than nests shaded by coastal plants. She argues that if the shaded parts of the beach are cleared for development, the beach will produce an even higher share of female hatchlings.

data.title: Female Hatchlings from Sea Turtle Nests on a Beach in Bahia, Brazil

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Teixeira's argument?

choices.A: Most of the hatchlings from partly shaded nests, 71 percent, were female rather than male.
choices.B: Nests in open sand produced a smaller share of female hatchlings than nests shaded by plants did.
choices.C: More turtles laid their eggs in open sand than in the shaded parts of the beach, where plants grow.
choices.D: Nests shaded by plants produced 42 percent female hatchlings, while nests in open sand produced 93 percent.

explanation.why: Teixeira's argument depends on shaded nests producing fewer females than open-sand nests, so that removing shade would raise the share of females. The graph shows 42 percent females from shaded nests and 93 percent from open-sand nests.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (71 percent), but it does not compare shaded nests with open-sand nests, which is what the argument about losing shade depends on.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Open-sand nests produced 93 percent females, compared with 42 percent for shaded nests, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The graph shows the share of female hatchlings, not how many nests were in each location.
explanation.D: Correct. Shaded nests produced far fewer females than open-sand nests, so losing the shaded areas would leave mostly nests that produce females.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When a regional railway in Poland introduced a smartphone ticket app in 2021, transport researcher Agnieszka Wróbel tracked how passengers at one station bought their tickets. She found that the app did not mainly replace the ticket counter, as many staff had feared. Instead, its growth came mostly at the expense of the station's ticket machines, while the counter's share fell only slightly.

data.title: Share of Tickets Sold at One Station, by Method (%)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Wróbel's finding?

choices.A: In 2023, 40 percent of tickets were bought through the app, more than through either of the other methods.
choices.B: The share of tickets bought through the app rose in every year after the app was introduced in 2021.
choices.C: From 2020 to 2023, the machines' share fell from 62 to 26 percent, while the counter's share fell only from 38 to 34 percent.
choices.D: From 2020 to 2023, the counter's share of ticket sales fell by more percentage points than the machines' share did.

explanation.why: Wróbel's finding is about where the app's growth came from, so the support must compare how much the counter and the machines each lost. The machines dropped from 62 to 26 percent, while the counter dropped only from 38 to 34 percent.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only how popular the app became, not which method lost the most sales to it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes the app alone and does not compare the losses of the counter and the machines.
explanation.C: Correct. The machines lost 36 percentage points while the counter lost only 4, which shows that the app's growth came mostly from the machines.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The counter's share fell by 4 points and the machines' share by 36 points, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In winter, a layer of snow acts like a blanket, slowing the loss of heat from the ground beneath it. Near Fairbanks, Alaska, soil scientist Ivan Petrov measured soil temperatures 10 centimeters below the surface in plots kept clear of snow and in plots left under natural snow cover. He concluded that the insulating effect of snow was strongest during the coldest months.

data.title: Average Monthly Temperatures near Fairbanks, Alaska (°C)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Petrov's conclusion?

choices.A: In every month shown, the soil under natural snow was warmer than the air above it, often by more than 10°C.
choices.B: Snow-covered soil was 12°C warmer than cleared soil in January, the coldest month, but only 4°C warmer in March, the mildest.
choices.C: The soil under natural snow stayed between −2°C and −4°C from November through March, while the air ranged from −10°C to −24°C.
choices.D: The difference between cleared soil and snow-covered soil was largest in March, the mildest month shown.

explanation.why: The insulating effect of snow is the difference between soil under snow and soil without snow. Petrov's conclusion requires that this difference be largest in the coldest months. The difference is 12°C in January (−4 versus −16), when the air was coldest, but only 4°C in March (−3 versus −7).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it compares snow-covered soil with the air, not with cleared soil, so it does not show when the snow's insulating effect was strongest.
explanation.B: Correct. The snow made the biggest difference in the coldest month and a much smaller one in the mildest, which is what Petrov concluded.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it never compares snow-covered soil with cleared soil, so it cannot show when the snow's insulating effect was strongest.
explanation.D: Incorrect. In March the difference was only 4°C, the smallest of any month, so this misreads the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Plants of the same species can look quite different depending on where they grow. On windy hilltops, for example, they tend to be shorter and have thicker stems than plants in sheltered valleys. Botanist Lena Fischer thinks the wind itself causes this difference. She hypothesizes that when a plant's stem is bent again and again, the plant responds by growing shorter and sturdier.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Fischer's hypothesis?

choices.A: Plants on windy hilltops produce fewer flowers than plants of the same species growing in valleys.
choices.B: Plants growing on windy hilltops are often damaged by strong storms during the winter.
choices.C: Indoor plants bent gently each day grew shorter and thicker than identical plants left alone.
choices.D: Valley soils hold more water than hilltop soils, which allows valley plants to grow taller.

explanation.why: Fischer's hypothesis is that repeated bending of the stem causes plants to grow shorter and sturdier. The strongest support would be a test in which bending is the only difference between two groups of plants. If the bent plants turn out shorter and thicker, bending is shown to cause the change.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Flower numbers have nothing to do with stem bending, height, or thickness.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Storm damage is a different effect of weather and says nothing about how bending changes growth.
explanation.C: Correct. Bending was the only difference between the two groups, and the bent plants grew shorter and thicker, just as Fischer predicts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This offers a different cause (water in the soil) for the height difference, so it would weaken the hypothesis rather than support it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the mid-1800s, trips to the seaside became common among British factory workers for the first time. Historian Kwame Asante argues that the main cause was cheap railway fares rather than rising wages. In his view, many workers could already afford a day away from work, but they had no affordable way to reach the coast until trains made the journey short and inexpensive.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Asante's argument?

choices.A: Where cheap trains to the coast already ran, workers' seaside trips became common only after wages rose.
choices.B: Seaside trips by workers increased sharply in towns soon after cheap train service to the coast began.
choices.C: Wealthy families had visited seaside resorts for many decades before railway lines reached the coast.
choices.D: Many seaside towns built new hotels and piers to attract the large numbers of visitors who arrived by train.

explanation.why: Asante claims that cheap trains, not higher wages, made seaside trips common. A finding weakens this if it shows that trains were not enough on their own and that wages made the difference. If trips stayed rare where cheap trains already ran and grew only once wages rose, wages look like the main cause.
explanation.A: Correct. Cheap trains were available but trips did not become common until wages rose, which points to wages, not fares, as the main cause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Trips rising right after cheap trains arrived would support Asante's argument, not weaken it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The argument is about factory workers; the habits of wealthy families do not bear on it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How resorts responded to visitors says nothing about whether fares or wages caused workers to travel.

items.subject: science
items.passage: House sparrows were once a familiar sight in South Asian cities, but residents of some neighborhoods in Karachi say they now see far fewer of them than in the past. Ornithologist Farah Siddiqui suspects that the main cause is a shortage of places to nest. Older houses had gaps under roofs and holes in walls where sparrows built their nests, whereas the smooth concrete and glass of newer buildings offer few such spaces.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Siddiqui's hypothesis?

choices.A: Sparrows in Karachi feed mainly on seeds and insects found in gardens and markets.
choices.B: Sparrow numbers fell by similar amounts in neighborhoods of older houses and in neighborhoods of new buildings.
choices.C: Several other bird species have also become less common in Karachi in recent decades.
choices.D: Sparrow numbers rose in an area after nest boxes were added to its new buildings but not in nearby areas.

explanation.why: Siddiqui's hypothesis is that sparrows declined because newer buildings offer few places to nest. If adding nesting places brings sparrows back in one area but not in similar areas without them, then a lack of nest sites was holding their numbers down. That is direct support.
explanation.A: Incorrect. What sparrows eat is unrelated to the hypothesis, which is about nesting sites.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If old houses with many nesting gaps lost sparrows just as fast, nest sites would not explain the decline; this weakens the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Declines in other species could have many causes and do not show that sparrows lack nesting places.
explanation.D: Correct. Providing nest sites raised sparrow numbers only where they were added, which points to a shortage of nest sites as the cause.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When two languages come into close contact, speakers often borrow words from each other. Linguist Ngozi Eze has studied a coastal town where speakers of two languages have traded with each other for generations. She hypothesizes that the words most likely to be borrowed are those for things that were new to one community when the contact began, such as unfamiliar tools or foods, rather than words for familiar everyday ideas.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Eze's hypothesis?

choices.A: Speakers in the town use borrowed words more often when talking with traders than with family.
choices.B: Most borrowed words in the town name tools and foods that one group first encountered through trade.
choices.C: Words for body parts and family members are among the most often borrowed words in the town.
choices.D: Both languages spoken in the town have also borrowed many words from a third language used in schools.

explanation.why: Eze predicts that borrowed words will mostly name things that were new to one group when contact began, not familiar everyday ideas. A finding that most borrowings name tools and foods one group first met through trade matches this prediction exactly.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This concerns when people use borrowed words, not which kinds of words get borrowed.
explanation.B: Correct. Tools and foods first encountered through trade are exactly the "new" things Eze predicts will be borrowed most.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Body parts and family members are familiar everyday ideas, so heavy borrowing of these words would weaken the hypothesis.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Borrowing from a third language does not show which kinds of words the two trading communities borrow from each other.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Many nineteenth-century novels first reached readers in monthly installments, each containing several chapters. Literary scholar Henrik Lund argues that authors writing for this format deliberately shaped their stories around the installment breaks, saving moments of suspense for the end of each part so that readers would buy the next one. As evidence, Lund notes that in the serialized novels he examined, chapters that closed an installment ended on an unresolved situation far more often than chapters that fell in the middle of an installment did.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Lund's argument?

choices.A: Editors, not authors, chose where most installments would end, after each book was fully written.
choices.B: Readers of the period often discussed the latest installments of novels with friends and in letters to magazines.
choices.C: Authors' letters show that they planned in advance which chapter would close each installment of their novels.
choices.D: A few chapters in the middle of installments also ended on unresolved situations in some of the novels.

explanation.why: Lund's claim is about the authors' intentions: they deliberately placed suspense at the breaks. His evidence is a pattern (suspenseful endings cluster at breaks). If editors set the breaks after the books were written, authors could not have aimed suspense at them; the pattern would instead come from editors choosing suspenseful spots to cut. That offers another explanation for his evidence and undercuts his claim.
explanation.A: Correct. If the breaks were chosen by editors after the writing was done, the authors could not have shaped their stories around them, so the pattern Lund found has a different explanation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Readers' discussions show interest in the installments but say nothing about whether authors planned suspense around the breaks.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Authors planning the breaks in advance makes Lund's argument more likely, so this would support it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Lund says suspense came "far more often" at installment ends, not only there, so a few suspenseful mid-installment chapters fit his evidence.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Octopuses alternate between two states of sleep. In "quiet" sleep they are pale and still, but during brief bouts of "active" sleep their skin flickers through patterns of color and texture, and their eyes and arms twitch. Neuroscientist Aiko Tanabe hypothesizes that active sleep in octopuses serves a function similar to one proposed for dreaming in mammals: the strengthening of memories of recent experience. If so, she reasons, the skin patterns produced during active sleep should not be random but should reflect what the animal did while awake.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Tanabe's hypothesis?

choices.A: Octopuses kept from active sleep for one night spent more time in active sleep the following night.
choices.B: The skin patterns that appeared during active sleep showed no relationship to the octopuses' waking activities.
choices.C: Patterns an octopus displayed in active sleep closely matched those it had used while hunting or hiding that day.
choices.D: Researchers have also observed a similar active sleep state in cuttlefish, which are close relatives of octopuses.

explanation.why: Tanabe's hypothesis makes a specific prediction: if active sleep strengthens memories of recent experience, the sleep patterns should reflect what the octopus did while awake. A finding that sleep patterns matched the octopus's patterns from earlier that day confirms this prediction directly.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Making up for lost active sleep suggests that active sleep matters to octopuses, but it does not show that it involves recent experience.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If the patterns had no link to waking activity, Tanabe's prediction would fail; this weakens her hypothesis.
explanation.C: Correct. Sleep patterns that match the day's hunting and hiding patterns are exactly the link to waking experience that Tanabe predicts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Finding active sleep in another species says nothing about what the octopus's sleep patterns reflect.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The sixteenth-century ruler Sher Shah Suri is remembered for the sarais, or roadside rest houses, that he built along the great road running across northern South Asia. Because the sarais offered free food and lodging to travelers, they are usually described as an investment in commerce. Historian Saad Hashmi contends, however, that commerce was at most a secondary concern: in his view, the sarais were placed chiefly to serve the relays of horses that carried official news and orders, and whatever benefit merchants gained followed from, rather than motivated, the choice of where to build them.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Hashmi's claim?

choices.A: Merchants traveling the road in that period often stayed at the sarais and praised the hospitality they found there.
choices.B: Sarais stood far closer together along busy market routes than along stretches that only the relays used.
choices.C: Horses for the relays that carried official news were kept at nearly every sarai along the road.
choices.D: Rulers who came after Sher Shah Suri built additional sarais specifically to encourage trade along the road.

explanation.why: Hashmi's claim is about motive, shown through placement: the sarais were located to serve the news relays, and merchants benefited only as a side effect. To weaken it, a finding must show that placement followed trade rather than the relays. If sarais were packed densely where markets were busy but sparse where only the relays ran, commerce, not the relays, appears to have guided where they were built.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Hashmi already grants that merchants benefited; he argues only that this benefit did not decide where sarais were built.
explanation.B: Correct. Placement that tracks trade routes rather than relay routes shows commerce shaping where sarais went, which contradicts Hashmi's claim.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Relay horses at nearly every sarai fits Hashmi's view that the sarais served the relays, so this would support him.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Later rulers' reasons for building sarais do not reveal why Sher Shah Suri placed his where he did.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In several Paleolithic caves in France and Spain, researchers have reported that painted images tend to cluster at spots where sound resonates or echoes strongly. Archaeologist Céline Marchand argues that the artists sought out these spots deliberately, perhaps because echoes held ritual significance for them. Skeptics point out, however, that resonance is strongest in narrow passages and small chambers, and that such spaces also offer the smooth, sheltered rock surfaces best suited to painting; on this view, the clustering could arise even if the artists paid no attention to sound at all.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Marchand's argument?

choices.A: In the caves studied, images appear far more often in narrow passages and small chambers than in large open halls.
choices.B: Many painted surfaces in the caves are smoother and better protected from moisture than nearby unpainted ones.
choices.C: Echoes are described as important in the ceremonies of several present-day societies that live near caves.
choices.D: Artists chose resonant spots far more often than nonresonant ones whose rock surfaces were equally suitable.

explanation.why: Marchand says artists chose resonant spots because of the sound. The skeptics offer another explanation: resonant spots also have the best painting surfaces, so the pattern might have nothing to do with sound. Support for Marchand must rule out that explanation by comparing spots whose surfaces are equally good. If artists still preferred the resonant ones, sound itself seems to have guided their choice.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Narrow passages and small chambers have both strong resonance and good surfaces, so this pattern fits the skeptics' explanation just as well as Marchand's.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Painted surfaces being smoother and more sheltered points to surface quality as the reason for the choice, which supports the skeptics instead.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The customs of present-day societies do not show what Paleolithic artists were thinking when they chose where to paint.
explanation.D: Correct. Because surface quality is held equal, the skeptics' explanation cannot account for the preference, so attention to sound, which is Marchand's claim, becomes the best explanation.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Gray squirrels bury thousands of nuts each fall, placing them one at a time in separate spots scattered across a wide area. Months later, during the winter, they dig many of them up again. Biologist Rosa Delgado thinks squirrels find these nuts mainly by remembering where they buried them, not simply by sniffing out any buried nut that happens to be nearby.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Delgado's hypothesis?

choices.A: Squirrels dug up far more of their own buried nuts than nuts that researchers had buried nearby in similar spots.
choices.B: Squirrels dug up nuts that researchers had buried nearby just as often as the nuts they had buried themselves.
choices.C: Squirrels bury more nuts in years when oak and hickory trees produce especially large crops of acorns and nuts.
choices.D: Many of the buried nuts that squirrels never dig up later sprout in the spring and grow into new trees.

explanation.why: Delgado says squirrels rely on memory of their own hiding spots rather than on smell alone. If smell were enough, a squirrel would find any nearby nut equally well. A finding that squirrels recover their own nuts far more often than similar nuts buried by someone else points to memory.
explanation.A: Correct. The researchers' nuts smelled just as much like nuts, so finding mostly their own shows the squirrels remembered where they had dug.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Finding other nuts just as often suggests smell, not memory, is doing the work, so this would weaken the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. How many nuts squirrels bury says nothing about how they find them again.
explanation.D: Incorrect. What happens to forgotten nuts does not show whether the recovered ones were found by memory or by smell.

items.subject: history_social
