items.passage: In Mumbai, India, workers known as dabbawalas deliver around 200,000 home-cooked lunches to offices every working day, and very few boxes ever go to the wrong place. Many dabbawalas have had little schooling and do not read long written addresses. Researcher Priya Kulkarni argues that the system works so well mainly because of a short code of colors, letters, and numbers painted on each lunch box, which tells every worker where the box must go next.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kulkarni's argument?

choices.A: Dabbawalas usually travel between neighborhoods on Mumbai's crowded suburban trains, carrying dozens of boxes at once.
choices.B: In a trial, boxes marked only with full written addresses were misdelivered far more often than coded boxes.
choices.C: Many office workers in Mumbai say that they prefer home-cooked lunches to meals bought from nearby restaurants.
choices.D: In a trial, boxes with missing codes reached the right offices just as often as boxes with complete codes.

explanation.why: Kulkarni credits the painted code for the system's accuracy. To support her, a finding should show that accuracy depends on the code. If boxes without the code but with full addresses are misdelivered much more often, the code is clearly what keeps deliveries correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. How dabbawalas travel does not show what keeps the boxes going to the right place.
explanation.B: Correct. When the code was replaced by written addresses, mistakes rose sharply, which shows the code is what makes the system accurate.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Why customers like home-cooked food has nothing to do with how the boxes are sorted.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If boxes without codes did just as well, the code would not matter, so this would weaken the argument.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Folktales often change as they pass from one storyteller to another. Folklorist Amara Nwosu has been studying a West African tale in which a clever hare outwits a shark along the seashore. She proposes that storytellers adapt such tales to their own surroundings, keeping the basic plot but changing details so that the story takes place somewhere their listeners know well.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nwosu's proposal?

choices.A: The tale about the hare is among the oldest stories still told in the coastal villages that Nwosu visited.
choices.B: Storytellers in inland villages tell the tale with the same seashore setting that coastal storytellers use.
choices.C: In inland versions, the hare outwits a crocodile at a riverbank instead of a shark at the sea.
choices.D: Many listeners in the villages Nwosu visited said they enjoy tales about clever animals more than other tales.

explanation.why: Nwosu predicts that the plot stays the same while the setting shifts to match each storyteller's surroundings. Inland villages are far from the sea, so her idea predicts that their versions would replace the sea with something local. A version with the same plot set at a river does exactly that.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The age of the tale does not show whether storytellers change its details to fit where they live.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If inland storytellers keep the seashore setting, the tale is not being adapted to their surroundings, so this would weaken the proposal.
explanation.C: Correct. The plot stays the same, but the setting and animal change to match an inland landscape, just as Nwosu proposes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Listeners' favorite kinds of tales say nothing about how storytellers change a tale's details.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many songbirds that live in cities sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species living in quiet forests. Ecologist Johan Lindqvist suspects that city birds raise their pitch so that their songs can be heard over the low rumble of traffic. He also thinks that individual birds can adjust their pitch from moment to moment, depending on how noisy their surroundings are.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's hypothesis?

choices.A: City songbirds often begin singing earlier in the morning than forest songbirds of the same species do.
choices.B: City birds living beside quiet parks sang at the same high pitch as city birds living beside busy roads.
choices.C: City songbirds tend to build their nests higher off the ground than forest songbirds of the same species.
choices.D: Individual city birds sang at a higher pitch during noisy rush hours than during quiet weekend mornings.

explanation.why: Lindqvist links high pitch to traffic noise and says each bird can change its pitch as the noise level changes. The best support would show the same birds singing higher when it is noisy and lower when it is quiet.
explanation.A: Incorrect. When birds start singing is a different question from what pitch they use.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If birds near quiet parks sing just as high as birds near busy roads, noise does not seem to matter, so this would weaken the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nest height has nothing to do with the pitch of the birds' songs.
explanation.D: Correct. The same birds sang higher when traffic was loud and lower when it was quiet, which shows them adjusting their pitch to the noise.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Many medieval cathedrals in Europe took more than a century to finish, and work on them often stopped for years at a time. Historian Claire Moreau argues that these long pauses happened mainly because the people in charge of building ran out of money, not because of wars or other outside events.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Moreau's argument?

choices.A: Building records show that work usually stopped when wars broke out, even while donations kept arriving.
choices.B: Building records show that work usually stopped soon after the money collected for construction was spent.
choices.C: Many medieval cathedrals have stained-glass windows showing stories that were familiar to local people.
choices.D: Some skilled builders traveled from city to city, working on several cathedrals during their careers.

explanation.why: Moreau claims the pauses came mainly from a lack of money rather than from wars. A finding weakens her if it shows work stopping because of war at times when money was still available.
explanation.A: Correct. Work stopped during wars even though donations kept coming in, so a lack of money cannot explain these pauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Work stopping when the money ran out fits Moreau's argument, so this would support it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The windows' subjects say nothing about why construction stopped.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Builders moving between cities does not show what caused the long pauses.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In parts of Sri Lanka, wild Asian elephants sometimes wander onto farms and eat the crops. Some farmers have begun hanging beehives along the fences around their fields, and elephants seem to stay away from these fences. Wildlife biologist Nirmala Perera thinks the elephants avoid the fences because they are frightened by the sound of buzzing bees.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Perera's hypothesis?

choices.A: Elephants in Sri Lanka raid farms most often during dry months, when wild food is hard to find.
choices.B: Elephants walked away when researchers played recordings of buzzing bees but not recordings of wind.
choices.C: Fences with beehives cost farmers less to build and repair than electric fences do.
choices.D: Elephants stayed away just as often from fences hung with empty hive boxes that made no sound.

explanation.why: Perera's hypothesis is specifically about sound: elephants avoid the fences because buzzing frightens them. The best support would show elephants reacting to the buzzing itself and not to other sounds.
explanation.A: Incorrect. When elephants raid farms does not explain why they avoid the beehive fences.
explanation.B: Correct. The elephants left only when they heard bees, not when they heard another sound, so the buzzing itself seems to scare them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The cost of the fences says nothing about why elephants avoid them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If silent, empty hives work just as well, the buzzing cannot be the reason, so this would weaken the hypothesis.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Willa Cather spent much of her childhood in the small prairie town of Red Cloud, Nebraska. Her novel My Ántonia (1918) follows Jim Burden, who grows up on the Nebraska prairie alongside Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of a family of immigrants from Bohemia. Literary scholar Tomás Herrera argues that many of the novel's characters were based on real people Cather knew in Red Cloud, rather than being entirely invented.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Herrera's argument?

choices.A: My Ántonia sold well when it first appeared and is now often taught in American literature classes.
choices.B: Cather once wrote that she had always avoided basing characters on people she had actually met.
choices.C: Cather's letters describe a Red Cloud neighbor whose life closely matches the life of the character Ántonia.
choices.D: Several of Cather's other novels are also set on the prairie and describe the hard work of farming there.

explanation.why: Herrera claims that Cather drew her characters from real people in Red Cloud. The strongest support would link a specific character to a specific person Cather knew there.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The novel's sales and its place in classrooms say nothing about where its characters came from.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Cather saying she avoided real people as models would weaken Herrera's argument, not support it.
explanation.C: Correct. A real neighbor whose life matches Ántonia's is direct evidence that at least one major character was based on someone Cather knew.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This concerns the setting of other novels, not whether this novel's characters were based on real people.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Arctic foxes grow a thick white coat each fall and change to a thinner brown or gray coat in the spring. Zoologist Ingrid Solberg hypothesizes that the main signal that starts the change to a white coat is the shortening of the days in fall, not the drop in temperature that comes at the same time of year.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Solberg's hypothesis?

choices.A: Foxes kept in a warm room under shortening days still grew their white coats at the usual time.
choices.B: A thick white coat both keeps a fox warm and helps hide it from its prey against the snow.
choices.C: Arctic foxes sometimes follow polar bears in winter to feed on what is left of the bears' meals.
choices.D: Foxes kept in a cold room with long, summer-length days still grew their white coats at the usual time.

explanation.why: Solberg says shorter days, not colder weather, are the main trigger for the white coat. To weaken her, a finding should show the coat changing without shorter days. If foxes in long days but cold air still turn white, cold alone seems to be enough.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Foxes turning white with short days but no cold fits Solberg's hypothesis, so this would support it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This explains why a white coat is useful, not what signal starts the change.
explanation.C: Incorrect. How foxes find food in winter has nothing to do with what triggers the coat change.
explanation.D: Correct. The days never got shorter, yet the foxes turned white in the cold, which suggests temperature, not day length, triggers the change.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the last years of his life, the French painter Claude Monet suffered from cataracts, a condition that clouds the lens of the eye and can make colors look dull and yellowish. His late paintings of his garden show blurred shapes and strong reddish and brownish tones. Art historian Elena Ruiz argues that these features were caused by his failing eyesight rather than by a deliberate change in his style.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ruiz's argument?

choices.A: Paintings Monet made years before his eyesight began to fail already show the same blurred shapes and reddish tones.
choices.B: Monet complained in letters that he could no longer tell some colors apart as his cataracts grew worse.
choices.C: Monet's late paintings of his garden include some of the largest canvases he ever produced.
choices.D: Many visitors traveled to Monet's home at Giverny to see the garden that appears in his paintings.

explanation.why: Ruiz says Monet's late blurring and reddish colors came from his cataracts. If the same features appear in paintings made while his eyes were still healthy, his eyesight cannot be what produced them, which weakens her argument.
explanation.A: Correct. The same features appear before his eyesight failed, so they are more likely a choice of style than a result of cataracts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Monet's trouble seeing colors fits Ruiz's argument, so this would support it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The size of the canvases says nothing about why the shapes are blurred or the colors reddish.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Visitors to the garden have nothing to do with the cause of the paintings' features.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Along the coast of Kerala, India, fishers sell their catch at beach markets. Before the late 1990s, a boat usually landed at its nearest market, so on the same day fish could be very expensive at one market and very cheap at another. Economist Arjun Menon argues that mobile phones made prices more even, because fishers still at sea could call several markets and then sail to the one paying the most.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Menon's argument?

choices.A: After mobile phones arrived, many fishers also began using them to talk with their families while at sea.
choices.B: After mobile phones arrived, boats often sailed past their nearest market to sell at one paying more.
choices.C: Before mobile phones arrived, some markets sold fish caught by boats from several different villages.
choices.D: After mobile phones arrived, nearly every boat still landed at its nearest market, just as before.

explanation.why: Menon's explanation depends on a change in behavior: with phones, fishers chose the best-paying market instead of the nearest one. A finding that boats really did start sailing past their nearest market to sell elsewhere supports that explanation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Calling family members does not show that phones changed where fishers sold their catch.
explanation.B: Correct. This shows fishers using information to choose the higher-paying market, which is exactly how Menon says prices became more even.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This describes markets before phones and says nothing about how phones changed prices.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If boats kept landing at the nearest market, phones did not change where fish were sold, so this would weaken the argument.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a group of meerkats searches for food in the Kalahari Desert, one animal often climbs onto a rock or bush and keeps watch for eagles and jackals while the others dig. Biologist Hannah Botha hypothesizes that a meerkat takes on this guard role mainly when it has already eaten enough, so that it can afford to stop feeding for a while.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Botha's hypothesis?

choices.A: Meerkats live in groups that can include more than twenty animals.
choices.B: Meerkats that researchers gave extra food stood guard no more often than meerkats given no extra food.
choices.C: Meerkats that researchers gave extra food stood guard more often than meerkats given no extra food.
choices.D: A meerkat on guard gives one alarm call for eagles and a different one for jackals.

explanation.why: Botha links guarding to how full a meerkat is. If her hypothesis is right, meerkats that have eaten more should guard more often. A test in which well-fed meerkats guard more than others would support her.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The size of meerkat groups does not show when an individual chooses to stand guard.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If extra food made no difference, being well fed would not explain guarding, so this would weaken the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Correct. The meerkats given extra food guarded more often, which shows that being well fed leads to taking the guard role.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The kinds of alarm calls describe what guards do, not why a meerkat becomes a guard.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Great Zimbabwe, a city known for its massive stone walls, was the center of a powerful state in southern Africa from about 1200 to 1450 CE. Archaeologist Thandiwe Moyo argues that much of the city's wealth came from long-distance trade, in which gold from the region was carried to ports on the East African coast and exchanged for goods from distant lands.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Moyo's argument?

choices.A: The stone walls of Great Zimbabwe were built without mortar, using carefully shaped blocks of granite.
choices.B: Many families living near Great Zimbabwe grew crops such as sorghum and kept herds of cattle.
choices.C: Excavations at Great Zimbabwe have found almost no objects that were made outside the surrounding region.
choices.D: Excavations at Great Zimbabwe have uncovered glass beads from Persia and pieces of pottery from China.

explanation.why: Moyo claims the city grew rich through trade that reached faraway lands. Objects made in distant places, found at the site itself, would show that such trade really reached Great Zimbabwe.
explanation.A: Incorrect. How the walls were built says nothing about where the city's wealth came from.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Local farming describes everyday life near the city, not long-distance trade.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If almost nothing at the site came from outside the region, there is little sign of long-distance trade, so this would weaken the argument.
explanation.D: Correct. Goods from Persia and China at the site are direct evidence that Great Zimbabwe was connected to long-distance trade.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Bread left out on a kitchen counter turns hard within a few days. Baker Liam O'Connor claims that bread goes stale mainly because water escapes from the loaf into the surrounding air, leaving the inside of the bread dry. For that reason, he tells his customers to keep their loaves tightly wrapped at all times.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken O'Connor's claim?

choices.A: Loaves left unwrapped on the counter lost water and also became hard within a few days.
choices.B: Loaves sealed in airtight bags lost almost no water but became hard just as quickly as unwrapped loaves.
choices.C: Bread made with extra sugar or butter usually stays soft for a day or two longer than plain bread.
choices.D: Many of O'Connor's customers prefer to buy fresh bread every day rather than store it at home.

explanation.why: O'Connor says bread hardens mainly because it loses water. If bread that keeps almost all its water still hardens just as fast, water loss cannot be the main cause, so that finding weakens his claim.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Unwrapped loaves losing water and hardening fits O'Connor's claim, so this would support it.
explanation.B: Correct. The sealed loaves kept their water but still went stale at the same speed, so something other than water loss must be the main cause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is about ingredients, not about whether losing water is what makes bread stale.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Customers' shopping habits do not show why bread becomes hard.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Kantha is a style of embroidery from Bangladesh and eastern India in which several layers of old cotton saris are stitched together with rows of small running stitches. Today many kantha quilts are richly decorated with flowers, animals, and scenes from daily life. Textile historian Farida Rahman argues that kantha began mainly as a practical way to reuse worn cloth, and that its decoration developed later.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Rahman's argument?

choices.A: The oldest surviving kanthas are made of worn, patched cloth and have very little decoration.
choices.B: Today, kantha quilts are sold in shops around the world and are popular with collectors.
choices.C: The oldest surviving kanthas are covered with detailed scenes stitched in many different colors.
choices.D: Running stitches are also used in many other embroidery traditions in different parts of Asia.

explanation.why: Rahman says kantha started as a plain, practical craft and became decorative only later. The oldest examples are the best test: if they are mostly patched, worn cloth with little decoration, her account is supported.
explanation.A: Correct. The earliest kanthas are practical and plain, which fits the idea that decoration came later.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Kantha's popularity today says nothing about how the craft began.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Richly decorated early kanthas would suggest decoration was there from the start, so this would weaken the argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The use of running stitches elsewhere does not show why kantha began.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Chameleons are famous for their ability to change color. In a popular book about animals, nature writer Paolo Ricci claims that a chameleon changes color mainly to match whatever it happens to be sitting on, so that predators passing by cannot see it. He describes the chameleon as a living camouflage that copies the colors around it.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ricci's claim?

choices.A: Chameleons placed on a bright green leaf turned green within a few minutes.
choices.B: Chameleons catch insects by shooting out a sticky tongue that can be longer than their bodies.
choices.C: Chameleons placed on green, brown, and gray backgrounds stayed the same color on all three.
choices.D: Many species of chameleon live only on Madagascar, an island off the southeastern coast of Africa.

explanation.why: Ricci says chameleons change color mainly to match their surroundings. If chameleons put on very different backgrounds do not change color at all, matching the background cannot be the main reason they change, so that finding weakens his claim.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A chameleon turning green on a green leaf fits Ricci's claim, so this would support it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. How chameleons catch food has nothing to do with why they change color.
explanation.C: Correct. The chameleons did not change to match any of the three backgrounds, which goes against the idea that they change color to blend in.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Where chameleons live does not show why they change color.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Some orb-weaving spiders add bright zigzag bands of silk, called decorations, to the centers of their webs. Because spinning these bands costs the spider both silk and energy, biologists have long asked what purpose they serve. Arachnologist Mei-Ling Chou argues that their main purpose is to warn birds: a bird that notices the bright bands can swerve away in time instead of flying straight through the web and destroying it.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Chou's argument?

choices.A: Decorated webs are built most often by spiders that hunt during the day, when birds are most active.
choices.B: Orb-weaving spiders often eat their old webs and reuse the silk to spin new ones.
choices.C: Some spider species add decorations to their webs only while the spiders are young.
choices.D: Birds flew through webs with decorations just as often as through similar webs without them.

explanation.why: Chou claims the decorations exist mainly to keep birds from flying into webs. If that were true, decorated webs should be hit by birds less often. A finding that birds hit decorated and undecorated webs equally often shows the decorations are not doing that job, which weakens her argument.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Decorations being most common where birds are active fits Chou's argument, so this would support it rather than weaken it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Reusing silk explains how spiders save material, not what the decorations are for.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Knowing that only young spiders of some species decorate does not show whether decorations warn birds.
explanation.D: Correct. If decorations did not reduce how often birds broke through webs, they cannot be serving mainly as a warning to birds.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1291, the government of Venice ordered the city's glassmakers to move their furnaces to Murano, a small island nearby. The official reason was safety: Venice was crowded with wooden buildings, and glass furnaces could easily start fires. Historian Paolo Benedetti, however, argues that the order was mainly meant to protect the city's valuable glassmaking methods by gathering the craftsmen in one place where they could be closely watched.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Benedetti's argument?

choices.A: Glassmakers who moved to Murano were forbidden to leave Venetian lands or to teach their methods to outsiders.
choices.B: Several serious fires had broken out in Venice in the decades before the glassmakers were ordered to move.
choices.C: Glass made on Murano became famous and was sold to wealthy buyers in cities across Europe.
choices.D: In the centuries after the move, Murano glassmakers developed new kinds of especially clear glass.

explanation.why: Benedetti's claim is about the government's motive: keeping glassmaking secrets inside Venice, rather than preventing fires. Rules that stopped the glassmakers from leaving or sharing their methods would show that controlling the craftsmen and their knowledge was a central aim.
explanation.A: Correct. Forbidding glassmakers to leave or to teach outsiders shows that the government was focused on keeping their methods from spreading.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Earlier fires would make the official safety reason more believable, which works against Benedetti's argument.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Murano glass becoming famous shows the craft was valuable but not why the glassmakers were moved.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Later improvements in glassmaking do not reveal the government's reason for the move in 1291.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In Ladakh, a high, dry region of northern India, villages depend on meltwater from glaciers to water their fields in spring, but many of the glaciers there are shrinking. Some villages now build "ice stupas": tall cones of ice made in winter by spraying stream water into the freezing air. Engineer Stanzin Dolma argues that the cone shape is what lets this ice last into late spring, because a cone exposes much less of its surface to direct sunlight than a flat sheet of ice holding the same amount of water.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Dolma's argument?

choices.A: Ladakh receives very little rain or snow, so its farmers have long relied on melting glacier ice.
choices.B: At the same site, ice cones lasted several weeks longer than flat sheets of ice made from equal amounts of water.
choices.C: At the same site, flat sheets of ice lasted just as long as ice cones made from equal amounts of water.
choices.D: Ice stupas built at higher, colder sites lasted longer than ice stupas built lower in the same valleys.

explanation.why: Dolma credits the shape of the ice, not just the cold, for how long it lasts. A fair test would compare a cone and a flat sheet with the same amount of water in the same place, so that only the shape differs. If the cones last much longer, shape is shown to matter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This explains why villages need meltwater, not why cone-shaped ice lasts longer.
explanation.B: Correct. Only the shape differed between the two kinds of ice, and the cones lasted weeks longer, just as Dolma predicts.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If flat sheets lasted just as long, the cone shape would not matter, so this would weaken the argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This shows that colder sites help the ice last, which is about location and temperature, not about the cone shape.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In recent decades, the instrumental introductions of popular songs have grown much shorter, and many hit songs now reach the singer's voice within a few seconds. Musicologist Daniel Okafor links this change to music streaming services, which typically count a song as played only if a listener stays with it for about thirty seconds. He argues that songwriters began shortening their intros so that listeners would not skip ahead before reaching that point.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Okafor's argument?

choices.A: On streaming services, listeners are most likely to skip a song during the first few seconds of its intro.
choices.B: Short intros have become common in songs written for films as well as in popular music.
choices.C: Most of the shortening of intros took place years before streaming services became widely used.
choices.D: Some popular songs released in recent years still begin with intros longer than thirty seconds.

explanation.why: Okafor claims streaming caused songwriters to shorten intros. A cause must come before its effect, so if most of the shortening had already happened before streaming was common, streaming cannot be the main cause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Listeners skipping during intros gives songwriters a reason to shorten them, so this fits Okafor's argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Short intros in film songs do not show what caused the change, so this neither confirms nor undercuts the streaming explanation.
explanation.C: Correct. If intros mostly shrank before streaming spread, the change must have had a different main cause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Okafor describes an overall trend; a few long intros today do not show that streaming was not behind the trend.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mary Shelley began writing Frankenstein (1818) in June 1816 near Lake Geneva in Switzerland. That summer was unusually cold and stormy across Europe, partly because a huge volcanic eruption in Indonesia the year before had filled the sky with ash. Literary scholar Inés Navarro argues that the strange weather of that summer directly shaped the bleak, icy, and storm-filled settings that dominate much of the novel.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Navarro's argument?

choices.A: The ghost-story contest that led Shelley to begin the novel was proposed by the poet Lord Byron, who was staying nearby.
choices.B: Frankenstein became much more widely known in the 1820s after it was adapted into a play for the London stage.
choices.C: Many novels written in warmer, calmer years of the period also feature bleak, icy, and storm-filled settings.
choices.D: Shelley's journal from that summer describes storms over the lake in words that closely match scenes in the novel.

explanation.why: Navarro claims the weather of summer 1816 directly shaped the novel's settings. The best support would connect what Shelley actually experienced that summer to what she wrote. Journal descriptions of the storms that closely match scenes in the book make that connection.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Who proposed the contest explains how the novel started, not where its stormy settings came from.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The novel's later fame on the stage says nothing about what shaped its settings.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If such settings were common in novels written in calm years, they may simply have been a fashion of the time, which would weaken Navarro's argument.
explanation.D: Correct. Matching language shows Shelley drawing on the storms she saw that summer when she wrote the novel's scenes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the Namib Desert of southwestern Africa, where rain almost never falls, some darkling beetles climb to the tops of sand dunes on foggy mornings. There they lean forward with their backs raised into the wind, and fog droplets gather on their bodies and roll down toward their mouths. Some researchers suspect this headstand mainly helps the beetles cool down, but ecologist Yusuf Adeyemi argues that its main purpose is to collect drinking water.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Adeyemi's argument?

choices.A: On clear mornings just as cool as foggy ones, the beetles almost never took the headstand position.
choices.B: Beetles in the headstand position lost body heat faster than beetles resting flat on the sand.
choices.C: The beetles' dark bodies warm up quickly once the sun rises higher over the dunes.
choices.D: Several other desert animals, including some lizards, also get water from fog in their own ways.

explanation.why: Two explanations compete: cooling and water collection. To favor Adeyemi's, a finding must separate them. Comparing mornings with the same temperature but with and without fog does this: if the beetles do the headstand only when there is fog to catch, water is the likely purpose.
explanation.A: Correct. With temperature held the same, the beetles did the headstand only when fog was present, which points to collecting water rather than cooling.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Losing heat faster in the headstand fits the cooling explanation, so this would favor the researchers Adeyemi disagrees with.
explanation.C: Incorrect. How fast the beetles warm in the sun does not show why they do the headstand on foggy mornings.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Other animals using fog says nothing about the purpose of this beetle's posture.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Although India was among the world's largest tea producers by 1900, most of its tea was shipped abroad, and relatively few people in India drank it. By the 1960s, however, tea had become an everyday drink across much of the country. Historian Kavita Raghunathan attributes this change chiefly to the advertising campaigns that tea companies ran in India beginning in the 1930s, which included free tea stalls at railway stations and demonstrations of how to brew it.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Raghunathan's claim?

choices.A: Tea companies spent more money on advertising in India during the 1930s than in any earlier decade.
choices.B: Tea drinking spread just as fast in regions the campaigns never reached as in regions where they were most active.
choices.C: Even in the 1960s, a large share of the tea grown in India was still being shipped to buyers abroad.
choices.D: Many railway passengers who were given free tea at station stalls had rarely tasted the drink before.

explanation.why: Raghunathan says advertising was the main reason tea drinking spread in India. If the campaigns mattered most, tea should have spread faster where they were active. Equal growth in places the campaigns never reached suggests something else drove the change.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Heavy spending shows the campaigns were large, which fits Raghunathan's claim rather than weakening it.
explanation.B: Correct. If tea spread equally fast without any advertising, the campaigns cannot have been the chief cause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Continued exports do not show what made people in India start drinking tea.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Passengers being new to tea shows the campaigns reached new drinkers, which fits the claim instead of weakening it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Common vampire bats feed only on blood, and a bat that fails to find a meal for two or three nights in a row can starve. A bat that has fed well will often bring up part of its meal to share with a hungry bat in its roost. Biologist Ewa Nowak hypothesizes that this sharing is directed mainly toward close relatives, since helping a relative survive helps pass on the genes the two bats share.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Nowak's hypothesis?

choices.A: Mother bats regularly shared food with their own young, even after the young had begun to hunt on their own.
choices.B: Bats that received shared food from a roost mate were more likely to survive the following week.
choices.C: Bats shared food with unrelated roost mates that had once fed them as often as they shared with relatives.
choices.D: Vampire bats spend more time grooming their roost mates than most other kinds of bats do.

explanation.why: Nowak says bats share food mainly with relatives. To weaken this, a finding must show bats sharing just as readily with bats that are not related to them. If unrelated bats that once helped them get food as often as relatives do, relatedness is not the main factor.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Mothers feeding their young is sharing with close relatives, so this fits Nowak's hypothesis.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This shows that sharing helps bats survive, not whom the bats choose to share with.
explanation.C: Correct. Unrelated bats received food as often as relatives, so sharing is not directed mainly toward kin.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Grooming is a different behavior and says nothing about who receives shared food.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the late 1970s and 1980s, deaf children in Nicaragua who were brought together at new schools began creating a sign language of their own, now known as Nicaraguan Sign Language. Over the following years, its grammar became more regular and complex. Linguist Sofia Marchetti argues that this growth came mainly from the youngest learners, who reshaped the signs they picked up from older students into a more systematic language.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Marchetti's argument?

choices.A: Signers who joined as young children used the newer grammar more consistently than teenage joiners with equal years of use.
choices.B: Students who joined the schools as teenagers were the first to create signs for many common objects and everyday actions.
choices.C: Signers who joined the schools as teenagers used the newer grammar just as consistently as those who joined as young children.
choices.D: Nicaraguan Sign Language is now used by thousands of deaf people living in towns and cities across the country.

explanation.why: Marchetti credits the youngest learners with making the grammar more systematic. Support would show that learners who started young use the newer grammar more than those who started older, with experience held equal, so that age of starting is what makes the difference.
explanation.A: Correct. With years of use held equal, those who started young used the newer grammar more consistently, which points to young learners as the source of the change.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Older students creating many of the first signs concerns vocabulary, not who made the grammar more regular, and it fits the passage's account that young learners picked up signs from older ones.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If age of joining made no difference, there would be no reason to credit the youngest learners, so this would weaken the argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How widely the language is used today does not show who shaped its grammar.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Over the past century, temperatures in the European Alps have risen, and many plant species there are now found growing higher up the mountains than they once did. Botanist Rafael Stein attributes this upward shift mainly to the warmer climate. Others point out that during the same period, many farmers stopped grazing cattle on high pastures, which may have let plants spread uphill once they were no longer being eaten.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Stein's claim?

choices.A: The upward shift has been greatest for plant species whose seeds are carried long distances by the wind.
choices.B: Plants moved uphill just as far on slopes where grazing never changed as on slopes where grazing stopped.
choices.C: Plants moved uphill mainly on slopes where cattle grazing stopped, with little change on other slopes.
choices.D: Temperatures in the Alps have risen faster over the past century than the average for the world as a whole.

explanation.why: Two causes are offered for the same change: warming and the end of grazing. Since warming affected every slope, support for Stein must rule out grazing. If plants moved uphill as much where grazing never changed, the end of grazing cannot explain the shift, leaving warming as the main cause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This explains which plants moved fastest, not whether warming or the end of grazing caused the move.
explanation.B: Correct. The shift happened just as much without any change in grazing, which points to the warmer climate as the main cause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A shift found mainly where grazing stopped points to grazing, not warming, so this would weaken Stein's claim.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The passage already says the Alps have warmed; how fast they warmed compared with the world does not separate warming from the end of grazing as the cause.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: During the bicycle craze of the 1890s, many women in the United States and Britain took up cycling. In the same decade, women's fashions began to change: skirts grew shorter, and some women adopted loose trousers called bloomers. Historian Grace Whitfield argues that cycling was the main force behind these changes, since long, heavy skirts could catch in a bicycle's chain and wheels.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Whitfield's argument?

choices.A: Newspapers of the 1890s printed many complaints from women about long skirts tangling in bicycle chains.
choices.B: Bicycles became much cheaper during the 1890s as factories began producing them in very large numbers.
choices.C: Some women who rode bicycles in the 1890s went on wearing long skirts while they cycled.
choices.D: Skirts grew shorter just as fast among women who never cycled as among women who cycled often.

explanation.why: Whitfield claims cycling was the main force behind shorter skirts. If cycling drove the change, it should show up first and most among women who cycled. A finding that skirts shortened just as fast among women who never cycled suggests a different main cause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Complaints about skirts catching in chains show the problem Whitfield describes, so this would support her.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Cheaper bicycles explain why cycling spread, not whether cycling changed fashion.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Whitfield calls cycling the main force, not the only one; a few cyclists keeping long skirts does not undercut that.
explanation.D: Correct. Non-cyclists changed their skirts just as quickly, so cycling cannot have been the main reason for the change.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Trees usually add a wide ring of wood in a good growing year and a narrow ring in a poor one, so scientists can use tree rings to study past climates. In one mountain forest in the western United States, the ponderosa pines show a series of unusually narrow rings from the 1840s. Dendrochronologist Nadia Petrov interprets these rings as evidence of a severe drought in the area during that decade.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Petrov's interpretation?

choices.A: Ponderosa pines in a forest about thirty kilometers away also show unusually narrow rings from the 1840s.
choices.B: The same pines show unusually wide rings in the 1850s, a decade known for plentiful rain in the area.
choices.C: Douglas firs growing among the pines, which also grow less in dry years, show normal rings for the 1840s.
choices.D: Bark beetles, which can slow the growth of the pines they attack, are found in many western forests.

explanation.why: Petrov reads the narrow pine rings as a sign of drought. A drought would affect every tree in the forest that is sensitive to dry weather, not just the pines. If drought-sensitive firs growing right beside the pines grew normally in the 1840s, something that affected only the pines is a likelier cause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Narrow rings in a nearby forest suggest a dry period across the area, which fits Petrov's interpretation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Wide rings in a rainy decade show that the trees respond to rainfall, which fits Petrov's method rather than weakening her reading of the 1840s.
explanation.C: Correct. A drought should have narrowed the firs' rings too; their normal growth suggests the pines were slowed by something other than drought.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Beetles being common in western forests does not show that they attacked these pines in the 1840s.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In a few communities around the world, people can "speak" by whistling, turning the words of their everyday language into whistled melodies that can be understood far away. One well-known example is Silbo Gomero, used on La Gomera in the Canary Islands, where steep, deep valleys separate many villages. Linguist Aylin Demir argues that whistled speech tends to develop where rugged land or thick forest makes it difficult to travel or to shout across distances.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Demir's argument?

choices.A: On La Gomera, Silbo Gomero is now taught in schools so that children continue to learn it.
choices.B: Skilled whistlers on La Gomera can express complete sentences, not just simple calls or signals.
choices.C: Several whistled languages are used in open, flat grasslands where villages lie close together.
choices.D: A worldwide survey found that nearly all known whistled languages are used in mountains or dense forests.

explanation.why: Demir makes a general claim about where whistled speech develops: in rugged or forested places. One example, La Gomera, cannot prove a general pattern. A survey showing that nearly all whistled languages are found in such places supports her claim across many cases.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Teaching Silbo Gomero in schools concerns keeping the language alive, not where whistled languages arise.
explanation.B: Incorrect. How much whistlers can express says nothing about the kinds of places where whistled speech develops.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Whistled languages in flat, open land with nearby villages would go against Demir's argument.
explanation.D: Correct. If nearly all whistled languages are found in mountains or forests, whistled speech does tend to develop in such places, as Demir argues.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Hundreds of thousands of people rushed to California after gold was discovered there in 1848. Because nearly everything had to be brought in from far away, prices in the mining camps were often many times higher than in the eastern United States. A few miners did strike it rich, but economic historian Lucía Ferreira argues that the people who profited most reliably were not miners but the merchants who sold them food, tools, and clothing.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's argument?

choices.A: A small number of miners found gold nuggets worth more than a typical worker could earn in several years.
choices.B: Records from mining towns show that most shopkeepers there earned more each year than most miners did.
choices.C: Many merchants in the mining towns went out of business within a year or two because of their high costs.
choices.D: Many people who came to California during the gold rush arrived by ship after long voyages around South America.

explanation.why: Ferreira compares two groups and says merchants profited more reliably than miners. The best support compares typical earnings of the two groups: if most shopkeepers earned more than most miners, merchants did better as a group.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A few lucky miners do not show which group profited more reliably, and Ferreira already grants that some miners struck it rich.
explanation.B: Correct. Comparing most shopkeepers with most miners shows that merchants usually earned more, which is Ferreira's point.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If many merchants failed quickly, their profits were not reliable, so this would weaken the argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How people traveled to California says nothing about who made the most money once they arrived.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: In 1893, Arthur Conan Doyle, tired of his famous detective, sent Sherlock Holmes over a waterfall in the story "The Final Problem." Readers were dismayed, yet a new story set after Holmes's apparent death did not appear until 1903. Literary historian Owen Adebayo argues that Doyle brought the detective back at that point mainly because a publisher offered him an unusually large sum of money, not because readers had protested.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Adebayo's argument?

choices.A: Doyle's letters from 1903 say he agreed to revive Holmes only after a magazine offered him a far larger fee.
choices.B: Readers sent Doyle many angry letters in the months after "The Final Problem" first appeared in a magazine.
choices.C: During the years without new Holmes stories, Doyle wrote several historical novels and a number of plays.
choices.D: Doyle wrote in his diary that he returned to Holmes because so many readers had begged him to do so.

explanation.why: Adebayo claims money, not readers' protests, was the main reason Doyle revived Holmes in 1903. The best support would link Doyle's decision directly to a large payment. Letters in which Doyle says he agreed only after a much larger fee was offered make that link.
explanation.A: Correct. Doyle's own words tie his decision to the larger fee, which is exactly the reason Adebayo gives.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Angry letters show that readers protested, which supports the explanation Adebayo rejects rather than his own.
explanation.C: Incorrect. What Doyle wrote in the meantime does not show why he chose to bring Holmes back.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Doyle saying readers' pleas brought him back would weaken Adebayo's argument.

items.subject: science
items.passage: For many years, a popular explanation held that zebras' black-and-white stripes help them escape lions. When a herd runs together, the idea went, the moving stripes blur into a confusing pattern, making it hard for a predator to pick out a single animal.
items.passage_b: Biologists testing the purpose of zebra stripes have found support for a different explanation. In one experiment, horses wearing striped coats had far fewer biting flies land on them than horses wearing plain coats. The researchers concluded that the stripes' main benefit is protection from these insects, which can spread disease.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation in Text 1?

choices.A: By suggesting that evidence points to a different main purpose for zebra stripes
choices.B: By agreeing that the main purpose of zebra stripes is to confuse lions
choices.C: By arguing that zebras are rarely hunted by lions or other predators
choices.D: By pointing out that biting flies are most common where lions live

explanation.why: Text 1 says stripes help zebras escape lions. Text 2 describes an experiment in which striped coats kept flies away and concludes that the stripes' "main benefit is protection from these insects." So the author of Text 2 would answer that the evidence supports a different purpose.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 presents experimental evidence that stripes mainly protect zebras from biting flies, a different explanation from the one in Text 1.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the main benefit is protection from insects, not from lions, so it would not agree.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about how often lions hunt zebras.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 never compares where biting flies and lions are found.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In Pakistan, many trucks are covered in brightly painted flowers, birds, and mountain scenes, along with lines of poetry and jingling metal chains. For drivers who may spend weeks on the road, a richly decorated truck is a source of pride and a kind of home.
items.passage_b: Pakistani truck art is also a major trade. Workshops in cities such as Karachi and Rawalpindi employ painters, metalworkers, and woodcarvers who may spend weeks decorating a single truck. Today these artists also paint the same designs on furniture and other objects that are sold to collectors around the world.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the description of truck art in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that truck art matters only as a business, not as a source of pride
choices.B: By adding that truck art is also an important source of work for skilled artists
choices.C: By claiming that truck art is found only in Karachi and Rawalpindi
choices.D: By noting that the designs on trucks were first created for furniture

explanation.why: Text 1 describes truck art from the drivers' point of view: it is "a source of pride." Text 2 adds another side, saying truck art "is also a major trade" that employs "painters, metalworkers, and woodcarvers." Text 2 builds on Text 1 rather than disagreeing with it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says truck art is "also" a trade, which adds to Text 1's point rather than denying that drivers take pride in it.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 adds that truck art provides work for painters, metalworkers, and woodcarvers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 names Karachi and Rawalpindi as examples ("cities such as"), not as the only places truck art is found.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says artists now paint truck designs on furniture, so the designs moved from trucks to furniture, not the other way around.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Norse settlers lived in Greenland from about 985 CE but had abandoned their farms by the mid-1400s. A common explanation is that they clung to European ways of life, raising cattle and sheep as the climate grew colder, and failed to adopt the hunting practices that allowed Inuit communities in the region to thrive.
items.passage_b: Chemical analysis of Norse skeletons from Greenland shows that, over the centuries, the settlers' diets came to rely heavily on seals and other marine animals. Archaeologist Hanne Sørlie argues that the settlers' departure is better explained by the falling value of walrus ivory, their main export to Europe, than by a refusal to change.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation in Text 1?

choices.A: By accepting it but adding that the settlers also exported walrus ivory
choices.B: By suggesting that the settlers left mainly because their farms could no longer feed them
choices.C: By questioning it, citing evidence that the settlers did change how they obtained food
choices.D: By arguing that a change in the settlers' diet caused them to abandon Greenland

explanation.why: Text 1 says the Norse "failed to adopt" new ways of getting food. Text 2 reports that their diets "came to rely heavily on seals and other marine animals" and that their departure is better explained by falling ivory prices "than by a refusal to change." So Text 2 doubts Text 1's explanation and offers evidence of adaptation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 does not accept Text 1's explanation; it says the departure is better explained by something other than "a refusal to change."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 does not blame failing farms; it points to the falling value of walrus ivory.
explanation.C: Correct. The evidence that settlers shifted toward eating seals challenges Text 1's claim that they failed to adapt.
explanation.D: Incorrect. In Text 2 the diet change is evidence that the settlers adapted, not the cause of their leaving; the cause it proposes is the falling value of ivory.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In one experiment, researchers played recorded sounds of bees' wings to evening primrose flowers. Within minutes, the sugar concentration of the flowers' nectar increased. The researchers suggest that the bowl-shaped petals vibrate in response to such sounds, allowing the plant to detect nearby pollinators and offer them a sweeter reward.
items.passage_b: Studies showing that plants react to sound are intriguing, but the word "hearing" can mislead. Plants have no nervous system, so any response must arise from cells physically disturbed by vibration. Moreover, a single experiment, however striking, needs to be repeated by other laboratories before biologists can be confident that the effect is real.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Plants hear sounds in much the same way that animals do.
choices.B: The evening primrose results have already been confirmed by other laboratories.
choices.C: Evening primrose nectar becomes sweeter when the flowers are exposed to bee sounds.
choices.D: Any response of plants to sound would depend on plant parts being physically moved.

explanation.why: Text 1 explains the flowers' response through petals that "vibrate in response to such sounds." Text 2 says any plant response "must arise from cells physically disturbed by vibration." Both authors connect a plant's reaction to sound with physical movement of its parts.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 warns that the word "hearing" can mislead because plants have no nervous system, so its author would not agree.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the experiment still "needs to be repeated by other laboratories," and Text 1 mentions no repetition.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 1 reports this result, but Text 2 says biologists cannot yet be "confident that the effect is real," so only one author clearly accepts it.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 1 relies on vibrating petals, and Text 2 says responses must come from cells "physically disturbed by vibration," so both would agree.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Iliad and the Odyssey are thick with repeated phrases, such as "swift-footed Achilles" and "rosy-fingered Dawn," that once struck readers as mere padding. In the 1930s, scholars who studied living oral poets in the Balkans showed that such stock phrases are the working tools of singers who compose as they perform, fitting ready-made units to the meter. The density of these formulas in Homer, the scholars concluded, is the signature of poetry composed without writing.
items.passage_b: That the Homeric poems emerged from a tradition of oral composition is now hard to dispute. What the formulas cannot establish is how the particular texts we possess came to be fixed. A singer trained in oral techniques might well have dictated a performance to a scribe, or even revised it in writing, without abandoning the formulaic style in which he had learned to think. The formulas tell us about the poet's training, not about the circumstances of the poems' final composition.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?

choices.A: By accepting that the formulas reflect an oral tradition while denying that they show how the surviving poems were composed
choices.B: By rejecting the idea that the Homeric poems have any connection to a tradition of oral composition
choices.C: By arguing that the formulas were inserted into the poems by the scribes who later copied them
choices.D: By agreeing that the poems were composed without writing while doubting that Balkan poets are a valid comparison

explanation.why: Text 2 grants that the poems "emerged from a tradition of oral composition," which accepts part of Text 1. But it says the formulas "cannot establish" how the surviving texts were fixed, since a poet trained orally might have dictated or revised in writing. So Text 2 accepts the oral tradition but rejects the step from formulas to "composed without writing."
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 agrees the formulas point to an oral tradition and the poet's "training" but denies that they reveal how the final texts were composed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 calls an oral tradition behind the poems "hard to dispute," so it does not reject that connection. This choice exaggerates its disagreement.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says scribes may have taken down a performance, not that scribes added the formulas.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 does not agree that the poems were composed without writing; that is exactly the conclusion it questions. It also never criticizes the Balkan comparison.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Because snow leopards are rarely seen, ecologists often count them with camera traps: motion-triggered cameras placed along the ridges and trails the cats use. Each leopard's spot pattern is unique, so researchers can tell individuals apart in the photographs. Using this method over one winter in a valley in Pakistan's Gilgit-Baltistan region, a team led by ecologist Sana Mirza identified nine adults and concluded that the valley supports a small but stable population.
items.passage_b: Camera-trap counts of snow leopards are valuable, but a single survey can say little about trends. As zoologist Arjun Thapa points out, photographs taken over a few months show which individuals were present during that time; they cannot reveal whether the population is growing, shrinking, or holding steady. Only surveys repeated over several years in the same area can support such a judgment.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?

choices.A: By doubting that the photographs could reliably tell individual leopards apart
choices.B: By arguing that the valley most likely contains more than nine adult leopards
choices.C: By accepting the count of individuals but questioning the claim that the population is stable
choices.D: By suggesting that the population's stability could be confirmed by a longer survey in another valley

explanation.why: Text 2 calls camera-trap counts "valuable" and says photographs show "which individuals were present," so it accepts the count. But it says a single survey "cannot reveal whether the population is growing, shrinking, or holding steady." Text 1's claim that the population is "stable" is exactly the kind of judgment Text 2 says needs repeated surveys.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 calls camera-trap counts "valuable" and does not question the use of spot patterns to identify individuals.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 does not say the count is too low; its concern is about trends over time, not the number of leopards.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 accepts what the photographs show about who was present but says one survey cannot show that a population is stable.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says only surveys repeated "in the same area" can support a judgment about trends, so a survey in another valley would not confirm this valley's stability.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Why did mechanized industry first take hold in eighteenth-century Britain? One influential answer is economic. British wages were high relative to the cost of capital and of coal, which was abundant and cheap. Under those conditions, machines that replaced costly labor with cheap energy were profitable to adopt in Britain, whereas the same machines, even if they had been available elsewhere, would not have repaid their cost in regions where labor was cheaper and fuel more expensive.
items.passage_b: Explanations grounded in relative prices are persuasive about why British manufacturers were eager to buy labor-saving machines; they are less persuasive about why such machines were invented and steadily improved there in the first place. Prices create an incentive, but an incentive does not by itself produce the tinkerers, instrument makers, and networks of correspondence through which technical knowledge was shared and refined. Those owed as much to a culture that prized practical experiment as to any ledger of costs.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the economic answer in Text 1?

choices.A: By disputing the claim that British wages were high compared with the cost of coal
choices.B: By conceding that it explains why British firms adopted machines but not why they were invented there
choices.C: By arguing that cultural values, rather than prices, explain why British manufacturers chose to buy machines
choices.D: By questioning whether economic incentives played any part in Britain's technological development

explanation.why: Text 2 says explanations based on prices "are persuasive about why British manufacturers were eager to buy labor-saving machines," which concedes part of Text 1. It then says they are "less persuasive about why such machines were invented and steadily improved there," pointing to a culture of practical experiment. Text 2 accepts the answer for adoption but finds it incomplete for invention.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 never disputes the facts about wages and coal; it questions only how much those facts explain.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 grants that prices explain why machines were bought but says they do not explain why the machines were invented and improved in Britain.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that prices explain the eagerness to buy machines; it turns to culture only to explain invention and improvement.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says "Prices create an incentive" and that invention owed to culture "as much as" to costs, so it does not deny that incentives mattered.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Jane Austen's Persuasion (1817) is often read as a novel about the dangers of yielding to others. Eight years before the story begins, Anne Elliot broke off her engagement to Frederick Wentworth on the advice of her older friend Lady Russell, and the novel dwells on the cost of that decision: years of quiet regret, and a reunion that comes about only because Wentworth's feelings, like Anne's, proved more durable than the advice that divided them. On this reading, the book's title names the error its heroine must outgrow.
items.passage_b: Readers who take Persuasion as a warning against being persuaded must contend with its final chapters. There Anne, reflecting on the broken engagement, tells Wentworth that Lady Russell's advice was mistaken but that she herself was right to follow it, given what duty then required of a young woman in her position. Austen, in other words, separates the soundness of the advice from the rightness of submitting to it, a distinction that the title, read as a simple caution, tends to obscure.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading of Persuasion in Text 1?

choices.A: By rejecting the reading on the grounds that Text 1 misstates why Anne ended her engagement
choices.B: By arguing that Lady Russell's advice was sound and that Anne was right to accept it
choices.C: By claiming that the novel endorses following others' advice whenever duty seems to require it
choices.D: By contending that the reading overlooks Anne's view that following mistaken advice was nonetheless right

explanation.why: Text 1 treats being persuaded as "the error its heroine must outgrow." Text 2 points to the final chapters, where Anne says Lady Russell's advice "was mistaken but that she herself was right to follow it." Text 2's author would say Text 1's reading misses this distinction between bad advice and a right decision to submit to it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that Anne ended the engagement on Lady Russell's advice; it challenges what the novel concludes about that choice, not the facts of the plot.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says Anne calls the advice "mistaken," so the author would not argue that the advice was sound.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 discusses Anne's judgment about one decision "given what duty then required of a young woman in her position"; it does not claim the novel recommends obeying advice in general.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 argues that Text 1 misses Anne's own judgment that the advice was wrong but that submitting to it was right.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In autumn, the leaves of many trees turn yellow and orange. This happens because chlorophyll, the green pigment that leaves use to capture sunlight, breaks down as the days grow shorter. Yellow and orange pigments that were in the leaf all summer, hidden by the green, then become visible.
items.passage_b: Not every autumn color was hiding in the leaf all along. The bright reds of many maples, for example, come from pigments called anthocyanins. Botanists have found that many trees begin producing these red pigments only in autumn, making them fresh just as the chlorophyll disappears.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation of autumn leaf color in Text 1?

choices.A: By explaining why trees drop their leaves before winter
choices.B: By noting that some autumn colors come from pigments that are newly made
choices.C: By agreeing that all autumn colors are present in the leaf during summer
choices.D: By suggesting that red leaves capture more sunlight than green leaves

explanation.why: Text 1 says autumn colors appear because yellow and orange pigments that were "in the leaf all summer" are revealed. Text 2 begins, "Not every autumn color was hiding in the leaf all along," and explains that red pigments are made "only in autumn." So Text 2 adds that some colors are newly produced.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 never discusses why or when trees drop their leaves.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 explains that red anthocyanins are produced fresh in autumn rather than revealed, which adds to Text 1's explanation.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says the opposite: "Not every autumn color was hiding in the leaf all along."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 does not compare how much sunlight red and green leaves capture.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: A claim repeated in many books and classrooms holds that the Great Wall of China is the only human-made structure that can be seen with the naked eye from space. Because the wall stretches for thousands of kilometers across northern China, the claim seems easy to believe.
items.passage_b: Astronauts who have orbited Earth tell a different story. Although the Great Wall is very long, it is only a few meters wide in most places, and its stone and earth are close in color to the land around it. Many astronauts report that they could not pick it out at all without a camera lens, while airports and large cities were much easier to spot.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the wall's great length makes it easy to see from orbit
choices.B: By arguing that the Great Wall is shorter than most books report
choices.C: By explaining that the wall is easiest to see where it is widest
choices.D: By pointing out that the wall is too narrow and plain to see easily from space

explanation.why: Text 1 reports the claim that the Great Wall can be seen with the naked eye from space. Text 2 says the wall is "only a few meters wide" and close in color to the land, so astronauts "could not pick it out" without a lens. Text 2 therefore rejects the claim and explains why.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says that "although the Great Wall is very long," it is still hard to see, so it would not agree.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that the wall "is very long"; it never says books exaggerate its length.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 never says the wall is easier to see in some places than in others.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 explains that the wall's narrow width and its color, similar to the land around it, make it hard to see from orbit.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In Sindh, a province in southern Pakistan, ajrak is far more than a piece of cloth. These block-printed shawls, patterned in deep red, indigo blue, black, and white, are worn at festivals and given to guests as a sign of respect. For many people, an ajrak is a symbol of Sindhi identity.
items.passage_b: Ajrak is also one of the most demanding crafts in the region. Printers carve wooden blocks by hand, then wash, print, and dye each cloth in more than a dozen separate stages, using natural dyes such as indigo. A single shawl can take two weeks or more to finish, and the skills are usually passed down within families.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the description of ajrak in Text 1?

choices.A: By adding that making ajrak is a long and skilled process
choices.B: By arguing that ajrak is no longer worn at festivals in Sindh
choices.C: By claiming that ajrak is valued only for the work needed to make it
choices.D: By noting that most ajrak is now printed by machines in a single day

explanation.why: Text 1 describes what ajrak means to people: it is worn at festivals, given to guests, and seen as "a symbol of Sindhi identity." Text 2 says ajrak "is also" a demanding craft with "more than a dozen separate stages" that can take "two weeks or more." Text 2 adds to Text 1 rather than disagreeing with it.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 explains that ajrak is made by hand in many stages over weeks, which adds to Text 1's account of its meaning.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 never mentions festivals, and nothing in it suggests that people have stopped wearing ajrak.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says ajrak is "also" a demanding craft, so it adds a point instead of replacing Text 1's view of its meaning.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 describes hand-carved blocks and a process that takes two weeks or more, the opposite of fast machine printing.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Daniel Defoe's novel Robinson Crusoe (1719) is usually remembered as an adventure story. Readers recall the shipwreck, the lonely island, and the moment Crusoe discovers a single human footprint in the sand, a scene that has thrilled audiences for three centuries.
items.passage_b: Anyone who rereads Robinson Crusoe may be surprised by how little of it is adventure. Page after page describes ordinary work: Crusoe plants barley, teaches himself to make pots, builds fences, and keeps careful records of his days. In many ways, the novel is a detailed study of how a person builds a working life from almost nothing.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the description of Robinson Crusoe in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the footprint scene is the most important part of the novel
choices.B: By arguing that the shipwreck in the novel was added by later editors
choices.C: By pointing out that much of the novel focuses on everyday work rather than adventure
choices.D: By claiming that readers have always valued the novel mainly for its record keeping

explanation.why: Text 1 says the novel is "usually remembered as an adventure story." Text 2 says readers may be surprised "by how little of it is adventure," since "page after page describes ordinary work." So Text 2 would respond that the novel is largely about daily labor.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 never mentions the footprint scene or ranks the novel's scenes by importance.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about editors or about how the shipwreck came to be in the novel.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 stresses that much of the novel describes farming, pottery, building, and record keeping rather than adventure.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 suggests the opposite: rereaders "may be surprised" by the focus on work, so readers have not always valued it for that.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Films and plays about Shakespeare's London often show his audiences as crowds of poor, noisy "groundlings," who paid a penny to stand in the open yard in front of the stage. Some writers have concluded that Shakespeare wrote his plays mainly for these working people.
items.passage_b: The yard was only part of the playhouse. Around it rose covered galleries, where seats cost more and where merchants, lawyers, and even nobles watched the plays. Historians who study the Globe therefore describe an audience that mixed people from nearly every level of London society.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the yard was the most expensive part of the theater
choices.B: By arguing that Shakespeare's plays were rarely performed at the Globe
choices.C: By claiming that nobles attended the theater more often than workers did
choices.D: By noting that wealthier people also attended, so the audience was more varied

explanation.why: Text 1 reports the conclusion that Shakespeare wrote mainly for poor "groundlings." Text 2 points out that the galleries held "merchants, lawyers, and even nobles," so the audience "mixed people from nearly every level" of society. Text 2 would answer that the audience was not mainly poor.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says gallery seats "cost more," so the yard was not the most expensive part.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 assumes plays were performed at the Globe; it never suggests otherwise.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says the audience was mixed; it never says nobles outnumbered workers.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 shows that wealthier people sat in the galleries, so the audience included many groups, not mainly poor workers.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Khewra Salt Mine in Pakistan's Punjab province is one of the largest salt mines in the world. A popular legend says that the salt was discovered around 326 BCE, when the horses of Alexander the Great's army stopped to rest nearby and were seen licking the rocks.
items.passage_b: The story of Alexander's horses is charming, but historians doubt that it explains how the salt was found. The salt lies in a range of hills where people had lived for many centuries before Alexander arrived, and the rock salt shows clearly in many places. Local communities, these historians argue, were very likely using it long before any foreign army came.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the legend in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that Alexander's army was the first to make use of the salt
choices.B: By suggesting that local people probably knew of the salt long before Alexander
choices.C: By arguing that the Khewra mine is smaller than it is often said to be
