choices.D: By claiming that Alexander's army never traveled through the region

explanation.why: Text 1 reports the legend that Alexander's horses led to the salt's discovery. Text 2 says historians doubt this, since people had lived in the hills "for many centuries before Alexander arrived" and were "very likely using it long before any foreign army came." So Text 2 offers a different, earlier discovery.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 argues that local people were likely using the salt before Alexander's army arrived.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 says local communities were "very likely using it long before any foreign army came."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 never discusses the size of the mine.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 doubts only that the horses explain the discovery; it does not deny that Alexander's army came to the region.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 2006, the International Astronomical Union decided that Pluto is not a planet but a "dwarf planet." Under the union's definition, a planet must orbit the Sun, be massive enough to pull itself into a round shape, and have cleared its orbit of other large objects. Pluto shares its region of space with many icy bodies, so it fails the third test.
items.passage_b: Some planetary scientists reject the union's definition. A world's own features, they argue, such as being round and having mountains, glaciers, and an atmosphere, are what make it a planet, not what else happens to orbit near it. By that standard, Pluto, whose glaciers and hazy atmosphere were photographed by the New Horizons spacecraft in 2015, clearly qualifies.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the decision in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the decision judges Pluto by its surroundings rather than its own features
choices.B: By agreeing that Pluto is not a planet because it has not cleared its orbit
choices.C: By claiming that Pluto is not round enough to meet the union's definition
choices.D: By suggesting that the New Horizons photographs were taken before the decision

explanation.why: Text 1 explains that Pluto lost planet status because it has not cleared its orbit of other objects. Text 2 argues that a world's "own features" should decide, "not what else happens to orbit near it," and says Pluto "clearly qualifies." So Text 2 objects that the decision uses the wrong kind of test.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 says planets should be defined by their own features, "not what else happens to orbit near it," which is exactly the test that ruled Pluto out.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says Pluto "clearly qualifies" as a planet, so it would not agree with the decision.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 lists being round among Pluto's qualifying features; neither text says Pluto is not round.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 dates the photographs to 2015, which is after the 2006 decision.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When sound films arrived in the late 1920s, audiences flocked to hear actors speak and sing on screen. Many film histories describe the change simply as progress: movies gained a powerful new tool, and nothing important was lost.
items.passage_b: Early sound recording came with real costs. Because cameras were noisy, they were often shut inside soundproof booths and could hardly move, and actors had to stay close to hidden microphones. As a result, many early sound films look stiff compared with the flowing camera work of the best silent films made just a few years before.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view of sound films in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that early sound films improved on silent films in every way
choices.B: By arguing that audiences preferred silent films to sound films
choices.C: By pointing out that the change to sound also limited how films could be shot
choices.D: By suggesting that actors refused to work near microphones

explanation.why: Text 1 says film histories treat sound as pure progress in which "nothing important was lost." Text 2 says sound "came with real costs": cameras "could hardly move" and actors had to stay near microphones, making films "look stiff." So Text 2 would point to a loss Text 1 ignores.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says early sound films often looked stiff compared with silent films, so it does not see them as better in every way.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 discusses how films were made, not what audiences preferred; Text 1 says audiences "flocked" to sound films.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 explains that cameras in soundproof booths could barely move, a real limit on filmmaking.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says actors had to stay close to microphones, not that they refused to.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sea turtle eggs hatch in nests buried in sandy beaches, usually at night. Biologists have found that the newly hatched turtles crawl toward the brightest part of the horizon. On a natural beach, that is the open sea, which reflects light from the Moon and stars.
items.passage_b: Brightness is only part of the story. In experiments, hatchlings also turned away from tall, dark shapes, such as sand dunes and trees, which normally stand on the land side of a beach. Together, these clues help the young turtles head toward the water.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Hatchlings mainly follow the sound of breaking waves to find the sea.
choices.B: Hatchlings use what they see to find their way to the ocean.
choices.C: Hatchlings reach the ocean most easily on very dark, moonless nights.
choices.D: Hatchlings move away from tall shapes such as sand dunes and trees.

explanation.why: Text 1 says hatchlings crawl "toward the brightest part of the horizon." Text 2 adds that they also turn "away from tall, dark shapes." Both clues are things the turtles see, so both authors would agree that hatchlings use vision to find the ocean.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Neither text mentions sound; both describe visual clues.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 1 describes turtles following brightness, and Text 2 adds turning away from dark shapes; both are visual clues.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 1 says the sea is bright because it reflects light from the Moon and stars, so neither author suggests dark nights help.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is stated only in Text 2; Text 1 mentions brightness alone.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For centuries, popular books and films showed the pyramids of Giza being built by enslaved people forced to work under the whip. The image grew partly from ancient Greek writers, who described the kings who built the pyramids as cruel rulers.
items.passage_b: Excavations near the pyramids since the 1990s suggest a different picture. Archaeologists have uncovered a town with bakeries and large amounts of cattle and fish bones, showing that the workers were well fed. They have also found the workers' own tombs, built beside the pyramids, an honor unlikely to be given to enslaved people.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the image of the pyramid builders in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that Greek writers described the pyramid builders accurately
choices.B: By arguing that the pyramids were built much later than most books claim
choices.C: By claiming that the workers' town was larger than the pyramids themselves
choices.D: By presenting evidence suggesting that the builders were not enslaved people

explanation.why: Text 1 describes the popular image of enslaved pyramid builders. Text 2 reports evidence that "suggests a different picture": the workers were "well fed" and were buried in tombs beside the pyramids, "an honor unlikely to be given to enslaved people." Text 2 challenges the image with evidence.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 offers "a different picture," so it does not support the Greek account.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Neither text discusses when the pyramids were built.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 never compares the size of the town with the size of the pyramids.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 points to good food and honored tombs as signs that the workers were not enslaved.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: At the end of Louisa May Alcott's Little Women (1868–1869), the independent Jo March, who once dreamed of fame as a writer, marries Professor Bhaer. Some readers have been disappointed by this ending, seeing it as the moment Jo gives up her ambitions for a quiet married life.
items.passage_b: Jo's marriage does not end her story of ambition. In the final chapters she and her husband turn her aunt's old house, Plumfield, into a school for boys, which Jo helps run with great energy. Her dreams change shape, but she remains an active, ambitious woman.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading of the novel's ending in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that Jo continues to pursue her ambitions, though in a new form
choices.B: By agreeing that Jo gives up all of her ambitions when she marries
choices.C: By claiming that Jo becomes a famous writer by the end of the novel
choices.D: By noting that Jo's aunt opposed the idea of opening a school

explanation.why: Text 1 reports the view that Jo "gives up her ambitions" when she marries. Text 2 says her marriage "does not end her story of ambition": she helps run a school, and "her dreams change shape." So Text 2 would say her ambition continues in a different form.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 says Jo's "dreams change shape" but she "remains an active, ambitious woman."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 directly disagrees, saying the marriage "does not end her story of ambition."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 describes Jo running a school, not becoming a famous writer.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the school is in her aunt's old house but never mentions the aunt's opinion.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 2009, scientists studying data from India's Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft announced a surprise. An instrument on the orbiter had detected the chemical signature of water spread across much of the Moon's surface. News reports celebrated the finding, since the Moon had long been thought to be completely dry.
items.passage_b: The discovery was real, but the water on the Moon's sunlit surface is extremely scarce. Later measurements suggest that its soil holds far less water than the sand of the Sahara Desert. Planetary scientists who hope to supply future lunar bases with water are looking instead at ice inside deep craters near the Moon's poles, where sunlight never reaches.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the finding in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the Chandrayaan-1 instrument did not actually detect any water
choices.B: By agreeing that the Moon's surface soil holds enough water to supply lunar bases
choices.C: By accepting the finding while stressing that the surface water is very scarce
choices.D: By claiming that the ice near the Moon's poles was also found by Chandrayaan-1

explanation.why: Text 1 reports that Chandrayaan-1 detected water across much of the Moon's surface. Text 2 says "the discovery was real" but adds that this water is "extremely scarce," with less water than Sahara sand. Text 2 accepts the finding but limits how much it means.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says "the discovery was real," so it does not deny that water was detected.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says scientists looking for water for lunar bases are "looking instead" at polar ice, because the surface water is so scarce.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 accepts the discovery but says the soil holds very little water.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 does not say which spacecraft or instrument found the polar ice.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1993, a small study reported that college students who listened to a Mozart sonata for ten minutes scored better on a spatial reasoning task than students who sat in silence. News reports soon claimed that Mozart's music could make listeners smarter, and some parents began playing classical music to their babies.
items.passage_b: Later studies told a more modest story. When researchers repeated the experiment, any improvement was small and lasted only minutes. It also appeared after people listened to other music they enjoyed, suggesting that a good mood, not Mozart in particular, briefly sharpened their thinking.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claims in the news reports in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that Mozart's music has a lasting effect on intelligence
choices.B: By suggesting that the effect was brief and was not special to Mozart's music
choices.C: By arguing that babies benefit more from music than college students do
choices.D: By claiming that listening to music has no effect at all on thinking

explanation.why: Text 1 says news reports claimed Mozart "could make listeners smarter." Text 2 says the improvement "was small and lasted only minutes" and also followed "other music they enjoyed." So Text 2 would answer that the effect was short-lived and not unique to Mozart.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says any improvement "lasted only minutes," so it was not lasting.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 reports that the effect was brief and also appeared with other enjoyable music.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Neither text compares the effects of music on babies and on college students.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says a good mood "briefly sharpened their thinking," so it does not deny every effect.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Taxila, an ancient city in what is now Pakistan's Punjab province, was a famous center of learning more than 2,000 years ago. Students traveled there from distant regions to study medicine, law, and military skills. Travel guides and websites often call Taxila the world's first university.
items.passage_b: Historians admire Taxila's teachers but question the label "university." Ancient accounts suggest that students learned from individual teachers in their homes, with no shared campus, set courses, or formal exams. Nalanda, founded centuries later in eastern India, had large shared buildings and organized studies, so it fits the word far better.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the label that travel guides give Taxila in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that Taxila's way of teaching does not match what the word suggests
choices.B: By denying that Taxila was an important center of learning
choices.C: By claiming that Nalanda was founded before Taxila became a center of learning
choices.D: By suggesting that students at Taxila studied only medicine

explanation.why: Text 1 reports that travel guides call Taxila "the world's first university." Text 2 "admire[s] Taxila's teachers" but questions the label, because students learned from individual teachers with "no shared campus, set courses, or formal exams." Text 2 says Taxila's teaching did not work like a university.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 says Taxila lacked the campus, courses, and exams that the word "university" suggests.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says historians "admire Taxila's teachers"; it questions only the label.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says Nalanda was founded "centuries later," not before Taxila.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 1 lists medicine, law, and military skills, and Text 2 never limits the subjects.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many people grow up believing that the sky is blue because it reflects the color of the oceans, which cover most of Earth's surface. The idea seems sensible, since the sky and the sea often appear to be similar shades.
items.passage_b: Physicists explain the blue sky without the oceans at all. Sunlight contains all colors, and as it passes through the atmosphere, tiny molecules of air scatter the shorter, bluer wavelengths far more than the red ones. This scattered blue light reaches our eyes from every direction, which is why the sky looks blue even over deserts far from any sea.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the oceans give the sky its blue color
choices.B: By arguing that the sky is not really blue but appears blue only over the sea
choices.C: By claiming that sunlight contains only blue and red wavelengths
choices.D: By explaining that the sky's color comes from the way air scatters sunlight

explanation.why: Text 1 describes the belief that the sky is blue because it reflects the oceans. Text 2 says physicists explain the color "without the oceans at all": air molecules scatter blue light most, so the sky is blue "even over deserts far from any sea." Text 2 replaces the belief with a different explanation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 explains the sky's color "without the oceans at all," so it would not agree.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the sky looks blue "even over deserts far from any sea," the opposite of this choice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says sunlight "contains all colors," not only blue and red.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 explains that air molecules scatter blue light more than red light, which makes the sky look blue.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most planetary scientists accept that the Moon formed about 4.5 billion years ago, when an object roughly the size of Mars, often called Theia, struck the young Earth. In the standard version of this "giant impact" model, most of the debris that later gathered into the Moon came from Theia rather than from Earth.
items.passage_b: Rocks brought back by the Apollo astronauts complicate that picture. The Moon's rocks turn out to be nearly identical to Earth's in their mix of oxygen isotopes, a chemical fingerprint that usually differs between bodies that formed in different parts of the solar system. Geochemist Lucía Ferrer argues that the collision must have been violent enough to mix material from both bodies thoroughly, or else that the Moon was built mostly from Earth itself.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the standard version of the giant impact model in Text 1?

choices.A: By rejecting the idea that a collision with another body led to the Moon's formation
choices.B: By arguing that Theia formed in the same part of the solar system as Earth
choices.C: By questioning where the Moon's material came from while accepting that an impact occurred
choices.D: By claiming that the Apollo rocks show the Moon to be older than Earth

explanation.why: Text 1's standard model says most of the Moon's material came "from Theia rather than from Earth." Text 2 says matching oxygen isotopes "complicate that picture," and Ferrer proposes that the material was thoroughly mixed or came "mostly from Earth." Both of her explanations still involve the collision, so Text 2 challenges only the source of the Moon's material.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Ferrer's explanations still assume "the collision" happened; Text 2 questions the details, not the impact itself.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 never says where Theia formed. It notes that bodies from different regions usually have different isotopes, but it does not use this to place Theia near Earth.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 accepts that a collision occurred but doubts that the Moon is made mostly of Theia's material.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 compares the chemistry of Earth and Moon rocks, not their ages.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Silk Road is often pictured as a single great highway along which caravans of merchants carried silk from China all the way to the Mediterranean. In this popular image, travelers such as the Venetian Marco Polo, who reached China in the 1270s, were typical of the people who used the routes.
items.passage_b: Surviving documents from oasis towns along the routes, such as contracts and travel permits, tell a different story. Most traders, historian Tomasz Wielgosz notes, traveled only a few hundred kilometers between neighboring markets, where they sold their goods to the next set of merchants. Silk reached the Mediterranean by passing through many hands, and long-distance travelers like Marco Polo were rare exceptions.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the popular image in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that most goods were carried in short stages by many different traders
choices.B: By claiming that documents from oasis towns are too few to support any conclusion
choices.C: By agreeing that most merchants traveled the full length of the routes
choices.D: By arguing that Marco Polo never actually traveled as far as China

explanation.why: Text 1 describes the image of merchants carrying silk the whole way and of Marco Polo as a typical traveler. Text 2 says most traders went "only a few hundred kilometers" and that silk moved "through many hands," with travelers like Polo "rare exceptions." Text 2 replaces the image of one long journey with many short ones.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 says goods passed between neighboring markets and "through many hands" on the way west.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 relies on these documents as evidence; it never questions whether there are enough of them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says most traders covered "only a few hundred kilometers," the opposite of this choice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 calls Marco Polo a rare long-distance traveler, which assumes he did make the journey.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Sri Lankan architect Geoffrey Bawa (1919–2003) designed houses and hotels in which the line between inside and outside almost disappears. Rooms open onto shaded verandas and courtyards, and breezes move freely through the buildings. Many critics have praised these features as Bawa's own modernist inventions, a break with the past suited to a newly independent country.
items.passage_b: Bawa's buildings certainly feel modern, but much of what makes them distinctive is old. Traditional Sri Lankan manor houses were arranged around open courtyards, and their deep, overhanging tiled roofs shed heavy monsoon rain while letting air pass beneath. Bawa, architectural historian Dilini Perera argues, studied these older buildings closely and reworked their ideas rather than inventing new ones.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the critics' praise in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that Bawa's open designs broke completely with earlier Sri Lankan buildings
choices.B: By arguing that Bawa's buildings do not suit Sri Lanka's monsoon climate
choices.C: By claiming that Bawa's buildings are not modern in any meaningful way
choices.D: By pointing out that the features praised as new were adapted from older local buildings

explanation.why: Text 1 reports that critics praised Bawa's open designs as "modernist inventions, a break with the past." Text 2 says that "much of what makes them distinctive is old," since traditional manor houses already had courtyards and deep roofs, and that Bawa "reworked their ideas rather than inventing new ones." Text 2 credits tradition, not pure invention.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 argues the opposite: Bawa reworked ideas from traditional buildings instead of breaking with them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the traditional features Bawa used were suited to monsoon rain, so it does not say his buildings fail in that climate.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 grants that the buildings "certainly feel modern"; it questions only where their ideas came from.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 traces courtyards and deep roofs to traditional manor houses that Bawa studied.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Neanderthals disappeared from Europe around 40,000 years ago. Paleoclimatologist Henrik Aas links their decline to the climate of the time, which swung rapidly between cold and milder periods. Each cold spell, he argues, shrank the forests and grasslands on which Neanderthals depended, splitting their populations into small groups cut off from one another.
items.passage_b: Ancient DNA shows that late Neanderthals had very little genetic variety, a sign that they lived in small, scattered bands for many generations. Anthropologist Teresa Quispe argues that such groups were fragile: a few bad hunting seasons or the arrival of competing modern humans could have been enough to make them disappear.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Competition with modern humans was the main cause of the Neanderthals' disappearance.
choices.B: Living in small, isolated groups left Neanderthals vulnerable to dying out.
choices.C: Rapid climate swings were the main reason Neanderthal populations became small.
choices.D: Neanderthals had more genetic variety than early modern humans did.

explanation.why: Text 1 says cold spells split Neanderthals "into small groups cut off from one another," and links this to their decline. Text 2 says they lived "in small, scattered bands" that were "fragile" and could easily disappear. Both authors connect small, separated populations with the Neanderthals' extinction, though they differ on what caused it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 mentions modern humans only as one possible final blow ("could have been"), and Text 1 does not mention them at all.
explanation.B: Correct. Both texts describe small, separated populations and link them to the Neanderthals' disappearance.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Only Text 1 blames climate swings; Text 2 explains the small groups using DNA evidence and never mentions climate.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says late Neanderthals had "very little genetic variety," and neither text compares them with modern humans.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Charles Dickens first ended Great Expectations (1861) with Pip and Estella meeting briefly and parting for good. When his friend, the novelist Edward Bulwer-Lytton, urged a happier conclusion, Dickens rewrote the final scene so that the two leave the ruined garden together. Many critics see this revision as a betrayal of the novel's sad, clear-eyed logic.
items.passage_b: The published ending is far less cheerful than its reputation suggests. Pip and Estella meet as two people worn down by years of disappointment, and the closing words, "I saw no shadow of another parting from her," are strangely hesitant; they describe what Pip did not see rather than what will happen. Read closely, the revised ending keeps the novel's somber tone and leaves the couple's future uncertain.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the critics' view of the revised ending in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the revision gives the novel a simple, happy conclusion
choices.B: By claiming that Dickens never wrote any ending other than the published one
choices.C: By arguing that the revised ending is more uncertain and somber than critics suggest
choices.D: By suggesting that Bulwer-Lytton wrote the final scene of the novel himself

explanation.why: Text 1 reports that critics see the revised ending as a happy betrayal of the novel's "sad, clear-eyed logic." Text 2 says the ending is "far less cheerful than its reputation suggests": the final words are "strangely hesitant," and the ending "keeps the novel's somber tone." So Text 2 would say the revision does not betray the novel's mood.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 argues that the ending only seems happy; read closely, it is somber and uncertain.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 discusses only the published ending and never denies that Dickens first wrote a different one.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 points to the worn-down characters and the hesitant final words to show that the ending stays somber.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 1 says Bulwer-Lytton urged a change and Dickens rewrote the scene; neither text says Bulwer-Lytton wrote it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: As the climate warms, mountain glaciers around the world are losing ice. In the Himalayas, satellite images show that many glaciers have shrunk and pulled back over recent decades. Some writers conclude that every glacier in the high mountains of South and Central Asia is now retreating.
items.passage_b: In the Karakoram range of northern Pakistan, the record is surprisingly mixed. Since the 1990s, glaciologists have found that many glaciers there have stayed about the same size, and some have even grown slightly. Researchers are still testing explanations for this "Karakoram anomaly," such as heavier winter snowfall and cooler summers in the region, but none of them doubt that most of the world's glaciers are shrinking.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?

choices.A: By accepting the general trend while pointing out a region where it does not hold
choices.B: By arguing that satellite images of Himalayan glaciers are unreliable
choices.C: By claiming that glaciers in the Karakoram are growing faster than others are shrinking
choices.D: By rejecting the idea that most of the world's glaciers are losing ice

explanation.why: Text 1 ends with the conclusion that "every glacier" in the high mountains of South and Central Asia is retreating. Text 2 reports that many Karakoram glaciers "have stayed about the same size" and some have grown, though no researcher doubts "that most of the world's glaciers are shrinking." So Text 2 accepts the overall trend but rejects the word "every."
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 agrees that most glaciers are shrinking but gives the Karakoram as an exception to Text 1's claim about "every glacier."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 never questions the Himalayan satellite images; it discusses a different range.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says only that some Karakoram glaciers have grown "slightly"; it makes no comparison with the losses elsewhere.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says researchers do not "doubt that most of the world's glaciers are shrinking."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Violins made by Antonio Stradivari in Cremona, Italy, around 1700 now sell for millions of dollars. Many musicians and collectors believe that these instruments produce a tone no modern violin can equal. Researchers have spent decades searching for the cause, proposing secrets in the wood Stradivari chose or in the varnish he applied.
items.passage_b: Before searching for the secret, it is worth asking whether the difference can be heard at all. In several blind tests, professional violinists wearing goggles that hid the instruments played old Italian violins, including ones by Stradivari, alongside fine new violins. Most players could not reliably tell which was which, and many preferred the sound of a new instrument.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that Stradivari's varnish explains the violins' superior tone
choices.B: By arguing that Stradivari's violins are worth far less than collectors pay
choices.C: By claiming that new violins sound better than old ones to every listener
choices.D: By questioning whether the tone of these violins is truly better than that of new ones

explanation.why: Text 1 describes the belief that Stradivari violins have a tone "no modern violin can equal." Text 2 asks "whether the difference can be heard at all" and reports that players in blind tests "could not reliably tell which was which." So Text 2 doubts that the tone is really superior.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 questions whether there is any superior tone to explain, so it would not credit the varnish.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 tests how the violins sound, not what they are worth; it never discusses their price.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says "many" players preferred a new violin, not every listener.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2's blind tests suggest that players cannot reliably hear the difference Text 1 describes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: New Caledonian crows, found on islands in the South Pacific, are famous for making tools: they shape twigs and strips of leaf into hooks and probes that pull insects out of holes in wood. Young crows stay with their parents for up to two years, and ornithologist Mele Taufa argues that this long period of watching adults is how the birds learn to make and use tools.
items.passage_b: In one study, young New Caledonian crows were raised by people, with no adult crows to watch. Within a few months, the birds began poking sticks into crevices on their own. Their early tools were simple and clumsy compared with those of wild adults. The researchers concluded that the basic urge to use tools is inborn, though experience and observation may help the birds refine their skills.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that young crows cannot use tools until they have watched adults
choices.B: By suggesting that watching adults may refine tool use but is not where it begins
choices.C: By arguing that young crows learn tool use mainly from crows other than their parents
choices.D: By claiming that observation plays no part in how crows develop tool skills

explanation.why: Taufa argues in Text 1 that young crows learn tool use by watching adults. In Text 2, crows with "no adult crows to watch" still began using sticks, so the basic urge is "inborn," though "observation may help the birds refine their skills." Text 2 would say watching adults explains the refinement of tool use, not its origin.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The crows in Text 2 used sticks "on their own" with no adults to watch, the opposite of this choice.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 says the basic urge is inborn, while observation may help refine skills.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 never compares learning from parents with learning from other crows.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says observation "may help the birds refine their skills," so it does not rule observation out.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When the modern Olympic Games were founded in the 1890s, their organizers looked to ancient Greece for an ideal. Ancient athletes, they claimed, were amateurs who competed purely for honor, receiving nothing but a crown of olive leaves for victory. Professional sport, in this view, was a modern corruption of the Greek spirit.
items.passage_b: It is true that the official prize at Olympia was an olive crown. But historian Nikos Andreou points out that victors could expect far more once they returned home. Their cities rewarded them with cash, statues, and free meals for life, and at other Greek festivals winners received valuable prizes such as large jars of olive oil. The amateur athlete, Andreou concludes, was largely an invention of the modern Olympic movement.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the organizers' claim in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that ancient athletes competed only for the honor of winning
choices.B: By arguing that the modern Olympics should stop awarding prizes
choices.C: By pointing out that ancient winners in fact received valuable rewards
choices.D: By claiming that olive crowns were never given to winners at Olympia

explanation.why: Text 1 reports the organizers' claim that ancient athletes received "nothing but a crown of olive leaves." Text 2 grants that the olive crown was the official prize but says winners received "cash, statues, and free meals for life" at home and valuable prizes elsewhere. So Text 2 would reject the image of the purely amateur Greek athlete.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 lists cash, statues, meals, and olive oil as rewards, so athletes did not compete for honor alone.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 discusses ancient rewards and never recommends any change to the modern Games.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 shows that victors received money and other valuable rewards from their cities and at other festivals.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says, "It is true that the official prize at Olympia was an olive crown."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the 1980s, conservators cleaned Michelangelo's frescoes on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome, removing centuries of candle soot and old layers of glue. The ceiling that emerged was startlingly bright, full of vivid pinks, greens, and oranges. Art historian Chiara Bellandi argues that the cleaning revealed Michelangelo to be a far bolder colorist than scholars had believed.
items.passage_b: No one disputes that the cleaned ceiling looks dramatically brighter than it did before. Some critics, however, worry that the cleaning went too far. They argue that Michelangelo added final touches of shadow after the plaster had dried and that the solvents used may have stripped these away along with the dirt, leaving the colors harsher than he intended.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: The cleaned ceiling looks much brighter than it did before the work began.
choices.B: The cleaning removed final touches of shadow that Michelangelo added himself.
choices.C: The colors now visible are the ones Michelangelo intended viewers to see.
choices.D: The ceiling should be cleaned again to remove the remaining layers of glue.

explanation.why: Text 1 says the ceiling that emerged "was startlingly bright." Text 2 begins, "No one disputes that the cleaned ceiling looks dramatically brighter than it did before." The authors disagree about whether the cleaning was faithful to Michelangelo, but both accept that the ceiling is now much brighter.
explanation.A: Correct. Both texts state that the ceiling is much brighter after cleaning.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Only the critics in Text 2 raise this worry, and Text 1 treats the bright colors as Michelangelo's own.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 1 suggests this, but Text 2 says the colors may be "harsher than he intended."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Neither text suggests further cleaning; Text 1 says the glue was removed.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Woolly mammoths had vanished from nearly all of their mainland range by about 10,000 years ago, but a small population survived on Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean, until roughly 4,000 years ago. Paleontologist Sergei Volkov argues that the island's isolation protected the mammoths from human hunters, who did not reach Wrangel until after the animals were gone.
items.passage_b: Genetic studies of the last Wrangel Island mammoths reveal a population in poor health. Descended from a small group that was cut off when rising seas flooded the land around the island, the mammoths carried harmful mutations and had little genetic diversity. Geneticist Hana Novák suggests that this weakened population, which held on for thousands of years after its mainland relatives died out, may finally have been wiped out by a sudden event such as a disease outbreak.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Human hunters caused the final extinction of the Wrangel Island mammoths.
choices.B: Harmful mutations were the direct cause of the mammoths' extinction.
choices.C: The island's isolation protected the mammoths from human hunters.
choices.D: Mammoths survived on Wrangel Island long after they disappeared from the mainland.

explanation.why: Text 1 says mammoths survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago, long after they had vanished from the mainland. Text 2 says the population "held on for thousands of years after its mainland relatives died out." Both authors accept this late survival, though they focus on different reasons for it and for its end.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 1 says hunters reached Wrangel only "after the animals were gone," and Text 2 suggests a sudden event such as disease.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the mutations weakened the population but suggests that a sudden event finally wiped it out; Text 1 never mentions mutations.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Only Text 1 makes this claim; Text 2 does not discuss hunters.
explanation.D: Correct. Both texts say the island's mammoths outlasted the mainland populations by thousands of years.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: A familiar story holds that when Christopher Columbus proposed sailing west from Spain to Asia in the 1480s, most learned Europeans believed the Earth was flat. In this telling, scholars warned that his ships would fall off the edge of the world, and Columbus bravely proved them wrong in 1492.
items.passage_b: Educated Europeans of Columbus's time already knew that the Earth was round; Greek scholars had shown this nearly 2,000 years earlier, and one of them, Eratosthenes, had even estimated its size. The real argument concerned distance. Columbus's critics believed, correctly, that Asia lay much too far west for his ships to reach with the supplies they could carry. His voyage succeeded only because two continents unknown to Europeans lay in between.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the familiar story in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that most Europeans of the time had never heard of Eratosthenes
choices.B: By explaining that the dispute was about the distance to Asia, not the Earth's shape
choices.C: By arguing that Columbus's critics underestimated how far away Asia was
choices.D: By agreeing that fear of a flat Earth delayed Columbus's voyage for years

explanation.why: Text 1 tells the story that scholars feared Columbus would sail off a flat Earth. Text 2 says educated Europeans "already knew that the Earth was round" and that "the real argument concerned distance": critics thought Asia was too far away. Text 2 corrects the story by naming the true dispute.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says Greek scholars' knowledge was shared by educated Europeans; it never says how many people had heard of Eratosthenes.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 says the argument "concerned distance," since educated Europeans already knew the Earth was round.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says the critics were correct that Asia was "much too far west," so they did not underestimate the distance.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says educated Europeans knew the Earth was round, so it would reject any role for fear of a flat Earth.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For centuries, historians called the period after the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 CE the "Dark Ages." In this view, as cities shrank and trade declined, Europeans lost much of the learning of the ancient world, and scholarship nearly died out until its revival in the 1300s and 1400s.
items.passage_b: Recent historians reject the label, or at least its gloom. Cities and long-distance trade did decline in much of western Europe, but monasteries from Ireland to Italy continued to copy and study ancient texts. Around 800, scholars at Charlemagne's court even promoted a clear new style of handwriting that made books easier to read, and many Roman works survive today only because they were copied during this period.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view of the period in Text 1?

choices.A: By denying that cities and trade declined after the fall of Rome
choices.B: By arguing that ancient learning was lost during Charlemagne's reign
choices.C: By accepting that some decline occurred while arguing that learning was preserved
choices.D: By claiming that the early Middle Ages were a time of growth in every area of life

explanation.why: Text 1 presents the view that learning "nearly died out" after Rome fell. Text 2 grants that "cities and long-distance trade did decline" but says monasteries kept copying ancient texts and that many Roman works "survive today only because" of copies made then. Text 2 concedes some decline but rejects the claim that learning vanished.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 explicitly says cities and trade "did decline," so it does not deny this.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says scholars at Charlemagne's court helped preserve ancient works, the opposite of this choice.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 admits that cities and trade declined but shows that monasteries and scholars preserved ancient learning.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 concedes decline in cities and trade, so it does not claim growth in every area.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When Emily Dickinson's poems were first published in 1890, four years after her death, the editors made many changes. Among other things, they replaced most of her frequent dashes with commas, periods, and semicolons. The editors believed these changes made the unusual poems easier for readers to follow, and the volume sold well.
items.passage_b: Readers of the 1955 edition, which restored the punctuation of Dickinson's manuscripts, met a different poet. Her dashes, many scholars argue, are not careless marks but part of the poems' meaning: they create pauses, leave thoughts open, and let a line point in more than one direction at once. Replacing them with ordinary punctuation made the poems tidier, but it also narrowed them.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the editors' changes in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the changes brought the poems closer to Dickinson's intentions
choices.B: By arguing that the 1890 volume failed because readers found the poems confusing
choices.C: By claiming that Dickinson's manuscripts contained very few dashes
choices.D: By suggesting that the changes made the poems neater but lost some of their meaning

explanation.why: Text 1 says the editors replaced Dickinson's dashes to make the poems "easier for readers to follow." Text 2 says the dashes are "part of the poems' meaning" and that replacing them "made the poems tidier, but it also narrowed them." So Text 2 grants a gain in neatness but sees a loss in meaning.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says the dashes are part of the poems' meaning, so removing them moved the poems away from what Dickinson wrote.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 1 says the volume "sold well," and Text 2 never claims it failed.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says the 1955 edition restored the punctuation of the manuscripts, including the dashes, so the manuscripts had many.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 calls the edited poems "tidier" but "narrowed," meaning they lost some of their range of meaning.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Dutch painter Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675) left no written record of how he worked, but some art historians believe he used a camera obscura, a darkened box that projects an image through a lens. They point to features of his paintings that resemble optical effects, such as small, blurry dots of light on shiny surfaces, like those in an out-of-focus photograph.
items.passage_b: The resemblance is real, but it proves less than it seems. A painter with a sharp eye could notice how highlights glitter and soften and copy that effect by hand. Moreover, the list of Vermeer's possessions made after his death mentions no lenses or optical devices. Without such evidence, art historian Saskia Mertens argues, the camera obscura remains an interesting possibility rather than an established fact.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief of some art historians in Text 1?

choices.A: By granting the visual similarity but arguing that it does not prove Vermeer used the device
choices.B: By claiming that Vermeer's paintings show no effects resembling those of a lens
choices.C: By arguing that the camera obscura had not yet been invented in Vermeer's time
choices.D: By suggesting that the list of his possessions proves Vermeer never used the device

explanation.why: Text 1 says some historians think Vermeer used a camera obscura because his paintings show lens-like effects. Text 2 agrees "the resemblance is real" but says a careful painter could create the effect by hand and that no optical devices appear among his possessions. Mertens calls the idea "an interesting possibility rather than an established fact."
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 accepts the resemblance but says it "proves less than it seems."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 begins by saying "the resemblance is real," so it does not deny the effects.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 never discusses when the camera obscura was invented.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 treats the idea as still "an interesting possibility," so it does not claim proof that Vermeer never used one.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: At exactly noon, the old clocks in Mr. Adeyemi's repair shop ______ all at once, filling the narrow room with chimes, bells, and the cry of a wooden cuckoo. His new apprentice, Tunde, still jumps at the sound every day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: rings
choices.B: ring
choices.C: is ringing
choices.D: has rung

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "clocks," which is plural; "in Mr. Adeyemi's repair shop" only tells where the clocks are. A plural subject needs a plural verb, and the rest of the passage is in the simple present ("jumps"), so "ring" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Rings" is singular and agrees with "shop," but the subject is the plural "clocks."
explanation.B: Correct. The plural verb "ring" agrees with the plural subject "clocks."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Is ringing" is singular, but the subject "clocks" is plural.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Has rung" is singular, but the subject "clocks" is plural.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Louvre in Paris first opened as a public museum in 1793, during the French Revolution. Today, ______ collection holds hundreds of thousands of objects, so only a small fraction of them can be displayed at any one time.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it's
choices.B: their
choices.C: its
choices.D: its'

explanation.why: The blank must show that the collection belongs to the Louvre, a single museum. The possessive form of "it" is "its," with no apostrophe.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "It's" is a contraction of "it is" or "it has"; "it is collection" makes no sense.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Their" is plural, but it refers to the Louvre, which is singular.
explanation.C: Correct. "Its" is the singular possessive pronoun, showing the collection belongs to the Louvre.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Its'" is not a word in Standard English; the possessive "its" never takes an apostrophe.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Rosetta Stone, found in Egypt in 1799, records a single royal decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic, and ancient Greek. Because the scholars who studied it could already read Greek, the stone gave ______ a way to work out the meaning of the other two scripts, though fully deciphering the hieroglyphs still took more than twenty years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: them
choices.B: it
choices.C: they
choices.D: him

explanation.why: The ones who were given a way to work out the other scripts are "the scholars," a plural noun. The pronoun is also the object of "gave," so it must be the plural object pronoun "them."
explanation.A: Correct. "Them" is plural, matching "scholars," and is the object form needed after "gave."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "It" is singular, but it must refer to the plural "scholars"; the stone did not give a way to itself or to the Greek text.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "They" is a subject pronoun; after the verb "gave," the object form "them" is needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Him" is singular and refers to no one in the text; the antecedent "scholars" is plural.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Before 1869, traveling from New York to San Francisco meant a long wagon journey or a sea voyage of several months. When the first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed at Promontory Summit, Utah, in May of that year, it ______ the trip to about a week. The celebrations, however, largely ignored the thousands of Chinese immigrant workers who had built much of the line through the Sierra Nevada.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: shortens
choices.B: has shortened
choices.C: will shorten
choices.D: shortened

explanation.why: The sentence describes a single finished event at a stated past time: "When the first transcontinental railroad … was completed … in May of that year" (1869). The other verbs in the passage, such as "was completed" and "ignored," are also in the past, so the simple past "shortened" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The present tense "shortens" doesn't fit an event the text places in 1869.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The present perfect "has shortened" isn't used with a specific finished past time such as "in May of that year."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The future "will shorten" doesn't fit an event that already happened in 1869.
explanation.D: Correct. The simple past "shortened" matches the past time "in May of that year" and the past-tense verbs around it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The 1977 discovery of hydrothermal vents along the Galápagos Rift, where scientists aboard the submersible Alvin found tube worms, clams, and crabs crowded around openings in the seafloor roughly 2,500 meters below the surface, ______ one of the most consequential findings in modern biology. It showed that entire communities of animals can depend on bacteria that draw energy from chemicals rather than from sunlight.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: remain
choices.B: remains
choices.C: have remained
choices.D: are

explanation.why: Strip away the long modifiers and the sentence reads "The 1977 discovery … remains one of the most consequential findings." The subject is the singular noun "discovery"; "vents," "scientists," "worms," "clams," "crabs" and "openings" all sit inside phrases that describe it. A singular subject needs the singular verb "remains."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Remain" is plural and seems to agree with nearby plural nouns such as "vents" or "openings," but the subject is the singular "discovery."
explanation.B: Correct. The singular verb "remains" agrees with the singular subject "discovery."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have remained" is plural, but the subject "discovery" is singular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Are" is plural, but the subject "discovery" is singular.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: In the 1840s, many reviewers judged a novel differently depending on whether they believed its author was a man or a woman. Publishing under the pen name Currer Bell, a name she chose partly because it did not reveal her sex, ______ Reviewers soon began guessing about who the mysterious author really was.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Charlotte Brontë's novel Jane Eyre was published in 1847 and quickly became a success.
choices.B: the novel Jane Eyre was published by Charlotte Brontë in 1847 and quickly became a success.
choices.C: Charlotte Brontë released Jane Eyre in 1847, and the novel quickly became a success.
choices.D: in 1847 Jane Eyre, a novel by Charlotte Brontë, appeared and quickly became a success.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Publishing under the pen name Currer Bell, a name she chose …" describes the person who published. An introductory modifier applies to the subject that comes right after it, so that subject must be Charlotte Brontë herself, not her novel.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "Charlotte Brontë's novel Jane Eyre," so the sentence says the novel was publishing under a pen name and chose it; the modifier dangles.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "the novel Jane Eyre," so the novel, not Brontë, seems to be publishing under the pen name.
explanation.C: Correct. "Charlotte Brontë" comes right after the introductory phrase, so she is the one publishing under the pen name she chose.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "Jane Eyre," the novel, so the introductory phrase wrongly describes the book as the one choosing a pen name.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Gitanjali (Song Offerings), the 1912 collection of devotional poems that Rabindranath Tagore translated from his own Bengali verse into spare English prose and that so impressed the Irish poet W. B. Yeats that Yeats agreed to write its introduction, ______ Tagore the Nobel Prize in Literature the following year, making him the first non-European writer to receive the award.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: earning
choices.B: having earned
choices.C: to earn
choices.D: earned

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is "Gitanjali (Song Offerings)"; everything from "the 1912 collection" to "its introduction" is a long description of it, and the verbs inside it ("translated," "impressed," "agreed") belong to the "that" clauses. The sentence still needs its own main verb, so the blank must be a finite verb: "earned."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Earning" is a participle, not a main verb, so the sentence would have no main verb and would be a fragment.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Having earned" is a participle phrase, not a main verb, so the subject "Gitanjali" would be left without a verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "To earn" is an infinitive, which can't serve as the main verb of a sentence.
explanation.D: Correct. The past-tense verb "earned" gives the subject "Gitanjali (Song Offerings)" its main verb and fits the past time of the passage.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Leonardo da Vinci painted The Last Supper on a dry plaster wall in Milan in the 1490s, experimenting with a technique that, unlike traditional fresco, did not bind the pigment into wet plaster; within a few decades the paint had begun to flake. A team of conservators spent more than twenty years, from 1978 to 1999, cleaning the mural. The ______ choice to strip away centuries of earlier retouching, and to fill the resulting gaps with pale watercolor rather than reconstruct Leonardo's lost brushwork, divided critics.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: conservator's
choices.B: conservators'
choices.C: conservators
choices.D: conservators's

explanation.why: The choice belonged to "a team of conservators," so the word in the blank must be plural and possessive. A plural noun that already ends in s forms its possessive by adding only an apostrophe: "conservators'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Conservator's" is the possessive of one conservator, but the text says the work was done by a team of conservators.
explanation.B: Correct. "Conservators'" is the plural possessive, showing that the choice belonged to the whole team.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Conservators" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it doesn't show that the choice belonged to them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to show possession; "conservators's" is not standard.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Plants take in carbon dioxide through tiny pores in their leaves called stomata, but water vapor escapes through the same pores. Most plants open their stomata during the day. Many cacti, however, open their stomata only at night, when the desert air is cooler and more humid. Since less water evaporates into cool, humid air, this habit most likely helps cacti ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: survive without taking in any carbon dioxide at all.
choices.B: grow taller than plants that open their stomata in daylight.
choices.C: lose less water than they would by opening their stomata during the day.
choices.D: lose more water at night than they do during the hot daytime hours.

explanation.why: The text gives two facts: water escapes through open stomata, and less water evaporates into cool, humid air. Cacti open their stomata only at night, when the air is cool and humid, so this timing must reduce how much water they lose.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says plants take in carbon dioxide through their stomata; cacti still open them, just at night.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says nothing about how tall cacti grow compared with other plants.
explanation.C: Correct. Opening the stomata only in cool, humid air means less water escapes than would escape in daytime heat.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the logic; the cool, humid night air reduces water loss rather than increasing it.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In many earlier European churches, thick walls had to hold back the heavy outward push of stone ceilings, so windows had to stay small; large openings would have weakened the walls. In the late twelfth century, builders began using flying buttresses, stone arches on the outside of a building that carry much of that push down to supports beyond the walls. With less force pressing on the walls, builders could ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: make the walls even thicker than they had been before.
choices.B: cut larger window openings without weakening the walls.
choices.C: build the ceilings out of wood instead of heavy stone.
choices.D: place every window in the ceiling rather than the walls.

explanation.why: The text explains that windows stayed small because large openings would weaken walls that were resisting the push of heavy ceilings. Flying buttresses took much of that force off the walls, so the reason for keeping windows small was removed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Less force on the walls means they need less thickness, not more.
explanation.B: Correct. Once the walls bore less force, larger openings would no longer weaken them dangerously.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions changing the material of the ceilings.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text gives no reason to move windows into the ceiling; it is about openings in the walls.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Archaeologists working at sites of the Indus Valley Civilization, which flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BCE in what is now Pakistan and northwestern India, have found hundreds of small stone cubes that were used as weights. The cubes follow the same system of sizes whether they come from Harappa, from Mohenjo-daro, or from settlements hundreds of kilometers away. Because the civilization's writing has never been deciphered, no surviving text explains how this system was kept in place. Even so, the uniformity of the weights suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: people in widely separated settlements shared common standards for measuring goods.
choices.B: every one of the weights was produced in a single workshop in Mohenjo-daro.
choices.C: scholars have learned how the weights were used by reading Indus inscriptions.
choices.D: trade between distant Indus settlements was rare and of little importance.

explanation.why: The key fact is that weights from many distant sites follow the same system of sizes. Even without written records, matching weights across far-apart places point to a shared standard that people in those places followed.
explanation.A: Correct. Identical weight systems in settlements hundreds of kilometers apart indicate shared measuring standards.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says nothing about where the weights were made; uniform sizes could result from many makers following one standard.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the Indus writing has never been deciphered, so no one can read such inscriptions.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A shared system of weights across distant places suggests that exchange mattered, not that it was rare.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Bloodroot, a woodland wildflower of eastern North America, produces seeds with a small fatty attachment called an elaiosome. Native ants carry the seeds to their nests, eat the elaiosomes, and discard the intact seeds in waste piles, where many later sprout. Ecologist Anneke de Vries compared two forests: one with plenty of native ants and one where those ants had been replaced by an invasive ant species that ignores the seeds. Bloodroot seeds sprouted equally well in both forests, but in the second forest nearly every seedling grew within half a meter of a parent plant. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the invasive ants eat bloodroot seeds, which keeps most of the seeds from sprouting.
choices.B: bloodroot seeds can sprout only after native ants have placed them in waste piles.
choices.C: bloodroot will soon disappear from every forest that the invasive ants have entered.
choices.D: native ants help bloodroot spread to new spots but are not needed for its seeds to sprout.

explanation.why: Two findings must be combined. Seeds sprouted equally well with or without native ants, so ants are not needed for sprouting. But without native ants, seedlings stayed right next to parent plants, so the ants are what move seeds to new places.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the invasive ants ignore the seeds, and seeds sprouted equally well in both forests.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Seeds sprouted just as well in the forest without native ants, so they do not need the waste piles to sprout.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text shows only that seedlings stayed near parent plants, not that the species will disappear.
explanation.D: Correct. It matches both findings: equal sprouting in both forests, but movement away from parent plants only where native ants were present.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Prussian blue, often described as the first modern synthetic pigment, was first made in Berlin in the early 1700s and was unavailable to painters before then. A landscape in a private collection bears an inscription dating it to 1690, yet conservator Hiroshi Tanabe detected Prussian blue in its sky. That detection alone would not settle the matter, since restorers routinely repaint damaged areas with pigments of their own era. Tanabe's cross-sections, however, place the Prussian blue in the lowest layer of paint, beneath layers that show no sign of having been scraped away or disturbed. Taken together, these observations suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the date in the inscription is unlikely to reflect when the landscape was actually painted.
choices.B: a later restorer added the Prussian blue when repairing a damaged area of the sky.
choices.C: the landscape was most likely painted in Berlin, where Prussian blue was first produced.
choices.D: the inscription was added to the landscape by someone other than the artist who painted it.

explanation.why: The pigment did not exist before the early 1700s, so a 1690 date is suspicious. The text then rules out the other explanation, a later restoration, because the blue sits in the very first layer under undisturbed paint. The blue was therefore part of the original painting, which means the painting was probably made after 1690.
explanation.A: Correct. If the original paint contains a pigment not available until the early 1700s, the 1690 date is probably not the true date of the painting.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the explanation the cross-sections rule out: the blue lies in the lowest layer, beneath undisturbed paint, so it was not added during a repair.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Knowing where the pigment was invented says nothing about where this painting was made; the pigment could have been sold elsewhere.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The evidence shows only that the date is probably wrong; the artist could have written the inaccurate date, so who added the inscription is not established.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The transit method detects a planet by the slight dimming that occurs when it passes in front of its star. Such a passage is visible only if the planet's orbit happens to be tilted so that, from Earth, the planet crosses the face of its star. For a giant planet orbiting very close to a sunlike star, only about one orbit in ten is tilted this way, and the fraction is far smaller for planets on wider orbits. Surveying 50,000 sunlike stars, astronomer Chidi Nwosu's team detected transits by close-orbiting giant planets around 26 of them, roughly one star in 2,000. Assuming these detections are accurate, the results imply that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: about one in ten of the stars the team surveyed has a close-orbiting giant planet.
choices.B: most close-orbiting giant planets went undetected because they were too small to dim their stars.
choices.C: considerably more of the surveyed stars have close-orbiting giant planets than the team directly detected.
choices.D: the transit method is unable to detect any planet that orbits far from its star.

explanation.why: Only about one in ten close-orbiting giant planets has an orbit tilted so that it transits. So for each such planet the team saw, roughly nine others around surveyed stars would have produced no transit at all. The true number of stars with these planets must therefore be well above the 26 detected.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "One in ten" is the share of orbits that are tilted the right way, not the share of stars that have such planets; the data point to roughly one star in 200.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives orbital tilt, not planet size, as the reason planets go undetected, and giant planets are the easiest to see.
explanation.C: Correct. Because most such orbits are not tilted toward Earth, the 26 detections must be only a fraction of the planets actually present.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the fraction of detectable orbits is "far smaller" for wider orbits, not that such planets can never be detected.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Historians of trade often treat customs ledgers as rough measures of commerce, since officials recorded the cargoes that passed through a port. Akosua Mensah's study of one Mediterranean port complicates that practice. The port's ledgers list pepper and cloves in nearly every year from 1620 to 1649, record almost none from 1650 to 1671, and list them regularly again thereafter. Mensah also located a city charter that, hoping to lure merchants away from a rival port, exempted spice cargoes from customs duties between 1650 and 1671, and she observes that clerks entered a cargo in the ledgers only when duty was owed on it. Mensah's findings therefore suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the port's spice imports fell sharply between 1650 and 1671 before recovering to their earlier level.
choices.B: the exemption succeeded in drawing spice merchants away from the rival port to Mensah's port.
choices.C: customs ledgers cannot serve as reliable evidence for the trade of any port in any period.
choices.D: the ledgers' near silence about spices from 1650 to 1671 may reflect the exemption rather than the trade.

explanation.why: Combine the two facts Mensah found: clerks recorded only cargoes that owed duty, and spice cargoes owed no duty from 1650 to 1671. Spices would then vanish from the ledgers during exactly those years whether or not they kept arriving, so the gap cannot be read as a drop in trade.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This takes the ledgers at face value, which is exactly the reading Mensah's findings call into question.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The charter shows what the city hoped for, but because exempt cargoes went unrecorded, the ledgers cannot show whether more spice merchants actually came.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Mensah's point concerns one gap at one port caused by a specific exemption; it does not show that all ledgers everywhere are unreliable.
explanation.D: Correct. Since untaxed cargoes went unrecorded, the missing spice entries could result from the exemption rather than from fewer spices arriving.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Indus river dolphin, found mainly in Pakistan, has eyes so reduced that it is nearly blind; it finds prey in the river's muddy water by echolocation, interpreting the echoes of its own rapid clicks. Biologist Saima Qureshi recorded the dolphins along two stretches of the river that held similar numbers of fish. Along the stretch with heavy motorboat traffic, the dolphins clicked far more often than along a quiet stretch. Qureshi points out that animals relying on echolocation tend to repeat their signals when background noise drowns out the returning echoes. If her reasoning is correct, the higher click rate in the busy stretch most likely indicates that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the busy stretch offered the dolphins more prey to locate than the quiet stretch did.
choices.B: the dolphins there needed more clicks to perceive their surroundings, not that they had more to find.
choices.C: motorboat noise has left the dolphins in the busy stretch unable to catch enough food to survive.
choices.D: the dolphins there were clicking to keep in contact with one another over the noise of the boats.

explanation.why: Two pieces of the text must be combined. The stretches held similar numbers of fish, so the extra clicking was not caused by more prey. Qureshi's point about noise drowning out echoes then explains it: in the noisy stretch, the dolphins had to click more to get usable echoes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says both stretches held similar numbers of fish, which rules out more prey as the cause.
explanation.B: Correct. With prey similar in both places and noise masking echoes, extra clicks most likely reflect the extra effort needed to sense the surroundings.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text shows that the dolphins clicked more, not that they were failing to catch food or were in danger of starving.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text describes the clicks as a tool for echolocation; it never says the dolphins use them to communicate.

items.subject: science
notes: Venus and Earth are similar in size: Venus's diameter is about 95 percent of Earth's.
Venus has a thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide.
The average surface temperature on Venus is about 465 degrees Celsius.
The average surface temperature on Earth is about 15 degrees Celsius.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between Venus and Earth. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Venus and Earth are similar in size, as Venus's diameter is about 95 percent of Earth's.
choices.B: Venus has a thick atmosphere that is made mostly of carbon dioxide.
choices.C: The average surface temperature on Venus is about 465 degrees Celsius, while on Earth it is about 15 degrees Celsius.
choices.D: Venus, a planet about the size of Earth, has an average surface temperature of about 465 degrees Celsius.

explanation.why: To emphasize a difference, the sentence must mention both planets and show how they are unlike each other. Only one choice sets a fact about Venus directly against the matching fact about Earth.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This sentence emphasizes a similarity in size, the opposite of the goal.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This describes Venus's atmosphere but says nothing about Earth, so no difference is shown.
explanation.C: Correct. It contrasts the two average surface temperatures, about 465 degrees Celsius on Venus and about 15 degrees Celsius on Earth.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It gives Venus's temperature but not Earth's, and it mentions how similar the planets are in size, so it does not emphasize a difference.

items.subject: humanities
notes: The kora is a stringed instrument from West Africa.
Its body is made from a large gourd covered with cowhide.
A traditional kora has 21 strings.
Griots, musicians who preserve history through song, often play the kora.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce the kora to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The kora, a stringed instrument from West Africa, has a body made from a large gourd covered with cowhide.
choices.B: A traditional kora has 21 strings and a body made from a large gourd.
choices.C: Griots are musicians who preserve history through song.
choices.D: Griots often play the kora, which has 21 strings.

explanation.why: Readers who have never heard of the kora first need to know what it is and where it comes from. The best choice names the kora, identifies it as a stringed instrument, gives its region, and adds a detail about how it is made.
explanation.A: Correct. It tells a new reader what the kora is (a stringed instrument), where it is from (West Africa), and what it is made of.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It gives details about the kora's strings and body but never says what the kora is or where it comes from, so it assumes the reader already knows.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This sentence introduces griots, not the kora.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It mentions the kora's strings but does not explain that the kora is an instrument from West Africa, so an unfamiliar reader is left guessing.

items.subject: history_social
notes: The Shalimar Gardens in Lahore were built in 1641–1642 under the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan.
The gardens are laid out on three descending terraces.
They contain more than 400 fountains.
In 1981 they were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with Lahore Fort.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the age of the gardens to an audience unfamiliar with them. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Built in 1641–1642 under the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, the Shalimar Gardens in Lahore are nearly four centuries old.
choices.B: The Shalimar Gardens contain more than 400 fountains spread across three terraces.
choices.C: In 1981, the Shalimar Gardens and Lahore Fort were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
choices.D: The Shalimar Gardens in Lahore are laid out on three descending terraces.
