choices.D: To hide the water supply from neighboring communities

walkthrough: The key words are "why" and "underground," which lead to the second sentence.
That sentence gives the reason: water in an open channel "would evaporate quickly."
C restates that reason.
A is the strongest trap because it uses real words from the text, but the shafts explain how the tunnels were dug and repaired, not why they were underground.

cards.title: Advanced: main ideas that come after a turn
steps: Notice the old view or expectation that opens the text and the word that turns away from it.
Build your summary around what comes after the turn, keeping any hedge such as "suggests" or "may."
Check the scope of each choice: does it claim "all" when the text says "some" or "several"?
Reject choices that state the old view, a single piece of evidence, or a conclusion stronger than the text.

worked_example.passage: Feathers were long regarded as an adaptation for flight, since they are essential to the way modern birds fly. Fossils discovered in China since the 1990s have complicated that view. Several small dinosaurs preserved there were covered in simple, hairlike feathers, yet their short arms and body shapes show that they could not fly. Many paleontologists now think that feathers first evolved for other purposes, such as keeping warm or attracting mates, and were only later used for flight.
worked_example.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Fossils from China show that every dinosaur was covered in hairlike feathers.
choices.B: Feathers may have evolved for purposes other than flight before birds used them to fly.
choices.C: Feathers are essential to the way that modern birds are able to fly.
choices.D: Feathers first evolved to help dinosaurs keep warm rather than to attract mates.

walkthrough: The text opens with the old view (feathers were for flight) and turns at "have complicated that view."
After the turn, the point is that feathers probably first served other purposes, a view held by "many paleontologists," not proven.
B states that point and keeps the hedge with "may."
A is too broad because the text says "several small dinosaurs," not every dinosaur, and D picks one purpose when the text gives warmth and attracting mates only as examples.

cards.title: Challenge: implied ideas in literary passages
steps: Track what the character does and notices, not only what the character says.
Look for a gap between the character's expectation and what actually happens.
Summarize the feeling or change the passage shows, using only actions and details in the text.
Reject choices that make the feeling more dramatic, or more negative, than the details support.

worked_example.passage: For thirty years Nadia had described the footbridge behind her grandfather's house as enormous, a swaying span over a river so wide that she had once refused to cross it. When she finally returned to the village, she found a few planks over a stream she could have jumped across. She stood on it for a long while, gripping the rail exactly where her small hand had once gripped it, and was surprised to find that she felt no disappointment at all, only a kind of tenderness toward the child who had needed the bridge to be so large.
worked_example.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Nadia is upset to discover that the village has replaced her grandfather's bridge with a smaller one.
choices.B: Nadia regrets that she was too frightened to cross the bridge when she was a child.
choices.C: Nadia realizes that the bridge has been poorly maintained since her grandfather's death.
choices.D: Nadia's return shows her how much her memory had enlarged the bridge, and she responds with affection rather than letdown.

walkthrough: The gap is between the "enormous" bridge in Nadia's stories and the "few planks" she actually finds.
Her response is stated through her surprise: "no disappointment at all, only a kind of tenderness."
D captures both the enlarged memory and the affectionate response.
A is the most attractive trap because the bridge is smaller than she said, but nothing suggests it was replaced, and she is not upset.

lessons.title: Command of Evidence (Quantitative)
lessons.what_is_tested: These questions pair a short text with a table or graph and test whether you can choose data that completes a statement or supports a claim. The right answer must be both accurate according to the data and relevant to what the text says.
lessons.how_to_spot: There is a table or graph, and the question asks which choice "most effectively uses data from the table" or "from the graph" to complete a statement or support a claim.
method: Read the text first and find the exact statement or claim the data must serve.
Read the title, labels, and units of the table or graph before looking at any numbers.
Decide what comparison the claim needs: highest value, change over time, or a difference between two groups.
Check each choice against the data; cross out any choice with a wrong number or a reversed comparison.
From the accurate choices, pick the one that matches the claim, not just the topic.
pitfalls: Choosing a true data point that does not address the claim (true but irrelevant).
Mixing up rows, columns, or series, or reading a comparison backward (reversed).
Choosing a statement that fits the claim but is not shown in the data at all (not in the text).
Picking a total or an average when the claim is about a difference between two groups.
Skipping the labels and units, then misreading what a number measures.

cards.title: Foundations: read the labels, then find the number
steps: Read the sentence with the blank and note what it asks for (most, least, or a specific value).
Read the table's title and column headings so you know what each number means.
Find the row or bar that answers the question.
Choose the answer that names it with the correct number, and check that number against the data.

worked_example.passage: Students at a school in Lahore counted the bird species they could identify during one spring morning in each of four city parks. They found that the park with the greatest variety of birds was ______

data.title: Bird Species Identified in Four City Parks on One Spring Morning

worked_example.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: Market Park, where 265 individual birds were counted.
choices.B: Hill Park, where 23 bird species were identified.
choices.C: Canal Park, where 212 individual birds were counted.
choices.D: River Park, where 31 bird species were identified.

walkthrough: The statement asks for the park with the "greatest variety of birds," which means the most species, not the most birds.
The "Bird species identified" column shows River Park highest, with 31.
D names River Park with the correct number.
A is the trap: Market Park had the most individual birds, but many birds of a few species is not variety.

cards.title: Medium: support a claim about every case
steps: Underline the claim's scope words, such as "every," "each," "most," or "only."
Work out which comparison in the data would prove the claim at that scope.
Check each choice for accuracy first, then for whether it covers the whole scope.
Reject choices that are accurate but describe only one row or a different comparison.

worked_example.passage: Covering soil with a layer of straw, called mulch, slows the evaporation of water from the ground. Agronomist Bilal Chaudhry hypothesized that mulching would reduce the amount of irrigation water needed for each of the three crops he grew in a test field in Punjab, not just for one or two of them.

data.title: Irrigation Water Used per Season (millimeters)

worked_example.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Chaudhry's hypothesis?

choices.A: Tomatoes needed more irrigation water than wheat or chilies, both with and without mulch.
choices.B: Each of the three crops needed less irrigation water with straw mulch than without it.
choices.C: With mulch, wheat needed 335 millimeters of water, the least of any crop in the test.
choices.D: Mulching reduced the water needed for tomatoes by 90 millimeters.

walkthrough: The scope words are "each of the three crops," so the support must cover all three.
In every row, the "With straw mulch" number is smaller than the "Without mulch" number.
B states that for all three crops, so it supports the hypothesis at the right scope.
D is accurate (520 minus 430 is 90) but covers only one crop, which the hypothesis says is not enough.

cards.title: Advanced: compare two series
steps: Name the two groups or series the claim compares and the direction it predicts for each.
Find the start and end values for both series and note how each changed.
Prefer the choice that describes both series in the way the claim needs, with correct numbers.
Reject choices about one series only, or about a pattern both series share.

worked_example.passage: In 2019, farmers in the village of Khanpur, in a dry region of western India, built a small check dam to hold back seasonal streams so that rainwater could soak into the ground. Hydrologist Priya Nair compared well-water levels in Khanpur with those in the nearby village of Sonari, which has similar rainfall but no dam. Nair concluded that while groundwater kept sinking in Sonari, it recovered in Khanpur after the dam was built.

data.title: Average Depth to Water in Village Wells before the Monsoon

worked_example.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Nair's conclusion?

choices.A: Between 2019 and 2022, the depth to water in Khanpur's wells fell from 19 to 13 meters, while in Sonari it grew from 19 to 22 meters.
choices.B: In 2017, the depth to water was 18 meters in Khanpur and 17 meters in Sonari.
choices.C: Between 2019 and 2022, the depth to water grew from 19 to 22 meters in Sonari.
choices.D: In both villages, the depth to water was 19 meters in 2019.

walkthrough: The claim compares two villages after the dam: water kept sinking in Sonari but recovered in Khanpur.
On the graph, a smaller depth means the water is closer to the surface; Khanpur went from 19 to 13 meters and Sonari from 19 to 22 meters after 2019.
A gives both trends with correct numbers, so it supports the whole conclusion.
C is accurate and fits half of the claim, but without Khanpur's recovery it cannot show the contrast Nair describes.

cards.title: Challenge: find the comparison the claim really needs
steps: Rewrite the claim as a precise comparison ("group X gained more than group Y").
Calculate any differences the claim depends on; the key often uses a difference, not a raw value.
Watch for choices that are accurate and impressive but answer a different question, such as which group scored highest.
Pick the choice that would convince a skeptic of exactly this claim and nothing broader.

worked_example.passage: A school district introduced a daily small-group reading program for one year. District officials pointed to the rise in average scores, but education researcher Grace Mwangi argues that the program's main value lay elsewhere: in her view, it helped the weakest readers far more than it helped students who were already reading well.

data.title: Average Reading Scores before and after the Program, by Starting Level

worked_example.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Mwangi's argument?

choices.A: Students in the highest quarter had the highest scores after the program, at 84 points.
choices.B: Average scores increased in every group of students during the program.
choices.C: Students in the lowest quarter gained 19 points, while those in the highest quarter gained only 3 points.
choices.D: Students in the middle half scored 70 points after the program, up from 63 points.

walkthrough: Mwangi's claim is a comparison of gains: the weakest readers improved far more than strong readers.
The gains are 61 minus 42 = 19 for the lowest quarter and 84 minus 81 = 3 for the highest.
C states both gains correctly, which is exactly the comparison the claim needs.
B is the most attractive trap because it is true, but it supports the officials' point about overall improvement, not Mwangi's point about who benefited most.

lessons.title: Command of Evidence (Textual)
lessons.what_is_tested: These questions test whether you can tell which evidence would support or weaken a specific claim. The SAT asks them because judging evidence, not just collecting facts, is at the heart of academic reading.
lessons.how_to_spot: The question asks which finding, "if true," would "most directly support" or "most directly weaken" a claim, or which quotation "most effectively illustrates the claim."
method: Find the exact claim, hypothesis, or argument in the text and underline it.
Check the question word: support or weaken. Write it down so you do not flip it halfway through.
Turn the claim into a prediction: "If the claim is right, we should see ___."
Accept each finding as true, then ask whether it bears directly on that specific claim.
Choose the finding that fits your prediction (for support) or breaks it (for weaken).
pitfalls: Choosing a finding that is about the topic but supports a different claim (true but irrelevant).
Choosing a finding that would weaken the claim when the question asks for support, or the other way around (reversed).
Choosing a finding that goes beyond the claim or proves something larger (too broad).
Doubting whether a finding is true; the question tells you to accept it, so judge only its relevance.
Missing the alternative explanation that the best evidence must rule out at harder levels.

cards.title: Foundations: claim first, then evidence
steps: Underline the claim, often the sentence with "hypothesizes," "argues," or "thinks."
Note whether the question asks you to support or to weaken it.
Predict what you would expect to see if the claim were true.
Pick the finding that matches your prediction most directly.

worked_example.passage: Gray squirrels bury nuts in many separate spots each fall and dig most of them up in winter. Some people assume the squirrels simply sniff out any buried nut they come across. Biologist Hannah Price disagrees. She hypothesizes that each squirrel remembers the locations of the nuts it buried itself.
worked_example.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Price's hypothesis?

choices.A: Squirrels bury more nuts in years when trees produce especially large crops.
choices.B: Squirrels dug up nuts they had buried themselves far more often than nuts that other squirrels had buried nearby.
choices.C: Squirrels often dig up nuts buried by other squirrels as easily as their own.
choices.D: Squirrels have a strong sense of smell that they use to find many kinds of food.

walkthrough: The claim is that each squirrel remembers where it buried its own nuts.
If that is true, a squirrel should find its own nuts more often than nuts buried by others, which smell just as strong.
B is exactly that result.
C is the trap: it is about the same topic but would weaken the claim, since it suggests smell rather than memory.

cards.title: Medium: weakening a cause
steps: Identify the cause and the effect in the claim ("X caused Y").
To weaken, look for a finding where the effect happens without the cause, or the cause appears without the effect.
To support, look for a finding where the effect follows the cause and not otherwise.
Ignore findings that describe the cause or the effect alone without linking them.

worked_example.passage: In 2021, a city added protected bicycle lanes to several busy streets in its central district. Over the next two years, the number of traffic accidents in the district fell by about 20 percent. City official Daniel Okoro argues that the new bike lanes were responsible for the decrease.
worked_example.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Okoro's argument?

choices.A: More residents of the central district began cycling to work after the lanes were built.
choices.B: Accidents on the streets with new lanes fell more than accidents on other streets in the district.
choices.C: Traffic accidents fell by about the same amount in districts of the city that received no new lanes.
choices.D: Several other cities have also built protected bicycle lanes in recent years.

walkthrough: The claim links a cause (the bike lanes) to an effect (fewer accidents).
To weaken it, we want the effect without the cause: fewer accidents in places that got no lanes.
C shows that, which suggests something citywide, not the lanes, explains the drop.
B is the trap because it is about accidents and lanes, but it would support the argument, not weaken it.

cards.title: Advanced: match the exact scope of the claim
steps: Restate the claim with all its specific parts, including the proposed mechanism ("because of X, not Y").
Ask which part of the claim is actually in question; the best evidence tests that part.
Distrust findings that are consistent with the claim but equally consistent with other explanations.
Prefer a finding that changes only the factor the claim names while everything else stays the same.

worked_example.passage: Birds of several species that live in cities sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species that live in forests. Ecologist Marta Kowalczyk hypothesizes that the difference is caused specifically by traffic noise, which is mostly low-pitched and can drown out low notes, rather than by other features of city life such as tall buildings or different food sources.
worked_example.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kowalczyk's hypothesis?

choices.A: In several cities, the birds studied sang at a higher pitch than birds of the same species in nearby forests.
choices.B: City birds of these species eat different foods than forest birds of the same species do.
choices.C: Tall buildings in cities reflect sound in ways that can make songs harder to hear.
choices.D: Within the same city, birds lowered the pitch of their songs on days when a major road nearby was closed to traffic.

walkthrough: The claim has a specific part: traffic noise, not buildings or food, causes the higher pitch.
The best test changes only the traffic noise, keeping the same city, buildings, and food.
D does that: when the road closed, the birds sang lower, so the noise itself seems to matter.
A is the near miss: it is true of the pattern, but it does not separate traffic noise from the other city features the hypothesis rules out.

cards.title: Challenge: rule out the rival explanation
steps: Find both explanations in the text: the author's claim and the rival one (often introduced by "skeptics" or "however").
Ask what result each explanation predicts, and look for where the predictions differ.
Choose a finding that fits the claim and that the rival explanation cannot easily account for.
Reject findings that both explanations predict equally, however relevant they look.

worked_example.passage: At a site in Jordan occupied thousands of years before farming began in the region, archaeologists found many large, flat grinding stones. Archaeologist Layla Haddad argues that people at the site were already grinding wild cereal grains into flour. Skeptics respond that grinding stones were also used to crush mineral pigments such as red ochre, which people of the period used for decoration, so the stones alone do not show that grain was processed.
worked_example.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haddad's argument?

choices.A: Microscopic starch grains from wild barley and wheat were found on the grinding surfaces of the stones, which showed no traces of ochre.
choices.B: Many of the grinding stones were found close to hearths where people cooked food.
choices.C: Red ochre has been found at a number of other sites from the same period in the region.
choices.D: The grinding stones were heavy and made from a type of rock found only a few kilometers away.

walkthrough: Haddad says the stones ground grain; the skeptics say they might have ground pigment.
The two views predict different residues on the stones: grain starch versus ochre.
A finds grain starch and no ochre, which fits Haddad and is hard for the skeptics to explain.
B is the most attractive trap, but stones near hearths fit both views, since people could prepare pigment and food in the same living area.

lessons.title: Cross-Text Connections
lessons.what_is_tested: These questions give you two short texts on the same topic and test whether you can see how they relate. You must understand each author's position and then predict how one would react to the other, or find a point both would accept.
lessons.how_to_spot: There are two passages labeled Text 1 and Text 2, and the question asks how the author of Text 2 would respond to Text 1 or what both authors would agree with.
method: Read Text 1 and sum up its main claim in one short line.
Read Text 2 and sum it up in one line, then find the exact point where it touches Text 1.
Label the relationship: agrees, disagrees, adds information, offers a different explanation, or accepts one part and questions another.
Predict the answer in your own words before reading the choices.
Check each choice for who said what and for how much of Text 1 it says Text 2 rejects.
pitfalls: Assuming that Text 2 rejects everything in Text 1 when it really questions only one part (too broad).
Mixing up which author said what (reversed).
Choosing a statement that is true of one text only for a "both authors would agree" question (true but irrelevant).
Picking a response about a detail of Text 1 rather than the specific claim the question names.
Treating new information in Text 2 as disagreement when it simply adds to Text 1.

cards.title: Foundations: one line per text
steps: After Text 1, write or think one line: "Text 1 says ___."
After Text 2, do the same: "Text 2 says ___."
Ask whether the two lines agree, disagree, or simply add to each other.
Choose the answer that matches your label and mentions the right idea from each text.

worked_example.passage: A long-standing popular belief holds that the great pyramids of Giza in Egypt were built by enslaved people who were forced to labor under harsh conditions. This picture has appeared in many novels and films.
worked_example.passage_b: Archaeologists excavating near the Giza pyramids have uncovered the remains of a town where the builders lived, including bakeries and large stores of food. Some workers were buried in tombs close to the pyramids, an honor that would have been unlikely for enslaved laborers. These finds suggest that the builders were organized, fed, and respected workers.
worked_example.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief described in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the builders worked under harsh, forced conditions
choices.B: By arguing that the pyramids were built much later than people believe
choices.C: By noting that novels and films are the best sources about the builders
choices.D: By pointing to evidence that the builders were not treated as enslaved people

walkthrough: Text 1 in one line: the pyramids were built by enslaved people.
Text 2 in one line: town remains and honored tombs suggest the builders were respected workers.
Those lines disagree, and Text 2 disagrees by using evidence, which is what D says.
A is the trap because it repeats Text 1's view, which Text 2's evidence works against.

cards.title: Medium: agree, disagree, or add?
steps: Find the single claim each text makes most strongly.
For a "both would agree" question, list ideas that appear in both texts, not just in one.
If Text 2 adds a condition or a cost, it is usually adding to Text 1, not rejecting it.
Test each choice against both texts separately; it must pass both tests.

worked_example.passage: City planners in many hot regions now plant trees along streets to keep neighborhoods cooler. A tree's leaves shade the pavement from direct sunlight, and the water they release into the air takes heat with it as it evaporates. On summer afternoons, tree-lined streets can be several degrees cooler than bare ones.
worked_example.passage_b: Shade clearly lowers temperatures on city streets, but trees are not the right choice everywhere. In very dry cities, young trees need regular watering for years before they are established, and where water is scarce, that cost can be hard to justify. In such places, shade structures such as awnings and covered walkways may provide much of the cooling at a lower cost in water.
worked_example.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Trees are the most effective way to cool streets in every city.
choices.B: Shade can make city streets cooler than streets without it.
choices.C: Shade structures should replace street trees in hot regions.
choices.D: Young trees in dry cities rarely need to be watered.

walkthrough: Text 1 says street trees cool neighborhoods, partly by shading pavement; Text 2 says shade "clearly lowers temperatures" but that trees cost water in dry places.
Both texts accept that shade cools streets, so that is the shared idea.
B states it without adding anything either author would dispute.
C is the strongest trap because it comes from Text 2, but even Text 2 limits it to very dry cities, and Text 1 would not accept it.

cards.title: Advanced: accepts one part, questions another
steps: Split Text 1 into its evidence and its conclusion.
Check which of the two Text 2 accepts and which it questions.
Prefer an answer that captures this split over one that says Text 2 rejects Text 1 completely.
Reject choices that give Text 2 an objection it never makes, even if the objection sounds reasonable.

worked_example.passage: Pollen grains settle each year at the bottom of lakes, so layers of lake mud preserve a record of the plants that grew nearby. In mud cores from a lake in the hills of northern Thailand, researchers found that tree pollen fell sharply about 2,000 years ago while grass pollen rose. They concluded that early farmers had cleared the surrounding forest to plant crops.
worked_example.passage_b: The pollen record from the lake shows convincingly that forest gave way to grassland around 2,000 years ago. But pollen alone cannot tell us why. A long period of drought would produce the same pattern, since many trees die when rain fails while grasses survive. Unless the same layers also contain signs of human activity, such as charcoal from burning or pollen from crop plants, the farming explanation remains one possibility among others.
worked_example.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?

choices.A: By rejecting the claim that the forest around the lake declined about 2,000 years ago
choices.B: By accepting that the forest declined but arguing that the pollen does not show what caused the decline
choices.C: By arguing that drought, rather than farming, was clearly the cause of the forest's decline
choices.D: By questioning whether pollen can survive for 2,000 years in the mud at the bottom of a lake

walkthrough: Text 1's evidence is the pollen shift; its conclusion is that farmers cleared the forest.
Text 2 accepts the evidence ("shows convincingly") but says pollen "cannot tell us why," so it questions only the conclusion.
B captures that split.
C is the near miss: Text 2 offers drought as a possibility, not as the clear cause, so C is stronger than the text.

cards.title: Challenge: the exact scope of the disagreement
steps: State the precise question each text answers; harder pairs often answer slightly different questions.
Note what Text 2 grants before it objects; words like "granted," "may," or "did matter" mark a concession.
Predict a response that includes both the concession and the objection.
Compare the near-miss choices word by word for scope (all vs. some, start vs. spread, cause vs. effect).

worked_example.passage: Historians often credit the rapid rise of reading ability in nineteenth-century England to the Education Acts of the 1870s and 1880s, which made elementary schooling widely available and, from 1880, compulsory for young children. Once every child was required to attend school, the argument runs, the spread of literacy followed.
worked_example.passage_b: Records of the share of brides and grooms able to sign their names in marriage registers show that literacy in England had been climbing steadily for decades before attendance was made compulsory. Historian Ruth Penhaligon therefore argues that the laws did not set the rise in motion. They did matter, she grants, in reaching the children whom the earlier growth had passed by, especially those in the poorest districts, but the laws largely confirmed a change that families, churches, and charities had already begun.
worked_example.stem: Based on the texts, how would Penhaligon most likely respond to the argument in Text 1?

choices.A: By denying that the Education Acts had any effect on literacy in England
choices.B: By agreeing that compulsory schooling was what started the rise in literacy
choices.C: By arguing that the laws did not begin the rise in literacy, though they extended it to some children
choices.D: By claiming that marriage registers are unreliable evidence of a person's ability to read

walkthrough: Text 1 answers the question "what caused the rise?" with the laws; Text 2 shows literacy was rising before the laws.
Penhaligon's objection is about the start of the rise, and her concession is that the laws helped reach the poorest children.
C includes both the objection and the concession.
A is the most attractive trap because Text 2 does downplay the laws, but "any effect" ignores her statement that the laws "did matter."

lessons.title: Form, Structure, and Sense
lessons.what_is_tested: These questions test grammar inside a sentence: verbs that agree with their subjects, the right tense and verb form, pronouns that match what they refer to, plurals and possessives, and modifiers that describe the right word. The SAT asks them because these choices decide whether a sentence is clear and correct.
lessons.how_to_spot: The choices are different forms of the same word or phrase (for example "is" and "are," "its" and "their," or "researcher's" and "researchers'"), and the question asks which choice "conforms to the conventions of Standard English."
method: Look at the choices first and name what changes: verb, pronoun, possessive, or the start of a main clause.
For a verb, find its real subject and cross out phrases between them; then check the tense clues in the text.
For a pronoun, find the noun it replaces and match number (singular or plural) and case (they or them).
For a possessive, ask who owns what and how many owners there are.
For a sentence that begins with a describing phrase, make sure the word right after the comma is the thing being described.
pitfalls: Making the verb agree with the nearest noun instead of its real subject.
Confusing "its" (belonging to it) with "it's" (it is), or "their" with "they're."
Using "their" for a singular noun such as a company, a jury, or a species.
Choosing an "-ing" form or "to" form where the sentence needs a main verb, leaving it without one.
Picking a choice where the opening phrase describes the wrong person or thing (a dangling modifier).
lessons.us_uk: In American English, a collective noun such as team, committee, jury, government, or company usually takes a singular verb and pronoun ("the committee is announcing its decision"); the British habit of "the committee are announcing their decision" is marked wrong on the SAT.

cards.title: Foundations: find the real subject
steps: Find the verb at the blank and ask, "Who or what is doing this?"
Cross out phrases that begin with words like "of," "in," "that," or "which" between the subject and the verb.
Decide whether the subject is singular or plural.
Choose the verb form that matches and fits the tense of the rest of the text.

worked_example.passage: Each year, huge flocks of lesser flamingos gather at Lake Natron in Tanzania to breed. The pink feathers of these birds ______ their color from pigments in the tiny algae that the flamingos eat; birds that eat less of this food gradually turn paler.
worked_example.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: gets
choices.B: getting
choices.C: get
choices.D: to get

walkthrough: The thing that gets its color is "The pink feathers"; "of these birds" is a phrase in between.
"Feathers" is plural, and the text is in the present tense.
The plural present verb is "get," so C is correct.
B and D are traps because "getting" and "to get" are not main verbs, which would leave the sentence without one; A is singular.

cards.title: Medium: pronouns and possessives
steps: Find the noun the pronoun replaces; it may be a sentence or more away.
Decide whether that noun is singular or plural; a group acting as one unit (a jury, a company) is singular.
Use "its" and "their" to show belonging; use "it's" and "they're" only where "it is" or "they are" would make sense.
Read the sentence aloud in your head with your choice to confirm it is clear.

worked_example.passage: After reviewing more than two hundred entries over four months, the jury for the new science museum in Kuala Lumpur announced ______ choice: a design by a young architect that arranges the galleries like a series of overlapping leaves.
worked_example.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it's
choices.B: its
choices.C: their
choices.D: they're

walkthrough: The pronoun refers to "the jury," and the blank shows the choice belongs to the jury.
A jury acting as one group is singular in Standard American English.
The singular possessive is "its," so B is correct.
C is the trap many students choose because a jury has many members, but the noun "jury" is singular; A means "it is," which makes no sense here.

cards.title: Advanced: long gaps between subject and verb
steps: Find the first noun of the sentence's main subject, before any "of," "that," or "which."
Bracket everything between that noun and the blank, even if it contains several plural nouns.
Match the verb to the bracketed-out subject and keep the tense consistent with the time the text describes.
Reread the stripped-down sentence ("The collection... throws new light") to check it.

worked_example.passage: The collection of letters, diaries, and photographs that historian Nadia Haddad found in a forgotten storeroom of the old customs house in Beirut ______ new light on daily life in the port a century ago. Many of the letters were written by clerks who described the ships, cargoes, and travelers they saw each day.
worked_example.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: have thrown
choices.B: are throwing
choices.C: throw
choices.D: throws

walkthrough: The main subject is "The collection"; everything from "of letters" to "Beirut" describes it.
"Collection" is singular, even though plural nouns like "photographs" sit right before the blank.
The singular verb is "throws," so D is correct.
C is the strongest trap because it agrees with the nearby plural nouns, not with the real subject.

cards.title: Challenge: modifiers and main verbs
steps: When a sentence opens with a describing phrase and a comma, ask who or what that phrase describes.
Make sure that exact noun comes right after the comma, not a person who did something else or a possessive form of the noun.
In long sentences, check that the main subject has a real main verb, not an "-ing" or "to" form.
Eliminate choices that are grammatical on their own but make the opening phrase describe the wrong thing.

worked_example.passage: Discovered in 1974 by farmers digging a well near the city of Xi'an, ______ It includes thousands of life-size clay soldiers, horses, and chariots buried near the tomb of China's first emperor more than two thousand years ago.
worked_example.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the Terracotta Army is one of the most famous archaeological finds in the world.
choices.B: archaeologists have called the Terracotta Army one of the most famous finds in the world.
choices.C: Xi'an's Terracotta Army is one of the most famous archaeological finds in the world.
choices.D: there is the Terracotta Army, one of the most famous archaeological finds in the world.

walkthrough: The opening phrase describes something "discovered... by farmers digging a well," which is the Terracotta Army.
So "the Terracotta Army" must come right after the comma.
A does that, and the next sentence's "It" then refers clearly to the army.
B is the most tempting trap because it is a correct sentence on its own, but it says the archaeologists were discovered by farmers; C puts "Xi'an's" first, so the phrase describes the city.

lessons.title: Inferences
lessons.what_is_tested: These questions test whether you can draw the conclusion that follows logically from the information in a text. The SAT asks them because careful readers go one step beyond what is stated without jumping further than the evidence allows.
lessons.how_to_spot: The text ends with a blank, usually after words like "suggests that," "most likely," or "therefore," and the question asks which choice "most logically completes the text."
method: Read the text and list its key facts (the premises) in your head, one by one.
Look closely at the words just before the blank; they tell you what kind of conclusion is needed.
Ask, "Given these facts, what must be true?" and predict an ending in your own words.
Choose the ending that follows from the facts without adding new ideas.
Prefer a modest, careful conclusion over a sweeping one; "may" and "most likely" are often signs of the key.
pitfalls: Choosing a conclusion that goes further than the facts, such as "always" or "every" (too broad).
Choosing an ending that contradicts one of the facts (reversed).
Choosing an ending that brings in an idea the text never mentions, even if it is true in real life (not in the text).
Using only one premise when the conclusion needs two of them combined.
Treating a possible explanation as the only possible one.

cards.title: Foundations: one fact leads to one conclusion
steps: Find the fact that explains how something works.
Find the new situation the last sentence describes.
Apply the fact to the situation and predict the ending.
Choose the ending that matches; reject choices that add extra claims.

worked_example.passage: Leaves look green because they contain large amounts of chlorophyll, a green pigment plants use to capture energy from sunlight. Many leaves also contain yellow and orange pigments, but the much larger amount of chlorophyll usually hides them. In autumn, many trees stop producing chlorophyll, and the chlorophyll already in their leaves breaks down. As a result, the yellow and orange pigments ______
worked_example.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: disappear from the leaves along with the chlorophyll.
choices.B: become visible because the green color no longer covers them.
choices.C: start capturing more energy than chlorophyll ever did.
choices.D: are produced for the first time to replace the chlorophyll.

walkthrough: The fact: chlorophyll's green "usually hides" the yellow and orange pigments.
The new situation: in autumn, chlorophyll breaks down.
If what was hiding them is gone, the other colors can be seen, so B follows.
D is the trap: the text says the pigments were in the leaves already, so they are not produced for the first time.

cards.title: Medium: conclude only what the evidence shows
steps: Ask what the evidence actually measures (when, where, or what it records).
Predict the conclusion that the evidence directly supports.
Check each choice for a hidden extra step, such as a cause the text never establishes.
Choose the choice that needs no extra step.

worked_example.passage: In regions where tree growth is limited mainly by rainfall, trees add wide growth rings in wet years and narrow rings in dry years. The outermost ring of a beam shows the last year the tree grew before it was cut down. Researchers studying the wooden beams of an abandoned mountain village found that every beam ended with about eight very narrow rings in a row. These findings suggest that ______
worked_example.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the village was abandoned because a long drought destroyed its crops.
choices.B: the trees used for the beams died from lack of water before they were cut.
choices.C: rainfall in the region increased sharply after the beams were cut.
choices.D: the trees used for the beams were cut down at the end of a long dry period.

walkthrough: The evidence records the last years each tree grew before it was cut, and those years were all very dry.
So the direct conclusion is about when the trees were cut: after a run of dry years.
D says exactly that.
A is the most tempting trap, but the rings date when the trees were cut, not when the village was abandoned, and the text says nothing about crops.

cards.title: Advanced: combine two premises
steps: Number the premises: premise 1 is usually a general rule, premise 2 a specific observation.
Put them together: "If rule 1 is true and observation 2 happened, then ___."
Keep the hedge the text uses ("likely," "suggests"); the key rarely sounds more certain than the evidence.
Reject choices that use only one premise or that need a third fact the text never gives.

worked_example.passage: Many lichens are highly sensitive to sulfur dioxide, an air pollutant released by burning coal; one common species cannot grow where levels of the gas are more than very low. In a 1980 survey of a European industrial city, botanists found none of this species on the trees in the city center. When botanist Elena Varga repeated the survey in 2020, she found it growing on trees throughout the center. Taken together, these observations suggest that ______
worked_example.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: levels of sulfur dioxide in the city center have most likely fallen since 1980.
choices.B: the air in the city center is now completely free of all pollutants.
choices.C: the lichen spread to the city center because the climate there has become warmer.
choices.D: levels of sulfur dioxide in the city center have probably risen since 1980.

walkthrough: Premise 1: this lichen grows only where sulfur dioxide is very low. Premise 2: it was absent in 1980 but present in 2020.
Combined, the lichen's return means sulfur dioxide is probably now very low, lower than in 1980.
A states that and keeps the hedge "most likely."
B is the near miss: the lichen tells us about one gas, so claiming the air is free of "all pollutants" is too broad; C needs a fact about climate the text never gives.

cards.title: Challenge: when a change in method explains the result
steps: Separate what was observed from how it was observed or recorded.
Ask whether a change in the method, not a real change in the world, could explain the result.
Look for a second piece of evidence that settles which explanation is better.
Choose the carefully hedged conclusion that fits both pieces of evidence; reject sweeping claims about the method or the world.

worked_example.passage: Seabird researcher Tomás Arriaga counted the nests of a ground-nesting seabird on a small island using photographs taken from a drone in 2016 and again in 2023. The 2023 photographs showed about 30 percent fewer nests. However, new rules introduced in 2020 to protect the birds from disturbance required drones to fly much higher, and from that height, nests partly hidden under low shrubs are hard to see. Arriaga's team also counted nests on foot in several marked plots across the island in both years and found nearly identical numbers. These findings suggest that ______
worked_example.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the seabird population on the island declined by about 30 percent between 2016 and 2023.
choices.B: drone photographs can never provide useful counts of nesting seabirds.
choices.C: the drop in the drone count may reflect the change in how the photographs were taken rather than a real decline in nests.
choices.D: the new rules about drone flights caused many of the birds to abandon their nests.

walkthrough: The observation is fewer nests in the photos, but the method changed: higher flights hide nests under shrubs.
The second piece of evidence, the ground counts, showed almost no change, which favors the method explanation.
C combines both points and stays appropriately hedged with "may."
A is the most attractive trap because it takes the drone count at face value, ignoring the ground counts; B overreaches by saying drones can "never" help.

lessons.title: Rhetorical Synthesis
lessons.what_is_tested: These questions give you a student's research notes and a writing goal, and test whether you can pick the sentence that uses the notes to meet that goal. Every choice is accurate, so the skill is matching purpose, not checking facts.
lessons.how_to_spot: A list of bulleted notes appears with no passage, and the question begins "The student wants to..." and asks which choice "most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal."
method: Read the question first, before the notes, and underline the goal's key words (for example "difference," "similarity," "introduce," "aim and method," "generalization").
Note any audience in the goal; an "unfamiliar" audience needs a basic explanation of what something is.
Skim the notes only to see which facts would serve that goal.
Check each choice against the goal, not against the notes; every choice will be true.
Make sure the choice does every part of the goal, such as both items in a comparison.
pitfalls: Choosing the longest choice or the one with the most facts instead of the one that meets the goal (misses the goal).
Choosing a sentence that covers only half of a two-part goal, such as one item in a comparison (too narrow).
Choosing an accurate fact from the notes that is unrelated to the goal (true but irrelevant).
Reading the notes carefully before the goal, which wastes time and makes every fact seem important.
Forgetting the audience: for an unfamiliar audience, a sentence that assumes the reader already knows the subject misses the goal.

cards.title: Foundations: underline the goal
steps: Read the goal first and underline its key word, such as "difference" or "similarity."
For a difference or similarity, look for a choice that mentions both things being compared.
Check that the choice actually shows the difference or similarity, often with words like "while," "whereas," "both," or "like."
Ignore whether a choice is interesting or detailed; ask only whether it does the goal.

notes: The Thar Desert lies in northwestern India and southeastern Pakistan.
It covers about 200,000 square kilometers.
The Sahara stretches across much of North Africa.
It covers about 9 million square kilometers, making it the largest hot desert in the world.
worked_example.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference in size between the two deserts. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The Thar Desert, which covers about 200,000 square kilometers, lies in northwestern India and southeastern Pakistan.
choices.B: The Sahara, which stretches across much of North Africa, is the largest hot desert in the world.
choices.C: The Thar Desert covers about 200,000 square kilometers, while the Sahara covers about 9 million square kilometers.
choices.D: The Thar Desert lies in South Asia, and the Sahara stretches across much of North Africa.

walkthrough: The goal's key words are "difference in size between the two deserts."
So the sentence must give a size for both deserts and set them side by side.
C gives both areas joined by "while," which shows the difference, so it is correct.
D is the trap because it mentions both deserts, but it compares their locations, not their sizes.

cards.title: Medium: writing for an unfamiliar audience
steps: When the goal mentions an audience "unfamiliar" with the subject, the sentence must explain what the subject is.
Look for a choice that names the subject and gives a short description (what kind of thing it is, where it comes from).
Reject choices that assume the reader already knows the subject, even if they contain impressive facts.
Confirm that the choice still matches any other part of the goal.

notes: Jamdani is a traditional weaving technique from Bangladesh.
It produces fine, lightweight cotton cloth, often used for saris.
Weavers add the patterns by hand while the cloth is being woven on a loom, rather than printing or stitching them on afterward.
In 2013, UNESCO added the traditional art of jamdani weaving to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage.
worked_example.stem: The student wants to introduce jamdani to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 2013, UNESCO added the traditional art of jamdani weaving to its list of intangible cultural heritage.
choices.B: Jamdani, a traditional weaving technique from Bangladesh, produces fine cotton cloth with patterns woven in by hand on the loom.
choices.C: Jamdani patterns are added by hand during weaving rather than printed or stitched on afterward.
choices.D: Fine, lightweight jamdani cloth is often used to make saris.

walkthrough: The goal is to "introduce" jamdani to readers who have never heard of it.
Such readers first need to know what jamdani is and where it comes from.
B says it is a weaving technique from Bangladesh and briefly describes the cloth, so it introduces the subject.
A is the strongest trap: the UNESCO fact is impressive, but it never tells an unfamiliar reader what jamdani actually is.

cards.title: Advanced: aim, method, or finding?
steps: For a study, sort the notes into three labels: aim (what the researcher wanted to know), method (what was done), and finding (what was found).
Underline which of those labels the goal asks for; it may ask for two of them.
Check each choice for exactly those parts; a choice with the wrong pair misses the goal.
Do not reward a choice for including extra background that the goal does not ask for.

notes: Eurasian blackbirds usually begin singing shortly before dawn.
Ecologist Mei Lin Chou wanted to know whether artificial light at night affects when city blackbirds start their morning song.
Her team placed sound recorders at 12 sites in one city, each with a different level of night lighting.
Blackbirds at the most brightly lit sites began singing about 40 minutes earlier than those at the darkest sites.
worked_example.stem: The student wants to present the aim and the finding of Chou's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Chou's team placed sound recorders at 12 city sites with different levels of night lighting to study blackbirds.
choices.B: Eurasian blackbirds usually begin singing shortly before dawn, and Chou's team recorded them at 12 sites.
choices.C: Chou wanted to know whether artificial light at night affects when city blackbirds start their morning song, so her team placed sound recorders at 12 sites.
choices.D: Investigating whether artificial light at night affects when city blackbirds start singing, Chou found that birds at the brightest sites began about 40 minutes earlier than those at the darkest sites.

walkthrough: The notes contain an aim (note 2), a method (note 3), and a finding (note 4); the goal asks for the aim and the finding.
D states the question Chou investigated and the 40-minute result.
So D meets both parts of the goal.
C is the near miss: it gives the aim but pairs it with the method, so the finding, which the goal requires, is missing.

cards.title: Challenge: goals with a built-in contrast
steps: Underline every part of the goal, including words like "unusual," "challenge," or "compared with."
Find the note that supplies the background or expectation and the note that supplies the surprise.
Choose the sentence that puts both together, usually with "although," "unlike," or "while."
Reject choices that report the surprising fact alone; without the background, the contrast the goal asks for is missing.

notes: Bar-tailed godwits are shorebirds that breed in Alaska and spend the northern winter in Australia and New Zealand.
Most migrating birds stop several times along the way to rest and feed.
Godwits cannot rest on the ocean's surface.
In 2022, a five-month-old godwit fitted with a tracking tag flew from Alaska to Tasmania, Australia, without stopping.
The flight covered about 13,560 kilometers and took about 11 days.
worked_example.stem: The student wants to emphasize how unusual the young godwit's flight was compared with the journeys of most migrating birds. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Unlike most migrating birds, which stop several times to rest and feed, a young bar-tailed godwit flew about 13,560 kilometers from Alaska to Tasmania without stopping.
choices.B: In 2022, a five-month-old bar-tailed godwit flew from Alaska to Tasmania, a journey of about 13,560 kilometers that took about 11 days.
choices.C: Bar-tailed godwits, which cannot rest on the ocean's surface, breed in Alaska and spend the northern winter in Australia and New Zealand.
choices.D: A young bar-tailed godwit wearing a tracking tag flew for about 11 days in 2022, traveling from Alaska to Tasmania, Australia.

walkthrough: The goal has two parts: show the flight was unusual and compare it with "most migrating birds."
The comparison comes from note 2 (most birds stop) and the surprise from notes 4 and 5 (nonstop, 13,560 kilometers).
A joins them with "Unlike," so it meets the whole goal.
B is the most attractive trap because its numbers are impressive, but it never mentions other birds, so the comparison is missing.

lessons.title: Text Structure and Purpose
lessons.what_is_tested: These questions test whether you can see why a text was written and how its parts fit together. You may be asked for the main purpose, the overall structure, or the job of one underlined sentence.
lessons.how_to_spot: The question asks for "the main purpose of the text," "the overall structure of the text," or "the function of the underlined sentence."
method: Read the whole text before looking at the choices; purpose depends on where the text ends up, not where it starts.
Say the author's aim in your own words: "The author wants to ___."
Pick the verb that fits: explain, describe, argue, challenge, compare, show a change, or present a finding and its limit.
For an underlined sentence, read the sentences before and after it and name its job (evidence, example, contrast, background, qualification).
Check every word of your choice; one wrong verb or one wrong part makes it wrong.
pitfalls: Picking a choice that describes only one sentence or detail instead of the whole text (too narrow).
Picking a choice whose verb is stronger than the text, such as "argue" or "prove" when the author only explains or suggests (too broad).
Choosing the right topic with the wrong attitude, such as "criticize" when the author is neutral (wrong tone).
Getting the direction of an underlined sentence backward, saying it supports a claim when it actually qualifies or challenges it (reversed).
For literary texts, picking a dramatic interpretation the passage never shows.

cards.title: Foundations: name the author's job
steps: Read every sentence, not just the first one.
Finish this sentence in your head: "The author wants to ___."
Choose the verb that matches: explain how or why, describe, tell a story, or argue.
Cross out choices that cover only one sentence or that add opinions the text never gives.

worked_example.passage: Cutting an onion breaks open its cells and lets chemicals that were stored separately mix together. Their reaction produces a gas that drifts upward and irritates the eyes, which respond by making tears to wash it away. Chilling an onion before cutting it slows the reaction, so less of the gas reaches the eyes.
worked_example.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that onions should always be stored in a refrigerator
choices.B: To describe how onions are grown and harvested
choices.C: To explain why cutting onions can make people's eyes water
choices.D: To compare onions with other vegetables that irritate the eyes

walkthrough: Every sentence is about what happens when an onion is cut and why the eyes respond.
So the author wants to explain a cause: why cutting onions brings tears.
C states that aim with the right verb, "explain."
A is the strongest trap because chilling is mentioned, but the text only notes that it slows the reaction; it never argues for always refrigerating onions.

cards.title: Medium: the job of an underlined sentence
steps: Read the sentence just before and just after the underlined one.
Ask what the underlined sentence does for its neighbors: gives evidence, an example, a contrast, a correction, or background.
Put its job in your own words before you read the choices.
Check the direction of each choice: does the sentence support, correct, or limit the idea it connects to?

worked_example.passage: Many people believe that bats are blind, perhaps because most species fly at night and find insects by echolocation, listening for the echoes of their own calls. <u>In fact, every bat species can see, and many large fruit bats find their food mainly by sight and smell.</u> Echolocation is better understood as an extra sense that lets some bats hunt in darkness where eyes alone would not be enough.
worked_example.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It gives an example of how echolocation helps bats hunt at night.
choices.B: It corrects the common belief described in the previous sentence.
choices.C: It introduces fruit bats as the main subject of the rest of the text.
choices.D: It supports the idea that bats see poorly and must rely on echoes.

walkthrough: The sentence before states a belief ("bats are blind"), and the underlined sentence opens with "In fact," a signal of correction.
Its job, in our words, is "shows the belief is wrong."
B says exactly that.
D is the strongest trap because it is about bats' eyesight, but it reverses the sentence's direction: the sentence shows bats can see.

cards.title: Advanced: track the turn and the strength
steps: Mark where the text turns ("however," "though," "yet," "still") and note what changes there.
Separate what the evidence shows from what the author concludes about it.
Match the strength of the choice to the text: "suggests" and "qualifies" are weaker than "proves" and "rejects."
Reject choices that are accurate about one part but leave out the limit or the turn.

worked_example.passage: Homing pigeons released far from their lofts usually find their way back, but how they do so has long been debated. A team led by biologist Paula Lindqvist fitted some pigeons with small magnets on their backs and others with brass weights of the same size. On sunny days, both groups returned home equally well; on overcast days, the pigeons carrying magnets were far more likely to become lost. The results suggest that pigeons can navigate using Earth's magnetic field, though they seem to rely on it mainly when the sun is hidden. Exactly how the birds detect the field remains unclear.
worked_example.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To present a finding about how pigeons navigate and the conditions under which it applies
choices.B: To argue that pigeons depend mainly on Earth's magnetic field to find their way home
choices.C: To explain the process by which pigeons detect Earth's magnetic field
choices.D: To describe the methods used to train homing pigeons to return to their lofts

walkthrough: The text turns at "though": the magnetic sense is used "mainly when the sun is hidden," and it ends by saying the mechanism is unclear.
So the author presents a result and limits it, rather than making a big claim.
A captures both the finding and its condition.
B is the near miss: it uses the right topic but says "mainly," which is stronger than the text, since pigeons with magnets did fine on sunny days; C is wrong because the mechanism "remains unclear."

cards.title: Challenge: map the structure piece by piece
steps: Split the text into its parts and label each in two or three words (common claim, why it appeals, objection, explanation).
Compare your labels with each choice in order, one part at a time.
Test every verb in a choice: "dismisses," "concedes," and "qualifies" mean very different things.
Eliminate a choice as soon as one part does not match; a structure choice must be right all the way through.

worked_example.passage: A popular claim holds that the Great Wall of China is the only human-made structure visible from the Moon. The idea is easy to believe: the wall's many sections together stretch for thousands of kilometers. Yet length is not what makes an object visible from far away. Width and contrast with the surroundings matter more, and most of the wall is only a few meters wide and built of stone and earth close in color to the land around it. Astronauts who traveled to the Moon reported seeing continents and clouds but no individual human-made structures. The claim survives, perhaps, because it seems only fitting that so enormous a project should be visible from space.
worked_example.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents a claim, offers evidence that supports it, and then notes a minor exception to it.
choices.B: It compares the Great Wall with other large structures to show which can be seen from the Moon.
choices.C: It describes how the Great Wall was built and then explains why it is difficult to photograph.
choices.D: It presents a popular claim, grants why it seems believable, explains why it is mistaken, and suggests why it persists.

walkthrough: Labeling the parts gives: popular claim, why it is easy to believe, why it is wrong (width and color, astronauts' reports), and why the claim survives.
D matches all four parts in order.
A fails at its second part, because the text's evidence works against the claim, not for it.
B and C each describe something the text never does: it compares no other structures and says nothing about building methods or photographs.

lessons.title: Transitions
lessons.what_is_tested: These questions test whether you can choose the word or phrase that shows how one idea connects to the next. The SAT asks them because transitions tell a reader whether an idea continues, contrasts, explains, or illustrates what came before.
lessons.how_to_spot: A blank sits at the start of a sentence (or after a semicolon), the choices are words or phrases such as "However," "For example," and "As a result," and the question asks for "the most logical transition."
method: Cover the choices.
Read the sentence before the blank and the sentence with the blank, and sum up each in a few words.
Name the relationship between them: contrast, cause and effect, example, addition, concession, restatement, or sequence.
Choose the transition that expresses exactly that relationship.
Reread the two sentences with your choice to confirm they make sense together.
pitfalls: Choosing a transition from the right family but with the wrong meaning, such as "Instead" where "Nevertheless" is needed (wrong logic).
Reading only the sentence with the blank and ignoring the sentence before it.
Choosing "For example" when the second sentence is a result, or "As a result" when it is only an example.
Choosing "Moreover" (adds a new point) when the sentence only restates the previous one ("In other words").
Letting a contrast word inside the sentence trick you into choosing a contrast transition.

cards.title: Foundations: same direction or opposite?
steps: Cover the choices and read both sentences.
Ask: does the second sentence continue the first idea or go against it?
If it continues, ask whether it is a result, an example, or just one more point.
Choose the transition that names that relationship.

worked_example.passage: Honey contains very little water and is slightly acidic, and most bacteria and molds cannot grow in those conditions. ______ honey stored in a sealed jar can stay safe to eat for a very long time.
worked_example.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: However,
choices.B: For example,
choices.C: Because of this,
choices.D: Similarly,

walkthrough: The first sentence explains a property of honey; the second describes what follows from it.
The second sentence continues the first, as a result of it.
"Because of this" signals cause and effect, so C is correct.
A is the trap: "However" signals a contrast, but long storage life agrees with the fact that microbes cannot grow.

cards.title: Medium: example, addition, or result?
steps: Check whether the second sentence is general or specific compared with the first.
If it names one specific case of the general idea, it is an example.
If it is something the first idea causes, it is a result; if it is a separate point of equal weight, it is an addition.
Choose the transition for that relationship and reread.

worked_example.passage: Many desert animals avoid the fierce heat of the middle of the day by being active mainly at night. ______ the fennec fox of the Sahara spends the hottest hours resting in a cool underground burrow and comes out after sunset to hunt insects and small rodents.
worked_example.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: For instance,
choices.B: In contrast,
choices.C: As a result,
choices.D: Nevertheless,

walkthrough: The first sentence is general ("many desert animals"); the second names one animal.
The fennec fox does exactly what the first sentence describes, so it is an example.
"For instance" introduces an example, so A is correct.
C is the strongest trap because the fox's habits are linked to the heat, but the second sentence does not describe a result of the first; it gives one case of it.

cards.title: Advanced: telling contrast words apart
steps: When the relationship is a contrast, decide which kind it is.
Concession ("Nevertheless," "Even so," "Still,"): the first sentence gives a reason to expect something, and the second says it happened anyway.

Replacement ("Instead," "Rather,"): the second sentence says what happened in place of something the first sentence ruled out; plain contrast ("However," "In contrast,") simply sets two different facts side by side.
Test each contrast choice by asking what it would claim about the two sentences, and keep only the one that is true.

worked_example.passage: On its first flight in 1903, the Wright brothers' airplane stayed in the air for only about twelve seconds and covered roughly 37 meters, less than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet. ______ the flight is regarded as a turning point in history, because it was the first controlled, sustained flight of a powered airplane with a pilot aboard.
worked_example.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Instead,
choices.B: Therefore,
choices.C: Similarly,
choices.D: Nonetheless,

walkthrough: The first sentence makes the flight sound small; the second says it was a turning point anyway.
That is a concession: a reason to expect little, followed by importance despite it.
"Nonetheless" signals exactly this, so D is correct.
A is the near miss: "Instead" would mean the flight's importance replaced its short length, but both facts are true at once.

cards.title: Challenge: restating, specifying, or adding
steps: Check whether the sentence after the blank gives new information or says the same thing in different words.
If it says the same thing more simply, it is a restatement ("In other words," "That is,").
If it gives a precise detail of a broader statement, it is a specification ("Specifically,"); if it adds a separate new point, it is an addition ("Moreover,").
Compare the last two candidates carefully against the exact content of both sentences before choosing.

worked_example.passage: Ecologists distinguish between a species' fundamental niche, the full range of conditions in which it could survive, and its realized niche, the narrower range it actually occupies once competitors are present. On rocky shores in Scotland, for example, one species of barnacle can live across a wide band of the shore when a rival barnacle is removed but is limited to the upper shore when the rival is present. ______ the rival does not change where the first species is able to live; it changes where the species actually lives.
worked_example.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Moreover,
choices.B: In other words,
choices.C: For example,
choices.D: Specifically,

walkthrough: The barnacle sentence shows the rival affecting the realized niche but not the fundamental one.
The last sentence says the same thing in plainer terms, without adding new facts, so it is a restatement.
"In other words" signals a restatement, so B is correct.
A is the strongest trap, but "Moreover" would announce a new point, and the final sentence adds no new information.

lessons.title: Words in Context
lessons.what_is_tested: These questions test whether you can choose the word that fits a sentence both logically and precisely. The SAT asks them because strong readers use context to pin down meaning, including the exact shade of a word and its less common senses.
lessons.how_to_spot: The text has a blank and the question asks for "the most logical and precise word or phrase," or a word appears in quotation marks and the question asks what it "most nearly" means.
method: Read the whole text first; the clue is often after the blank, not before it.
Find the clue: a restatement (colon, "in other words"), a contrast ("although," "instead," "but"), or a cause and effect ("because," "so").
Cover the choices and say your own word for the blank, including whether it is positive or negative and how strong it is.
Uncover the choices and pick the one closest to your prediction.
Read the sentence again with your choice in place to make sure it fits the logic and the tone.
pitfalls: Choosing a word that suits the topic but not the sentence, such as a science word for a science passage (not in the text).
Missing a contrast signal and picking a word that means the opposite of what the context needs (reversed).
Accepting a near-synonym that is too strong, too weak, or slightly off in meaning (wrong tone or shade).
Choosing the most familiar meaning of a quoted word when the text uses a second, less common meaning.
Picking the most impressive-sounding word because it seems "SAT-like" instead of testing it in the sentence.

cards.title: Foundations: predict, then match
steps: Cover the answer choices so they cannot steer you.
Read the full text and underline the words that describe or explain the blank.
Say a simple word of your own that would fit the blank, even an everyday one.
Choose the answer closest to your word, then read the sentence once more with it in place.

worked_example.passage: The new public library in the town was designed to be ______: its ramps, wide doors, low shelves, and large-print signs allow visitors of all ages and abilities to find books and move around the building easily.
worked_example.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: ornate
choices.B: temporary
choices.C: accessible
choices.D: crowded

walkthrough: With the choices covered, the clue is the colon: everything after it explains what the blank means.
Ramps, wide doors, and large-print signs all let "visitors of all ages and abilities" use the building, so a prediction is "easy to use for everyone."
"Accessible" means exactly that, so C matches the prediction.
"Ornate" is the strongest trap because libraries can be decorated, but nothing after the colon is about decoration.

cards.title: Medium: follow the contrast or the cause
steps: Circle signal words such as "in fact," "instead," "although," "because," and "so."
Decide whether the blank must agree with the earlier idea or push against it.
Predict a word with the right direction (positive or negative) before looking at the choices.
Cross out choices that fit the topic but would reverse the logic of the signal word.

worked_example.passage: Many visitors expect the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, one of the driest places on Earth, to be lifeless. In fact, in the rare years when unusually heavy rain falls, seeds that have waited in the soil for years sprout all at once, and parts of its plains become ______ with flowers, an event known in Spanish as the desierto florido, or "flowering desert."
worked_example.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: carpeted
choices.B: barren
choices.C: threatened
choices.D: measured

walkthrough: The signal "In fact" pushes against the expectation that the desert is "lifeless," so the blank must describe something full of life.
Seeds sprouting "all at once" suggests the plains are thickly covered, so a prediction is "covered."
"Carpeted" means covered thickly across a surface, which matches.
"Barren" is the strongest trap because it fits the desert topic, but it repeats the expectation that "In fact" rejects.

cards.title: Advanced: match the strength, not just the direction
steps: Predict both the direction of the word and how strong it should be.
Look for hedges and limits nearby ("only," "but," "not entirely," "in some cases") that set the strength.
When two choices point the same way, compare their degree: "skeptical" is milder than "dismissive," "suggest" is milder than "prove."
Test the final choice against the sentence that follows the blank, since it often supplies the evidence.

worked_example.passage: Early reports claimed that a new battery design would make long charging times a thing of the past. Engineer Kofi Boateng's laboratory tests support a more ______ view. His batteries did charge about 30 percent faster than standard ones, but only at moderate temperatures; in cold conditions, the advantage disappeared almost entirely.
worked_example.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: enthusiastic
choices.B: dismissive
choices.C: arbitrary
choices.D: tempered

walkthrough: "More ______ view" is contrasted with the early reports' big claim, so the blank must be less excited than those reports.
The next sentence sets the strength: the batteries did improve, "but only at moderate temperatures," so the view is positive yet limited, something like "cautious."
"Tempered" means moderated or held back, which fits a real but limited benefit.
"Dismissive" points the right way but is far too strong, because the tests did show a 30 percent improvement.

cards.title: Challenge: hard words and second meanings
steps: Predict from context as usual; your prediction matters more than knowing every choice.
Eliminate the words you know do not fit, then judge the unfamiliar one by what is left and by its roots.
For "most nearly mean" questions, expect the common meaning of the word to be a trap and replace the word with each choice.
Check the whole passage, not only the sentence, because the deciding clue may be a clause or sentence away.

worked_example.passage: When coffee leaf rust, a fungal disease, was first noticed on plantations in Sri Lanka in 1869, few planters were alarmed; the orange spots on the leaves seemed a minor nuisance. Over the next two decades, however, the fungus spread from estate to estate, and because no treatment then available checked its advance, the island's coffee harvests collapsed. Many estates were replanted with tea, the crop for which Sri Lanka later became famous.
worked_example.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "checked" most nearly mean?

choices.A: examined
choices.B: halted
choices.C: marked
choices.D: confirmed

walkthrough: The sentence says no treatment "checked its advance," and as a result harvests "collapsed," so the word must mean something a treatment would do to a spreading disease.
A prediction is "stopped" or "held back."
Replacing the word, "no treatment halted its advance" keeps the cause and effect, so B is correct.
"Examined" is the trap: it is the everyday meaning of "checked," but examining the fungus would not have saved the harvests.

grammar.title: Grammar handbook
grammar.intro: The SAT tests a small, predictable set of Standard English rules, and every grammar question in the Reading and Writing section comes from the eight topics below. Learn each rule, study the wrong/right pairs, and pay special attention to the notes where British habits can lead you astray on an American test.

sections.title: Subject-verb agreement
sections.rule: A verb must match its subject in number: a singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. The hard part is finding the true subject when other words sit between it and the verb.
points: Cross out prepositional phrases ("of the samples," "in the northern valleys") before you match the verb; the subject is never inside one.
Two subjects joined by "and" are plural; with "or" or "nor," the verb matches the subject closer to it.
Phrases such as "along with," "as well as," and "together with" do not make a singular subject plural.
When the sentence is inverted ("Among the findings was..." or "There are..."), find the subject after the verb.
Collective nouns such as "team," "committee," "jury," and "government" are singular in American English.

examples.wrong: The collection of letters written by the early settlers were donated to the museum in 1952.
examples.right: The collection of letters written by the early settlers was donated to the museum in 1952.
examples.why: The subject is "collection," which is singular; "letters" and "settlers" sit inside modifying phrases.

examples.wrong: Each of the three proposals require a separate budget.
examples.right: Each of the three proposals requires a separate budget.
examples.why: "Each" is singular, so the verb must be "requires," even though "proposals" comes right before it.

examples.wrong: The lead engineer, along with her two assistants, have reviewed the bridge design.
examples.right: The lead engineer, along with her two assistants, has reviewed the bridge design.
examples.why: "Along with her two assistants" is an added phrase, not part of the subject; the subject "engineer" is singular.

examples.wrong: Hidden beneath the floor of the old library was several clay tablets.
examples.right: Hidden beneath the floor of the old library were several clay tablets.
