examples.why: In this inverted sentence the subject "tablets" comes after the verb, and it is plural.

examples.wrong: The research committee have published their annual report.
examples.right: The research committee has published its annual report.
examples.why: In American English a collective noun like "committee" is treated as one unit, so it takes a singular verb and the pronoun "its."

sections.us_uk: British English often treats collective nouns as plural ("the government are," "the team have"). On the SAT, which follows American usage, treat them as singular: "the government is," "the team has," "the orchestra performs its program."

sections.title: Pronoun-antecedent agreement
sections.rule: A pronoun must agree in number with the noun it refers to (its antecedent), and that noun must be clear. Use the correct case: subject pronouns (he, they, who) as subjects, object pronouns (him, them, whom) as objects.
points: Find the antecedent first, then check whether it is singular or plural.
Singular things, organizations, and collective nouns take "it" and "its"; plural nouns take "they," "them," and "their."
"Its" is possessive; "it's" means "it is" or "it has." "Their" is possessive; "they're" means "they are."
"Who" and "whom" refer to people; "which" refers to things; "that" can refer to either.
If a pronoun could point to two different nouns, the sentence is unclear; the SAT prefers a clear noun.
Keep the same point of view: do not switch from "one" to "you" or from "students" to "you" in a sentence.

examples.wrong: The university updated their admissions policy last spring.
examples.right: The university updated its admissions policy last spring.
examples.why: "University" is a single institution, so the pronoun must be the singular "its."

examples.wrong: Migratory birds use the Earth's magnetic field to guide its long journeys.
examples.right: Migratory birds use the Earth's magnetic field to guide their long journeys.
examples.why: The journeys belong to the birds, a plural noun, so the pronoun must be "their."

examples.wrong: The coral reef is losing it's color as ocean temperatures rise.
examples.right: The coral reef is losing its color as ocean temperatures rise.
examples.why: The sentence needs a possessive (the reef's color), which is "its" with no apostrophe; "it's" means "it is."

examples.wrong: The prize was shared between my lab partner and I.
examples.right: The prize was shared between my lab partner and me.
examples.why: "Between" is a preposition, so it takes the object pronoun "me." Test it by removing the partner: "shared with me."

examples.wrong: When the architect met the engineer, she explained the new load calculations.
examples.right: When the architect met the engineer, the engineer explained the new load calculations.
examples.why: "She" could mean either woman, so the reader cannot tell who explained; naming the person removes the ambiguity.

sections.us_uk: As with verbs, British writers often use "they" or "their" for a company or team ("the club announced their new coach"). In American English, and on the SAT, a single organization takes "it" and "its."

sections.title: Plurals and possessives
sections.rule: A plural simply means more than one and takes no apostrophe. A possessive shows ownership and uses an apostrophe: before the s for one owner, after the s for a plural owner that already ends in s.
points: Plural, no ownership: researchers, cities, species. No apostrophe.
Singular possessive: the researcher's notes (one researcher). Add 's.
Plural possessive: the researchers' notes (several researchers). Add only an apostrophe after the s.
Irregular plurals that do not end in s add 's: children's, women's, people's.
Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: its, their, whose, ours, yours.
Ask two questions: Is it one or more than one? Does it own the next word?

examples.wrong: The scientist's gathered in Nairobi to compare their data.
examples.right: The scientists gathered in Nairobi to compare their data.
examples.why: "Scientists" is only a plural here; nothing follows that they own, so no apostrophe is needed.

examples.wrong: Both farmers fields were damaged by the early frost.
examples.right: Both farmers' fields were damaged by the early frost.
examples.why: There are several farmers and they own the fields, so the plural possessive "farmers'" is needed.

examples.wrong: The novel's characters reveal it's author's interest in village life.
examples.right: The novel's characters reveal its author's interest in village life.
examples.why: The author belongs to the novel, so the possessive pronoun "its" is needed, not the contraction "it's."

examples.wrong: The museum opened a new wing devoted to childrens' art.
examples.right: The museum opened a new wing devoted to children's art.
examples.why: "Children" is already plural and does not end in s, so the possessive is "children's."

examples.wrong: The study's compared rainfall in Dhaka and Chittagong, and the studies' results were similar.
examples.right: The studies compared rainfall in Dhaka and Chittagong, and the studies' results were similar.
examples.why: The first noun is the subject of "compared" and owns nothing, so it is the plain plural "studies"; the second owns "results," so it is the plural possessive "studies'."

sections.title: Verb forms and tense
sections.rule: Use the tense that matches the time frame of the passage, keep tenses consistent unless the timing really changes, and make sure every sentence has a main (finite) verb. An -ing word or a "to" verb alone cannot be the main verb of a sentence.
points: Look at nearby verbs and time words ("in 1890," "currently," "by the time") to choose the tense.

Simple past (discovered) for a finished event; present perfect (has discovered) for something that began in the past and continues or matters now; past perfect (had discovered) for an event before another past event.
A sentence needs a finite verb: "The team analyzing the data" is not a sentence; "The team analyzed the data" is.
After a helping verb such as "has," "have," or "had," use the past participle: has begun, had written, have swum.
Keep parallel verbs in the same form: "to measure, record, and compare," not "to measure, recording, and compare."
In passages about literature or ongoing findings, the present tense is common: "In the novel, the narrator describes..."

examples.wrong: The geologist collecting rock samples from the riverbed for three summers.
examples.right: The geologist collected rock samples from the riverbed for three summers.
examples.why: "Collecting" cannot serve as the main verb, so the original is a fragment; "collected" gives the sentence a finite verb.

examples.wrong: By the time the rescue team arrived, the storm already passes.
examples.right: By the time the rescue team arrived, the storm had already passed.
examples.why: The storm passed before the team arrived, so the earlier past event takes the past perfect "had passed."

examples.wrong: Since 2010, the city plants more than forty thousand trees.
examples.right: Since 2010, the city has planted more than forty thousand trees.
examples.why: "Since 2010" signals an action that started in the past and continues to now, which calls for the present perfect.

examples.wrong: The poet had wrote most of her early work in Lahore.
examples.right: The poet had written most of her early work in Lahore.
examples.why: After "had," use the past participle "written," not the simple past "wrote."

examples.wrong: Volunteers were asked to count the nests, measuring the eggs, and record the weather.
examples.right: Volunteers were asked to count the nests, measure the eggs, and record the weather.
examples.why: The three actions form a list after "to," so all three verbs must be in the same base form.

sections.us_uk: American English prefers some past forms that British English spells differently: "learned" and "burned" (not "learnt" and "burnt"), "dreamed," "spelled," and "gotten" as a past participle ("has gotten"). It also uses the simple past where British speakers often use the present perfect ("I just finished" rather than "I've just finished"); on the SAT, time words in the passage decide the tense.

sections.title: Modifier placement
sections.rule: A descriptive phrase must sit right next to the word it describes. When a sentence opens with a descriptive phrase followed by a comma, the noun right after the comma must be the person or thing that phrase describes.
points: Ask "Who or what is doing this?" for an opening phrase, then make that noun the first word after the comma.
A dangling modifier has no correct noun to attach to: "Walking through the market, the spices smelled strong" (the spices were not walking).
Possessives do not fix a dangling modifier: "Born in Kandy, the artist's paintings..." is still wrong, because the paintings were not born.
Place words like "only," "almost," and "nearly" directly before the word they limit.
On the SAT, these questions often put the blank right after the comma; choose the option that starts with the correct noun.

examples.wrong: After analyzing thousands of seed samples, the drought-resistant variety was identified by the botanists.
examples.right: After analyzing thousands of seed samples, the botanists identified the drought-resistant variety.
examples.why: The botanists did the analyzing, so "the botanists" must come right after the comma.

examples.wrong: Born in a small village near Kathmandu, the climber's first ascent came at age nineteen.
examples.right: Born in a small village near Kathmandu, the climber made her first ascent at age nineteen.
examples.why: The ascent was not born in a village; the climber was. A possessive form does not make the climber the subject.

examples.wrong: Known for its bright blue tiles, tourists often photograph the old mosque.
examples.right: Known for its bright blue tiles, the old mosque is often photographed by tourists.
examples.why: The mosque is the thing known for its tiles, so it must follow the comma.

examples.wrong: The students almost read every article on the reading list.
examples.right: The students read almost every article on the reading list.
examples.why: "Almost" should limit "every article"; placed before "read," it suggests they nearly read but did not.

sections.title: Linking clauses
sections.rule: An independent clause has a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a sentence. Two independent clauses may be joined only by a period, a semicolon, a colon (when the second explains the first), or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).
points: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice, which is always wrong on the SAT.
Two independent clauses with no punctuation at all form a run-on sentence.
Words like "however," "therefore," "moreover," and "for example" are not conjunctions; between two clauses they need a semicolon or period before them and usually a comma after.
A semicolon must have a complete sentence on both sides.
A dependent clause (starting with "because," "although," "when," "which") cannot stand alone; join it to a main clause, usually with a comma or nothing.
Test each side of the boundary: can it stand alone? Then pick punctuation that is allowed between those two pieces.

examples.wrong: The glacier has retreated nearly two kilometers, scientists expect it to shrink further.
examples.right: The glacier has retreated nearly two kilometers; scientists expect it to shrink further.
examples.why: Both sides are independent clauses, so a comma alone creates a comma splice; a semicolon can join them.

examples.wrong: The experiment was repeated twice, however, the results did not change.
examples.right: The experiment was repeated twice; however, the results did not change.
examples.why: "However" is not a conjunction, so it cannot join two clauses with commas alone; it needs a semicolon (or period) before it.

examples.wrong: The ancient port city traded with Rome and China its merchants grew wealthy.
examples.right: The ancient port city traded with Rome and China, and its merchants grew wealthy.
examples.why: Two independent clauses with no punctuation make a run-on; a comma plus "and" joins them correctly.

examples.wrong: Although the drug performed well in trials; regulators asked for more data.
examples.right: Although the drug performed well in trials, regulators asked for more data.
examples.why: The first part starts with "although," so it is a dependent clause and cannot stand before a semicolon; a comma is correct.

examples.wrong: The results pointed to one cause. Rising soil salinity.
examples.right: The results pointed to one cause: rising soil salinity.
examples.why: "Rising soil salinity" is not a sentence. A colon after a complete clause can introduce the explanation.

sections.title: Supplements (nonessential elements)
sections.rule: A supplement is extra information that could be removed without breaking the sentence. It must be set off by a matching pair of punctuation marks: two commas, two dashes, or two parentheses, unless it begins or ends the sentence.
points: Remove the extra phrase: if the sentence still works and keeps its basic meaning, the phrase is nonessential.
Use the same mark on both sides: comma...comma, dash...dash, or parenthesis...parenthesis. Never mix a comma with a dash.
Essential information (needed to identify which one) takes no commas: "The student who won the award spoke first."
"Which" with commas introduces nonessential information; "that" introduces essential information and takes no commas.

A title or name directly after a description is often essential and takes no commas: "the physicist Abdus Salam." If the description already identifies one person, the name is set off: "Pakistan's first Nobel laureate in science, Abdus Salam, ..."
A colon or a single dash can add one explanatory element at the end of a complete sentence.

examples.wrong: The Indus River, which begins in Tibet flows through Pakistan to the Arabian Sea.
examples.right: The Indus River, which begins in Tibet, flows through Pakistan to the Arabian Sea.
examples.why: "Which begins in Tibet" is extra information, so it needs a comma on both sides.

examples.wrong: The telescope's mirror, more than six meters across — was built in segments.
examples.right: The telescope's mirror — more than six meters across — was built in segments.
examples.why: A supplement must open and close with the same mark; here a comma is paired with a dash.

examples.wrong: The novelist, Chinua Achebe, wrote Things Fall Apart in 1958.
examples.right: The novelist Chinua Achebe wrote Things Fall Apart in 1958.
examples.why: There are many novelists, so the name is needed to identify which one; essential information takes no commas.

examples.wrong: The vaccine that was developed in only eleven months, was tested on thousands of volunteers.
examples.right: The vaccine, which was developed in only eleven months, was tested on thousands of volunteers.
examples.why: If the vaccine is already known, the clause is extra detail: use "which" with a pair of commas. A single comma between subject and verb is never correct.

sections.us_uk: American English uses "that" (no commas) for essential clauses and "which" (with commas) for extra information much more strictly than British English, where "which" often appears without commas. American style also tends to write a dash with no spaces ("mirror—more than"); either spacing is fine, but the two marks must match.

sections.title: End and internal punctuation
sections.rule: Use colons, semicolons, apostrophes, quotation marks, and question marks according to their specific jobs. Never put punctuation where the sentence does not pause grammatically, such as between a subject and its verb or between a verb and its object.
points: A colon must follow a complete sentence; what comes after it explains, lists, or illustrates.
Semicolons can separate items in a list when the items already contain commas.
Do not place a colon right after a verb or a preposition ("The samples included: ..." is wrong).
No single comma between a subject and its verb, between a verb and its object, or before a preposition that completes the idea.
A direct question ends with a question mark; a reported question ("She asked whether...") ends with a period.
In American English, periods and commas always go inside closing quotation marks; colons and semicolons go outside.

examples.wrong: The expedition carried three essential tools, a compass, a rope ladder, and a water filter.
examples.right: The expedition carried three essential tools: a compass, a rope ladder, and a water filter.
examples.why: A complete sentence introduces a list, so a colon is needed; a comma would make "tools" look like one item in a series.

examples.wrong: The most surprising result of the survey, was the low rate of participation.
examples.right: The most surprising result of the survey was the low rate of participation.
examples.why: A single comma should never separate a subject ("result") from its verb ("was").

examples.wrong: The historian wondered why the treaty had failed so quickly?
examples.right: The historian wondered why the treaty had failed so quickly.
examples.why: This is a reported (indirect) question inside a statement, so it ends with a period.

examples.wrong: The festival featured musicians from Karachi, Pakistan, Colombo, Sri Lanka, and Kathmandu, Nepal.
examples.right: The festival featured musicians from Karachi, Pakistan; Colombo, Sri Lanka; and Kathmandu, Nepal.
examples.why: Each list item already contains a comma, so semicolons separate the items clearly.

examples.wrong: The guide called the trail "easy to follow", but many hikers disagreed.
examples.right: The guide called the trail "easy to follow," but many hikers disagreed.
examples.why: In American English the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.

sections.us_uk: British English usually uses single quotation marks ('like this') and places a period or comma outside the closing mark unless it belongs to the quotation. The SAT follows American rules: double quotation marks, with periods and commas always inside ("like this.") and colons and semicolons outside ("like this"; next). Question marks and exclamation points go inside only if they belong to the quoted words. Watch spelling too: color, center, analyze, organize, traveled, defense, program, and catalog are the American forms.

sections.title: How the Reading and Writing section works
body: The Reading and Writing section comes first on the digital SAT. It has **two modules**, and each module has **27 questions** and a time limit of **32 minutes**. That is 54 questions in 64 minutes for the whole section. After it, there is a short break before the Math section.

Every question has its own short passage (or a pair of passages, a table, a graph, or a set of notes) and one multiple-choice question with four answer choices. You never read one long passage for many questions.

The test is **adaptive by module**. Module 1 contains a broad mix of easier, medium, and harder questions. How well you do on Module 1 decides whether your Module 2 is a harder or an easier set. The harder Module 2 gives you access to the highest scores, so careful work in Module 1 really matters.
Inside a module you can move back and forth freely and change any answer until time runs out. Once a module ends, you cannot return to it.
A small number of questions in each module are unscored trial questions, and you cannot tell which ones they are. Treat every question as if it counts.
There is **no penalty for wrong answers**. Never leave a question blank: if you run short of time, pick your best guess.

sections.title: Pacing
body: 32 minutes for 27 questions gives you about **71 seconds per question**. Some questions, such as a short grammar item, take 30 seconds; others, such as a paired-passage or data question, can take two minutes. Aim for the average, not the same time on every question.
A useful checkpoint: by the 16-minute mark you should be at about question 14. If you are well behind, speed up on the grammar and transition questions, which are usually quicker.

If you have spent about 90 seconds on a question and still cannot decide, eliminate what you can, choose your best answer, mark the question for review, and move on. A guess is never blank, and you may come back to it with fresh eyes.
Save the last two or three minutes to visit your marked questions and make sure every question has an answer.

sections.title: Order of question types and where to spend time
body: Questions are grouped by skill, and the groups appear in the same order in each module: first **Craft and Structure** (Words in Context, Text Structure and Purpose, Cross-Text Connections), then **Information and Ideas** (Central Ideas and Details, Command of Evidence, Inferences), then **Standard English Conventions** (Boundaries; Form, Structure, and Sense), and finally **Expression of Ideas** (Transitions, Rhetorical Synthesis). Within a group, questions tend to get harder as you go.

Reading-heavy questions near the start, especially Cross-Text Connections, Command of Evidence, and Inferences, usually take the most time. Grammar, transition, and notes questions near the end are often faster and very learnable.

Because of this, do not let a hard reading question early in the module eat up the time you need for quick points later. Mark it, guess, and come back if time allows. Some students choose to answer the grammar and notes questions first and then return to the reading questions; try both approaches in practice tests and keep the one that gives you more correct answers.

sections.title: Tools in the digital test
body: The testing app gives you several built-in tools. Practice with them before test day so you use them without thinking.
**Highlighter and notes:** you can highlight words in a passage and add a short note. Use it to mark a contrast word, a claim, or a key number, but do not spend time decorating the passage.
**Answer eliminator:** you can cross out answer choices you have ruled out. Crossing out wrong answers keeps your focus on the choices that are left and helps when you return to a marked question.
**Mark for review:** you can flag any question. Flagged questions are easy to find again before the module ends.

**Question navigator:** a panel shows every question in the module, which ones you have answered, and which you have marked. Use it to jump straight to a question and to check that nothing is left blank.
**Timer:** a countdown clock shows the time left in the module. You can hide it if it makes you nervous, and the app warns you when only a few minutes remain.
You also get scratch paper, which is useful for quick predictions in Words in Context questions or for sorting the two texts in a Cross-Text question.

sections.title: The night before and the morning of
body: **The night before:** do not cram. A light review of the Grammar handbook and the Trap guide is enough. Make sure your testing device is fully charged, the testing app is installed and up to date, and your admission ticket and photo ID are ready. Pack a charger, pencils or pens, a water bottle, and a simple snack for the break. Check the route to your test center and how long it takes.
Get a full night of sleep. Rest helps your focus and memory much more than one extra hour of practice.

**The morning of:** eat a normal breakfast, dress in layers in case the room is cold or warm, and leave early so you arrive calm. Read one or two short practice passages to warm up your brain, but do not take a full practice test.
At the start of the test, take a slow breath and remember the plan: about 71 seconds per question, mark and move on when stuck, and never leave a blank.

sections.title: After the test
body: Scores usually arrive online within a few weeks. Your Reading and Writing score is reported on a scale of 200 to 800 and combined with your Math score for a total between 400 and 1600.

Look at your score report for the skill areas where you lost the most points, and come back to those lessons and drills in Module Up. Many students improve on a second attempt, and many colleges consider your best section scores across attempts.
Whatever the result, take a day off from practice. One test is a step in your preparation, not a final judgment.

traps.title: Trap guide
traps.intro: Wrong answers on the SAT are not random: they are built from a small number of patterns that catch rushed readers. Learn to name each trap, and you will be able to cross out choices with confidence instead of guessing.

traps.title: Too broad
traps.description: The choice claims more than the text supports. It may generalize from one case to all cases, turn a cautious finding into a certainty, or describe a bigger topic than the passage covers.
traps.example: Text: "In one survey of 200 farms in Punjab, drip irrigation cut water use by about a third." Trap: "Drip irrigation is the most efficient way to water crops everywhere." The text covers one survey in one region and never compares all methods.
traps.how_to_avoid: Watch for absolute words such as "all," "always," "proves," "never," and "most" in the choice. Check whether the text's own wording is just as strong; if the text says "may" or "in one study," the answer should be just as limited.

traps.title: Too narrow
traps.description: The choice is accurate but covers only one detail or one part of the text. It fails when the question asks for the main idea, main purpose, or the whole goal.
traps.example: Text: a passage that describes how a city built rooftop gardens and then explains that they lowered summer temperatures. Question: main idea. Trap: "Rooftop gardens were built on public buildings first." True, but it is only a detail from the first sentence.
traps.how_to_avoid: Before reading the choices, sum up the whole text in one short sentence. The right answer for a main idea or purpose question should match that summary, not just a sentence you remember.

traps.title: Not in the text
traps.description: The choice brings in an idea the text never states or implies. It may sound sensible or even be true in real life, but nothing in the passage supports it.
traps.example: Text: "The researchers found that the bees visited blue flowers more often than yellow ones." Trap: "Blue flowers produce more nectar than yellow flowers." Nectar is never mentioned, so this explanation comes from outside the text.
traps.how_to_avoid: For every choice, ask "Where does the text say that?" If you cannot point to a specific line, eliminate it. Use only what is written, not what you already know about the topic.

traps.title: Reversed
traps.description: The choice uses the right words but flips the relationship: cause and effect switched, increase turned into decrease, or one author's view given to the other. It is dangerous because it looks so familiar.
traps.example: Text: "Higher water temperatures led to more frequent coral bleaching." Trap: "More frequent coral bleaching led to higher water temperatures." Same ideas, opposite direction.
traps.how_to_avoid: Trace the direction of every relationship: what causes what, which number is larger, who believes what. In cross-text questions, label each claim with its author before you look at the choices.

traps.title: True but irrelevant
traps.description: The choice is accurate according to the text or the data, but it does not answer the question asked. It often supports a different claim than the one in the question.
traps.example: Claim: "Students who slept longer scored higher on the memory test." Trap: "Students in the study slept an average of seven hours." The statement may be true, but it says nothing about the link between sleep and scores.
traps.how_to_avoid: Reread the question and underline the exact claim or goal. A correct answer must be both true and directly connected to that claim. For data questions, check that the choice compares the groups the claim compares.

traps.title: Wrong tone or shade
traps.description: The choice is a near-synonym of the right answer, but its strength, attitude, or exact meaning does not fit the context. It appears most often in Words in Context and in questions about an author's attitude.
traps.example: Text: "The critic found the novel's ending ______: it was unexpected, though not entirely unwelcome." Key: "surprising." Trap: "shocking." Both relate to the unexpected, but "shocking" is far stronger and more negative than the mild reaction described.
traps.how_to_avoid: Predict your own word from the clues before looking at the choices, and note how strong and how positive or negative it should be. Then pick the choice whose meaning and intensity match your prediction most closely.

traps.title: Wrong logic
traps.description: The choice sets up the wrong relationship between two ideas, such as a contrast where the text shows a cause, or an example where it adds a new point. It is the main trap in Transitions questions.
traps.example: Text: "The region received almost no rain for six months. ______, the reservoir dropped to its lowest level in decades." Key: "As a result," Trap: "However," The second sentence is a consequence of the first, not a contrast.
traps.how_to_avoid: Cover the choices and decide the relationship yourself: contrast, cause and effect, example, addition, restatement, or sequence. Then choose the transition that names exactly that relationship. If two choices express the same relationship, neither is likely to be right.

traps.title: Misses the goal
traps.description: In Rhetorical Synthesis questions, the choice uses accurate facts from the notes but does not accomplish the specific goal stated in the question. It might describe, for example, when the goal is to compare.
traps.example: Goal: "emphasize a difference between the two dams." Trap: "The Tarbela Dam is on the Indus River and was completed in 1976." Accurate, but it mentions only one dam and shows no difference.
traps.how_to_avoid: Ignore the notes at first and read only the goal. Underline its key verb (emphasize, compare, introduce, explain) and any key words such as "difference" or "to an audience unfamiliar with." Then check each choice against the goal alone.

traps.title: Grammar rule broken
traps.description: The choice does not follow a rule of Standard English, such as subject-verb agreement, pronoun case, punctuation between clauses, or modifier placement. It may sound natural in casual speech but is wrong in formal writing.
traps.example: Text: "The ancient manuscripts were fragile ______ the archivists handled them with gloves." Trap: a comma alone ("fragile, the archivists"), which creates a comma splice. Key: "fragile, so the archivists."
traps.how_to_avoid: Look at what changes between the choices to find the rule being tested. Then apply that rule to the sentence instead of trusting what sounds right. The Grammar handbook lists the rules for every topic.

wordbank.title: Word bank
wordbank.intro: These are high-use academic words that often appear in SAT-style passages and in Words in Context answer choices. Level 1 words are common in academic reading; level 4 words are the sophisticated choices you meet in the hardest questions. Learn each word through its example sentence, and notice the shade of meaning, not just a synonym.

words.definition: to leave behind or give up completely
words.example: The team abandoned its original hypothesis after the second round of tests contradicted it.

words.definition: to become less strong or intense
words.example: Once the monsoon rains abated, engineers could finally inspect the damaged embankment.

words.definition: something that departs from what is normal or expected
words.example: The researchers treated the unusually cold summer as an aberration rather than the start of a trend.

words.definition: existing as an idea rather than as a physical, concrete thing
words.example: Young children often find abstract concepts such as fairness easier to grasp through stories.

words.definition: present in large amounts; more than enough
words.example: Fossils are abundant in the limestone cliffs, making the site ideal for student fieldwork.

words.definition: easy to reach, enter, use, or understand
words.example: The historian wrote her account in plain language to make it accessible to general readers.

words.definition: to make room for or adjust to fit someone's needs
words.example: The library extended its hours to accommodate students preparing for final exams.

words.definition: to gather or build up gradually over time
words.example: Sediment accumulates at the river's mouth, slowly forming new land.

words.definition: correct and free from error
words.example: Accurate measurements of rainfall are essential for predicting crop yields.

words.definition: to admit that something is true or exists
words.example: The author acknowledges that her sample was small before presenting her conclusions.

words.definition: to get or gain something, such as a skill or possession
words.example: Children acquire their first language mostly by listening to the people around them.

words.definition: sharp, severe, or very intense
words.example: Water shortages became acute during the third year of the drought.

words.definition: to change in order to suit new conditions
words.example: Some urban birds have adapted to city noise by singing at a higher pitch.

words.definition: enough to meet a need, though not more than that
words.example: The survey provided adequate data for a preliminary report but not for firm conclusions.

words.definition: to stick to something, or to follow a rule or belief closely
words.example: The architects adhered to traditional building methods while using modern materials.

words.definition: next to or very near something else
words.example: Researchers compared the forest plot with an adjacent field that had been cleared for farming.

words.definition: harmful or unfavorable
words.example: The study found no adverse effects on soil quality after five years of crop rotation.

words.definition: to publicly support or argue for a cause or policy
words.example: The economist advocates investing in rural roads to connect farmers with markets.

words.definition: related to beauty or artistic taste
words.example: The mosaic's aesthetic appeal comes from its careful balance of color and pattern.

words.definition: to state firmly or confirm that something is true
words.example: The second study affirmed the earlier finding that the plant tolerates salty soil.

words.definition: to make a problem or pain less severe
words.example: New wells helped alleviate the water shortage in the outlying villages.

words.definition: to set aside or distribute resources for a particular purpose
words.example: The city allocated most of its new budget to public transportation.

words.definition: to change something, usually in a small way
words.example: The editor altered only a few words, leaving the poet's meaning intact.

words.definition: open to more than one meaning; unclear
words.example: The ending of the story is deliberately ambiguous, leaving readers to decide the character's fate.

words.definition: requiring great effort, or having a strong desire to succeed
words.example: The project's ambitious goal was to map every glacier in the range within two years.

words.definition: having mixed or conflicting feelings about something
words.example: The narrator is ambivalent about leaving her village: she longs for the city yet fears losing her roots.

words.definition: willing to accept or be influenced by something
words.example: The council proved amenable to the residents' suggestion once the costs were explained.

words.definition: to make larger, louder, or more intense
words.example: Social media can amplify a minor rumor until it reaches millions of people.

words.definition: similar in a way that allows a useful comparison
words.example: The author argues that a cell's membrane is analogous to a city's border checkpoint.

words.definition: to examine something carefully and in detail
words.example: The students analyzed the speeches to identify the persuasive techniques each speaker used.

words.definition: based on personal stories rather than systematic research
words.example: Although reports of the remedy's success were anecdotal, they prompted a formal clinical study.

words.definition: something that does not fit the usual pattern
words.example: A sudden spike in the readings turned out to be an anomaly caused by a faulty sensor.

words.definition: to expect or predict something and sometimes prepare for it
words.example: Planners anticipated heavy traffic and added extra buses during the festival.

words.definition: a lack of interest, concern, or enthusiasm
words.example: Low turnout was blamed less on apathy than on the difficulty of reaching polling stations.

words.definition: clearly seen or understood; also, seeming true but not certainly so
words.example: The benefits of the new irrigation method became apparent after the first harvest.

words.definition: large enough to be noticed or measured
words.example: The filter produced no appreciable change in water quality.

words.definition: anxious or worried that something bad might happen
words.example: The young scientist was apprehensive about presenting her results to senior colleagues.

words.definition: based on chance or personal choice rather than a reason or system
words.example: The author criticizes the border as arbitrary, drawn without regard to local communities.

words.definition: very old or no longer in common use
words.example: Some archaic words in the poem required footnotes for modern readers.

words.definition: requiring great effort and endurance
words.example: The arduous climb to the monastery took the researchers two full days.

words.definition: to express an idea clearly in words
words.example: In her essay, the philosopher articulates a theory of justice based on shared needs.

words.definition: to find out for certain
words.example: Investigators used tree rings to ascertain the age of the wooden beams.

words.definition: to have a strong hope or ambition to achieve something
words.example: Many of the workshop's participants aspired to publish their own short stories.

words.definition: to state something firmly as true
words.example: The author asserts that the old trade routes shaped the region's languages.

words.definition: to judge or measure the quality, value, or size of something
words.example: Teachers assessed the program by comparing reading scores before and after it began.

words.definition: to absorb information or to become part of a larger group
words.example: Immigrant families in the novel assimilate gradually while keeping their own festivals.

words.definition: something accepted as true without proof
words.example: The model rests on the assumption that rainfall will stay the same each year.

words.definition: to reach or achieve something, usually after effort
words.example: Few climbers attained the summit before modern equipment became available.

words.definition: to regard something as caused by or belonging to someone or something
words.example: The researchers attribute the decline in fish populations to warmer water.

words.definition: to increase or add to something
words.example: The museum augmented its collection with textiles donated by local weavers.

words.definition: real and genuine, not copied or false
words.example: Experts confirmed that the manuscript was authentic by analyzing its ink.

words.definition: reliable because based on expert knowledge
words.example: Her study of monsoon patterns remains the most authoritative work on the subject.

words.definition: able to govern or act independently
words.example: The region became autonomous, with its own council and budget.

words.definition: kind and wishing to help others
words.example: The novel portrays the landowner as benevolent, though his tenants see him differently.

words.definition: harmless or gentle
words.example: Most of the bacteria found in the soil samples were benign.

words.definition: a tendency to favor one side unfairly
words.example: The researchers chose participants randomly to reduce bias in their results.

words.definition: to support or strengthen something
words.example: New fossil discoveries bolster the theory that the species migrated across a land bridge.

words.definition: shortness in time or in use of words
words.example: The poem's brevity makes its final image especially striking.

words.definition: honest and direct, even when the truth is uncomfortable
words.example: In a candid letter, the scientist admitted that his early measurements were flawed.

words.definition: to take advantage of an opportunity
words.example: Local weavers capitalized on growing tourism by opening small shops.

words.definition: something that causes or speeds up an important change
words.example: The invention of the printing press was a catalyst for wider literacy in Europe.

words.definition: careful to avoid risk or error
words.example: The authors are cautious, noting that their results apply only to one species.

words.definition: to give up power, land, or a right, often unwillingly
words.example: After the treaty, the kingdom ceded two coastal provinces to its neighbor.

words.definition: to criticize strongly and formally
words.example: The committee censured the journal for publishing data it had not checked.

words.definition: lasting for a long time or happening repeatedly
words.example: Chronic flooding has forced several farming families to move to higher ground.

words.definition: arranged in the order in which events happened
words.example: The exhibition presents the artist's paintings in chronological order.

words.definition: to find a way around a rule or obstacle
words.example: Traders circumvented the high taxes by using smaller mountain passes.

words.definition: to mention something as evidence or as a source
words.example: The author cites three experiments to support her claim.

words.definition: a statement that something is true, which may need evidence
words.example: The author supports her claim with records from three different ports.

words.definition: logical and consistent; clearly connected
words.example: The final chapter weaves the scattered observations into a coherent argument.

words.definition: to happen at the same time or to agree exactly
words.example: The rise in bird sightings coincided with the planting of native trees.

words.definition: to work together with others on a shared task
words.example: Engineers collaborated with village elders to design the new water system.

words.definition: to honor and remember an event or person
words.example: A statue in the square commemorates the city's first female mayor.

words.definition: able to exist or work together without conflict
words.example: The new software was not compatible with the lab's older equipment.

words.definition: convincing or holding strong attention
words.example: The documents offer compelling evidence that the bridge was built earlier than believed.

words.definition: having enough skill or knowledge to do something well
words.example: The apprentice became a competent potter within two years.
